Administration service-
1. Departmental administration, $130,406.
I think it is customary for the minister to make a general statement before any discussion takes place on his estimates. Is he going to follow that procedure to-day?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speechtext:
I had not intended to make any

extensive statement, Mr. Chairman, I think it will be remembered that I did not do so (last year) and I do not recall what I did the year before. I should like to call attention to the fact, however, that the estimates for this year are almost identical with those of last year. They are some slight changes, but not to any great extent.
Except for one item.

I presume the one item to which my hon. friend refers is the wheat acreage reduction. Even last year the estimates did not show the amount to be paid out under wheat acreage reduction; that was provided in the legislation itself. I should like to say, however, that the decision has been reached this year not to continue wheat acreage reduction, so that while the amount is shown in the estimates in exactly the same way as it was shown last year, when we indicated that some $26,000,000 would be paid out for this purpose, this year I shall indicate to the committee that no amount beyond what is shown in these estimates is expected to be paid out under this item. In other words there are some payments that will have to be made after the end of this fiscal year, and they will come out of this amount.
In addition there are expenditures made by the department of Agriculture out of the war appropriation, which of course are not shown in these estimates. If at all possible I should like hon. members to confine their discussion to the estimates now before the committee. There may be overlapping in some cases, which may require that the same questions be answered twice, but I think we can give more intelligent answers if we stay pretty close to these estimates while we are discussing them. The other matters can be fully discussed when the other items are under consideration by the committee. Apart from this I have nothing in particular to say at this time.

I wish the minister would elaborate a little on the connection between the war estimates and these civil estimates. After all, under the war appropriation a number of boards have been set up which are connected closely with the department of Agriculture, and it is difficult to know exactly when we are referring to the one and when to the other. Could the minister let us know a little more definitely the relationship between these estimates? There are a number of these boards; it is not necessary for me to mention them. If the minister does not wish us to go into the war estimates at all, he might explain the situation a little more fully, so that we may know just where we stand.

Supply-Agriculture

One board which has been in existence ever since the war started is the agricultural supplies board. It is true that the officials of that board are officials of the Department of Agriculture. We shall be discussing personnel in connection with these estimates, and that personnel will be found on those boards, or connected with them. But the expenditures actually made in connection with the different agreements made with Britain are amounts provided under the War Measures Act, and I think we would discuss those at another time to better advantage than we can while these estimates are before the committee.
Under the agricultural supplies board comes the bacon board, now known as the meat board. For the first three years of the war it was known as the bacon board, but the name has since been changed. Then we have the dairy products board, and the special products board, all of which operate under the agricultural supplies board, and with funds provided out of the war vote. The only other board about which we might speak in that connection is the food board, which has as its chairman the Deputy Minister of Agriculture. The food board, however, carries on its activities with funds provided from other sources. The officials in the Department of Agriculture naturally have the information respecting these other matters. They may not have it with them when we are discussing these items, but to the extent that questions are asked, the answers to which may be necessary for a reasonable discussion of the estimates, we shall try to answer. I hope, however, that there will not be an extensive discussion on the other items until we reach them.
The minister of course in his department assumes responsibility for what is done by these different boards.
Yes.
And to a very great extent the Department of Agriculture is responsible for the information supplied to those boards, and upon which they render their decisions.
Yes.
So that I cannot understand how some overlapping could be avoided.

I should like to ask a question with respect to the food board. The minister may decide that my question would more properly relate to the agricultural supplies board. I have in mind the conference held last fall, under the supervision of the agricultural supplies board, to decide upon the various amounts of agricultural productions for 1944. I believe it was decided at that conference that Canada in 1944 should not increase her wheat acreage production, but should endeavour to maintain the acreage she had in 1943. At the same time our neighbours to the south in the United States were asked to increase their wheat acreage production in 1944 by at least twenty-four per cent. When one considers that the four major wheat exporting countries, according to estimates published, used approximated *
464.000.	000 bushels of wheat for feeding live stock in 1942, on account of the shortage of usual feeding supplies, one wonders at this condition. I believe it is agreed among our experts that if we have a dry season in western Canada the best cereal crop is wheat, , and that we would have much better success in attempting to grow wheat, even if used for feeding purposes, than in attempting to grow oats or barley.
Our own wheat, storage has been greatly decreased. In fact, figures for the past year show that the decrease is approximately twenty-five per cent. While a year ago the wheat storage was more than 463,000,000 bushels, the present storage is only 348,000,000. At the same time our storage supplies of coarse grains have increased by twenty-three per cent from more than 61,000,000 bushels to
75.000.	000. As I have pointed out, the United States have asked for an increase. On January 1, 1943, they had in storage about 268,000,000 bushels of wheat and on January 1 of this year that amount had been reduced to 92,000,-
000.	Only a few days ago in the house the Minister of Trade and Commerce announced a sale of 175,000,000 bushels of wheat to the United States, for the current year 1944. It must be clear to anyone that there will be a very small carry-over of wheat this year, either in the United States or in Canada.
Moreover, the last issue of the Economic Annalist, published in February, 1944, and reaching my desk in to-day's mail, points out that-
The conference of the united nation's relief and rehabilitation administration which took place at Atlantic city during the latter part of November, 1943, was the second important international gathering held in the United States during world war II. The first, the conference on food and agriculture had already established a working basis for close and continued collaboration among all the united nations. In setting up the UNRRA, the united nations agreed to bring relief to victims of war immediately upon liberation of the countries enslaved by the enemy. According to the estimates, total import requirements for Europe from all sources will amount to over 45 million tons of foodstuff, feeds, oils, fat, chemicals, fertilizers, rubber, wood, paper, hides, leather, clothing, coal, metals, minerals, machinery,
Supply-Agriculture

vehicles, seeds, drugs and hospital supplies. One of Canada's major contributions will be food-especially wheat.
In the same issue Doctor Black summarizes his analysis of food production by saying that-
If labour is short as at present, we should get our calories so far as possible from cereals.
I do not like to take issue with the able experts on the board, or with the gentlemen before the minister to-day. It does seem to me however that in view of these facts, when our western wheat producers can produce wheat under natural land and climate condition much more easily than they can produce anything else, they should now be asked to increase their wheat acreage. In view of the weather conditions in these winter months it would not appear to me that we will have anything like as much precipitation or moisture in 1944 as we had in the last two years. I should like to have a more complete statement from the minister. I do not know what his personal views are about the present situation, but our producers are preparing for their spring operations, and any information they could get would be useful at this time. If the minister believes some change should be made, the producers should be told. If there is any reason why they should not increase their acreage, he should tell us why, because it must be apparent to all that the production could be used both for the winning of the war and for the feeding of people in the overrun countries immediately after the war.
My namesake, the hon. member for Moose Jaw, pointed out about a year ago that before the end of the next year we might easily have a shortage of cereals in North America. Judging from these figures I should think his prediction might not be far wrong.

The statement made respecting the facts related to the conference are pretty much as indicated by the hon. member. The acreage under wheat in 1943 was 17,488,000 acres. The objective for 1944 is 17,500,000, or 100 per cent of the 1943 figure. The production figure for 1943 is the actual acreage we had in that year. The figures for oats are 17,405,000 acres for 1943 and 16,377,000 for 1944. For barley the figure is approximately the same; the 1944 acreage is 101 per cent of the 1943. For mixed grains the figure is 120 per cent of the 1943 acreage; for rye, 87 per cent, and for corn, 153 per cent. For hay and clover we are asking the same, and also for alfalfa.
Those are the figures with regard to wheat and feed grains and forage crops. We are asking approximately thie same for all import-

ant crops. Corn for husking is not a big crop in Canada. There were 257,000 acres in this crop in 1943 and we are asking for 303,000 acres in 1944. While that is up 53 per cent it does not represent a considerable acreage. In answering the question asked by the hon. member if I were confining my discussion of grains largely to the first three items, I think I shall have pretty well covered the picture. The wheat and oats and barley acreages will be approximately the same as far as this country is concerned. The wheat acreage will be 100 per cent of the 1043 acreage; the oat acreage, 106 per cent, and the barley, 101 per cent. Those are the main crops we utilize for feeding purposes.
The suggestion has been made that at a conference held in the United States certain decisions were reached. An agreement has been signed by the four exporting nations, namely, Australia, the Argentine, the United States and Canada together with Britain. That agreement was signed some time ago and was announced through the press. Under it certain provisions were made for the establishment of price levels toward the end of the war and as to acreages in the different countries. The most important feature of the acreage agreement is the one which relates to wheat acreage reduction. We were parties to that agreement; we signed it at the time.
Since that time there have developed some changes in Canada and the United States which have perhaps made it necessary in certain areas to depart from a strict interpretation of the terms of the agreement. It is possible that this is true in the United' States. If I recall correctly, in the United States they asked their farmers to increase their acreage in wheat and feed grains by some 14,000,000 acres. In some places that has been interpreted as an expressed desire on the part of the United States government that the wheat acreage should be increased by 14,000,000. As I understand it, the intention in the United States was that
14,000,000 more acres of land should be seeded this year in order to provide feed for live stock. In so far as the growing of wheat to be used to provide food for human beings is concerned, I assume that they are following very much the idea contained in the agreement signed two or three years ago.
As the hon. member for Souris has stated, it is true in certain sections of western Canada that as many if not more pounds of feed can be grown in a dry area by seeding wheat rather than oats or barley. I think I can say that is true from experience. I do not think any objection would be taken-I suppose it would not make very much difference if we did take objection-to farmers seeding wheat.

Certainly no serious objection would be taken to the seeding of wheat as a substitute for barley for feeding purposes. That was the intention of the United States request to their farmers-to get more feed for live stock.
However, that is not what was in our minds when we discussed the matter in the conference. What was in our minds was whether we required more wheat for the purpose of providing flour with which to feed human beings. The hon. member for Souris has said that it is stated that the greatest contribution Canada is to make under U.N.R.R.A. is to supply wheat, but that contribution is to be only 25,000,000 bushels. Anyone looking at the figures of wheat supplies in Canada or wheat production will realize just what little effect one way or another the provision of
25,000,000 bushels of wheat would have upon our supply. At the time these discussions were being carried on we had 604,000,000 bushels carried over from preceding years. That represents about two years of average crops. At that time we had another crop which was being marketed and which is still being marketed. Therefore it was not considered wise when we had about three years' supply of wheat on hand to say to people this year that they should seed a greater acreage of wheat than they had last year. As a matter of fact, we asked them to seed the same acreage as they had last year. In so far as we have been able to study the statistics that come before us from time to time, we have not seen any reason up to date for changing that position. We thought it wise that our farmers should not seed more acreage this year for the production of wheat to be marketed for human consumption than they had seeded in 1943.
The question of feed is a different matter. We are asking our people to seed approximately a million more acres in oats, and we are asking them to seed approximately the same acreage in barley, or just a little more. We believe that with the carryover we have in the country at the present time our position will be well taken care of if our people follow these directions for 1944.
Will there be a carryover if we supply the United States with what they require in feed and wheat?

The other day the
Minister of Trade and Commerce pointed out that the United States were prepared to take
175,000,000 bushels of wheat if we could get the shipping facilities to take it to them. Up to date no transportation organization has been able to assure us that facilities can be supplied to handle 175,000,000 bushels. It will be 100-41
Supply-Agriculture
apparent that 175,000,000 bushels, plus, the
25,000,000 bushels spoken of a moment ago, total only 200,000,000 bushels, or one-third of what we carried into this crop year. Assuming that we have a poor crop next year-no one in the west ever assumes that until we actually have it; we always assume we are going to have a fair crop-the figures might look different next fall, but they certainly would not look sufficiently different to put us in the position of being short of feed in Canada.
That carryover already has been greatly reduced.
It is being reduced by certain wheat that is being shipped out.
Will the European market be larger than it was?
We are hoping it will, but we are, of course, not the only suppliers of that market.
Could the minister give the committee any figures with regard to the world picture of production-stocks, and probable demand?

The best information which can be had under war conditions is that there is no indication from crop conditions throughout the world this year that there is any pending shortage of grain. Of course we all know that, with armies moving, weather is not the only thing which counts.

We are now dealing with the first item, within the purview of which, naturally, may be discussed the general ramifications of the Department of Agriculture.
I have no desire at the moment to take the time of the committee with any general observations in connection with the matter. I rise for the single purpose of pointing out that during the last session of parliament, in the discussion of the agriculture estimates, there was 'brought to the minister's attention a matter which merits a little more consideration than the estimates would indicate it has received. I do not suppose that in many years as much interest has been shown in any suggestion respecting a vote in the house as there was in the suggestion last year that half a million dollars should be put aside for research laboratories and facilities for agricultural research in Canada. Many communications were received from agricultural sections regarding suggestions for the expenditure of this money in research for the benefit of agriculture. There is a feeling throughout the country that agriculture has not been able to

Supply-Agriculture

keep abreast with other lines of industry in regard to improvements and development. It is all very well to say that urban industry looks after its own research. Industry is in a very much better position to look after its own research than agriculture is. First of all, manufacturing industry is much more concentrated. Then, much of the money expended for this purpose is set aside by large concerns having their own research facilities. Further, the advantages of this research are sooner or later extended to branches of industry which perhaps are less fortunately placed. So far as the farmer is concerned he is not organized to the same extent to do that. It may be that in the future there will be some organization of a nature which will enable the farmer to make his contribution in a collective way to the advancement of research facilities, but for the moment that does not seem possible, at any rate on a very large scale. So that it becomes pretty definitely the obligation of the government to see that research facilities, laboratories or whatever may be needed, are provided through government assistance.
I noticed that last year a good deal of interest was taken in, and much support given to, the suggestion that a sufficiently large sum of money be set aside for this purpose. In the debate, which took place much nearer the end of the session than the present debate, many hon. members representing agricultural constituencies rose to express approval of the suggestion which was made. But as I look through the items of the estimates, both in the war appropriation measure and in the civil estimates which are now before us, I have not been able to find anything of a satisfactory or comprehensive nature with respect to any advance so far as those science services are concerned under which, I assume, the vote would occur. I notice a paragraph in the speech from the throne which says that "provision will be made to expand research activities." I have not a great hope that the speech from the throne, when it is brought down to earth, will look quite as attractive as when it remained up in the skies, in the clouds. Nevertheless I urge the minister and the government not to let the session pass without a substantial amount of money being set aside for agricultural research purposes. We must not under any circumstances fly in the face of agricultural opinion, which is insisting, in a way that agriculture seldom insists, upon this action. I want to summon every bit of emphasis I can to impress upon the minister the importance of his dealing with this matter. There may be a ray of hope in the paragraph of 
the speech from the throne which calls for an expansion of research activities. If that expansion covers other lines of activity as well as agriculture, I think agriculture should be given the very top place.
I leave the matter with the minister this afternoon. I was unable to discover in the details of the estimates where this vote is to be found. For that reason I rise on the general item in. order that the minister may be apprised of this urgent necessity. I do not think a day's delay should be countenanced in seeing to it that this most important contribution by the government to agriculture is made. It may be that the government does not want to go as far as was suggested in the session last year, but in my opinion not only is it justified in going that far but, if necessary, should go farther. The government must recognize that for many years the need has existed for this move to be made. It is strange that the governments of to-day and of yesterday have not recognized the urgent and essential nature of such provision for our agricultural populations. I am ready to lend every possible encouragement to the government in seeing to it that research for agriculture is not neglected, but that proper provision is made for it during this session.

The paragraph following item 32, namely, "appropriation not required for 1944-45, 8200,000", is the item which was placed in the supplementary estimates last year to provide for certain research work and the putting in of pilot plants relative to research in connection with agriculture. That item was only partly spent last year. Provision was made for the expenditure of some of it, but the expenditure is not yet completed. It may be necessary to bring down supplementaries later on to cover the expenditures which will be made this year in that connection. But on page 44 of the estimates there appears, under "trade and commerce", item 358, "expanded research on the utilization of farm crops, 8325,000", one of two items under "national research council". That
8325,000,	together with what is expended under the other item when we come to deal with it in supplementaries, will make up a total somewhere between $325,000 and the $500,000 which has been spoken of.
Is that the carrying out of the provision in the speech from the throne?

Yes; that is the intention, and I will explain why it is found where it is. Some years ago-I have not the exact date, but it was long before my time in Ottawa-the research council was set up. The objective which I understand that those who

Supply-Agriculture
set it up had in mind was to bring all research under one national research council. That organization was supposed to have taken over a great deal of the research work which previously had been carried' on in the Department of Agriculture, and all research work generally that had been carried on by the different departments of government, and considerable new research work was added to its activities.
There has always been a certain amount of discussion as to whether agricultural research can be as successfully carried on in an organization of that kind as it would be under a purely agricultural set-up. I was not present in the committee last year when the matter was discussed and it was recommended that half a million dollars be expended on research in connection with agricultural products, and I am therefore not in a position to say what views hon. members expressed on that question. Finally, however, 8200,000 was put in the agriculture estimates last year, and in the meantime a committee was appointed which was composed of persons right across Canada, under the chairmanship of the president of the university of Alberta, and of which the hon. member for Moose Jaw* (Mr. Ross) served as a member. They made certain recommendations as to how moneys voted for this purpose might be expended, or on what works they might be used.
Out of these discussions there has grown this vote which is placed in the Department of Trade and Commerce under national research council for the purpose of doing research work in connection with farm products to determine exactly what is stated here-"research on the utilization of farm crops." On the question whether there should be additional amounts in the estimates of the Department of Agriculture to carry on some more practical work in connection with the development of ideas found by research, that is something which perhaps the members of the committee might wish to discuss, but any money voted for that particular purpose would have to be voted this session in the supplementary estimates.

The reasons why I expected to find the vote in the estimates for agriculture were very well grounded, and that was the plan or scheme which was suggested by the hon. member for Moose Jaw, who brought up the question last year and was strongly supported by many members of the committee. The idea was to have a chain of laboratories across Canada for the purpose of doing this agricultural work. It had not occurred to me, but perhaps the minister, on consideration, may have felt that the vote could be more effectively spent by utilizing it through the research council.
I am not sure that the government's judgment on that point was very good. I am rather inclined to think that agriculture, at least as I understand from the general leanings, would like to have had, not only the amount here but whatever extended vote might be required, for work to be carried on through their own operations and within their own field. The minister will see why that should be, and I would point out that perhaps, in a reconsideration of the whole research field, that might be done.

There are a few general remarks I wish to make on agriculture. When the minister, with much gusto, proclaims that the farmer finds himself in a splendid position, and tries to create the impression that everything is well with agriculture, I think we should remember that it has only been in the fifth year of the war that the farmer's return for his labour has begun to show any proper relation to his cost of production.
The farmer in this country is to be complimented upon the work he has done. The production figures for Canada are figures to which we can point with pride and satisfaction, and the fact that labour shortages have existed only reveals the extent to which the older people have taken on the burden of producing food for our men as well as for the civilian population in this time of stress. If, however, we visited the farm homes across Canada we would find the people living in those homes not as well cared for as one would suppose they would be, looking over the slight increases in the farmer's income over the past year.
For twelve years, in most parts of Canada, this industry has suffered from a depression from which it will take years and years to recover. For the past twelve years there have existed in Canada conditions that should not exist in any country. In New Brunswick there are farmers who delivered barrels of potatoes containing over three bushels and sold them at twenty cents a barrel, and in many cases they could not sell their potatoes even at that price. Over long periods of depression agriculture finds itself in the position where it has constantly to meet debt costs, production costs and taxation, and these are not cancelled at the end of each year but are carried on indefinitely so that there has been irreparable loss which years of prices above parity will not offset.
The figures placed1 on the record the other evening by the hon. member for Melfort showed the extent to which farmers and farming communities have lost equity in their homes. Farm homes which were previously the property of the men who did the work have been taken over by the mortgage companies, and in far too many cases these people will
Supply-Agriculture

continue renting from the mortgage companies and will remain from now on tenants on their land. These losses can never be restored.
We must remember that our prosperity to-day is the result of a world conflict. The prices which we receive now are due to the fact that in Canada we have a market and that there are unusual circumstances at the present time. This machinery of ours, the system under which we operate, works all right in war time, but we are paying the price to keep the machinery working. There is the blood of our young men, the flower of our youth, which is being sacrificed from day to day, and which makes possible war, and the prices received at this time.
Agricultural prosperity is the very basis of national prosperity. We have not recognized that in the past. The Canadian wheat market has lagged for some time far behind the markets of the world; it was only in the fall of 1943 that we saw the Canadian markets catching up with those in the United States, and then the government stepped in and by order in council closed the grain exchange on wheat and prevented the farmer from receiving the value he might have obtained from the sale of his product.
It seems to me what we need in this whole set-up of agriculture itself and all those industries which are dependent upon it, is a new outlook, a new purpose. The purpose has to be the welfare of the producers and consumers who make up the majority of the population of our country. The basis upon which we should judge the success of the Department of Agriculture should be the living conditions of those engaged in that industry. If we were to use that as the basis of our judgment of the Department of Agriculture there is no doubt as to the verdict. It has failed entirely. If it is to be judged by the standard of living of the operators of the grain exchanges, those who run and operate the packing houses, the millers, the finance and mortgage loan companies, the bank directors and machine companies, then we can say that the agricultural industry of Canada has been a great success. The farmer who produces the product has no control at all of the price at which it shall be sold. The grain exchange, which was permitted to operate for years in the city of Winnipeg, dictated to him the price he was to receive for his toil. The milling industries, closely interlocked with the banking and financial interests of this country through directorships, received the product of his toil, sold it to the consumers east and west, placed a price on bread to the baker, and the consumers paid their price for the farmer's product. The con-
(Mr. Castleden.]
sumer and the producer should be working together in cooperative organizations, interlocked with wholesale cooperatives, to see that each got his proper share of the toil of the other, to exchange their toil on equitable terms and not allow those in the middle to clean up.
The farmer who raises stock must hand his product over to the packers and they control the prices. Recently a group of farmers in western Canada had a large quantity of feed cattle-cows in this case-ready for the market. They were told that there was no price on the market, no market there. The impression was created among those people that there was no room in the packing plants for those cattle. But we find that the packing companies were around offering seven and a half cents a pound for them. There must have been room somewhere. The packers tried to create the idea that there was a scarcity of room in the pack

g plants, or that there were no facilities for transportation, or something like that, but all the time there was a below-market price being offered by the packing companies. That seems to point to the fact that there is need of some control somewhere. Apparently they can create surpluses when they are required, and all kinds of excuses can be used.
The milk producers find themselves in the same position when they try to sell dairy' products to the large private monopolistic organizations that handle dairy products in the cities. The fruit producers found, although they did organize a cooperative in the Okanagan valley, that when they came to sell their products there was only one avenue through which to sell them and at a low price, in most cases a price below the cost of production. When the consumer comes to buy that commodity in the market the price is at the top. The same thing applies to farm machinery. When the agricultural producer goes to buy anything in the way of farm machinery he finds that apparently there is an agreement between companies with regard to prices. These things should not be. When it comes to repairs the price continues to rise year after year. Apparently there is no control, no price ceiling. The farmers should have cooperative organizations whereby they could manufacture their own farm machinery and own their own factories. That seems to be about the only solution.
When the farmer requires financial aid he has to go to the bank or the mortgage company. When wheat is at S2 a bushel money i3 loose. The farmer may' borrow a couple of thousand dollars and believes he will need only 1,000 bushels of wheat to pay off the debt.

Supply-Agriculture
But he finds when he comes to pay off the debt a few years later, that the price has gone away down. Instead of 1,000 bushels taking care of the debt he finds he has to grow 5,000, 6,000 or 8,000 bushels. Interest rates are away beyond what they should be. Mortgage and loan companies make him sign agreements containing clauses that are almost criminal. Legal fees are permitted which are disgraceful. The farmer finds himself constantly in debt. There are clauses in the agreement which make it almost impossible for him to meet his obligations, and foreclosure is usually the ultimate result.
When war broke out the government froze the price of commodities at one level and left the farmer's cost of production away higher than the price at which the commodity had to be sold. The farmer, realizing how he was the victim of so much exploitation, organized cooperatives in an attempt to solve the problem. Large groups organized cooperatively and said, we must enter into the purchasing field and control the sale of our commodities; we must have something to do with the sale of our products. The first thing they found was that it was opposed in almost every direction. The history of the Saskatchewan Cooperative Wheat Pool is a record of attempts by farmers to solve this problem in the marketing field in a cooperative way. They attempted to sell their products and return the actual sale of the products to those who produced them, so that all would share equally in the fruit of the toil. However, they found there were regulations set up against them. The grain board decided to step into the field. Storage facilities were required. Government regulations soon stepped in and prevented the farmer from delivering his grain to his own elevator at his own point. He was told there was a shortage of cars when he wanted to sell his grain to his own pool elevator. He was told: "You cannot sell your wheat to your own elevator. Since your elevator is filled you have to sell to those other line elevator companies. We will not permit you-"
He did not have to sell it at all.
"We will not permit you to sell it there because thp elevator space is used up."
He did not have to sell it; the government took it over at an advance.
He still has to deliver the grain to the line elevators.
Is there not a shortage of cars?
Why should that distribution be used to militate against the farmers cooperative organization?
It has not.
Why did they not allocate the cars in proportion to the business which these companies did in 1938, 1939 and 1940?
They received their fair share.

No, they did not. If you look over the records you will find that during the past year, instead of the cooperative business increasing as it should have year by year, and as it had done since 1935, the percentage of grain handled by the Saskatchewan pool elevator companies has gradually decreased. That decrease has taken place since the wheat board regulations came in, and the regulations with regard to the allotment of cars were put into force. Had the normal trend of business continued its upward graph their increase should have been almost sixty per cent of grain handled in 1943.
The distribution is based on 1938-39.
Are they getting cars on that rating?
At the present time, yes.

No. That is what they were informed was going to happen last July, but suddenly an emergency situation developed. The government said:	We must have
six million bushels out right away, the railway companies will take it wherever they can; and the car allotment cycle was all broken up. Then they said they were going to use the 1938-39 basis, and apparently the allotment committee has ceased to function. They are permitting the railway officials at each point to distribute cars as they see fit. We are told that the thing is to be handled on a quota basis, and that the quota system has been put in operation. But, though they fixed quotas for various points throughout the west, we find that cars are not available at these points even to fill those quotas. However, f believe this comes under the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and I can deal with it when his estimates are before the committee.
It seems to me that through government boards the advantage has always been given to the ordinary grain trade, to the line elevator companies and the milling companies which have their elevators buying grain at country points. It seems that assistance is always given to the operators of large businesses on the
Supply-Agriculture

grain exchange. The same thing appears to be true in the packing industry. There is a iloor placed under beef and pork, but there is no floor placed under cattle or hogs, which are what the farmer has to sell. If we could have an independent investigation of what has been happening in the meat packing industry in Canada; if we could ascertain the facts in regard to costs, processing, the returns to the packing firms-which in recent years have been amalgamating so that there are fewer and fewer companies in the business-and so on we would find out things that would shock every producer and consumer in this country. If the department and the government were operating in the interests of the producer and consumer they would curtail the activities of those who are exploiting the producers of this land1. Apparently the government is not only condoning the actions of these people; in its legislation and regulations it appears to aid and abet and legalize their operations. The result has been quite a rapid deterioration of the rural areas across this dominion, these small rural places which were the centre o( good living in this country. What is required is the establishment of parity prices, not only for the duration of the war and six months after, but for three or four years ahead at a time. There should be proper producer representation on the marketing boards. We should not have the government pick out some people they want to have representing the producers; we should have the producers themselves meet democratically and select from their own organizations those who would represent their point of view and their interests on these boards.
_ think one of the most effective contributions that could be made by the government to assist agriculture at this time would be the setting up of government or cooperative abattoirs throughout the country, where large surpluses of meat could be properly processed and held in storage, so that a large bank of food might be built up for the years of world scarcity which must necessarily follow this war; for the longer the war lasts the greater will be the need for such relief.
We should have the establishment on a cooperative basis of credit corporations and marketing and processing plants for each branch of agriculture, and assistance should be given those farmers who have endeavoured to organize their own cooperative farm machinery plants.
Governmental machinery should be set up for the proper estimation of the world supply and the world production. We know that in Argentine and other parts of the world cattle
{Mr. Castleden.]
production is being increased to an extent almost equal to the increase that has taken place in Canada. A long-range view must be taken of the possible world requirements and world production, in order to see what may be Canada's part in supplying the world with the food it is going to require.
I believe we should also take into consideration the nutritional standards and needs of this country of ours. Recent surveys made by service organizations and clubs throughout the country reveal some shocking conditions in regard to the nutrition of our people. Surely a country which can produce in one year ten times more wheat than it can eat should not be a land in which malnutrition and want prevail. What is wrong with this country of ours, when in almost every city we had thousands of people in need of food? Just before the war we found that in a place like Saint John, New Brunswick, there was considerable want and privation because the people were unable to obtain the food they required, while within a hundred miles of that city farmers growing potatoes could not get rid of them at fifteen or twenty cents for a three-bushel barrel. When we see things like that we realize that there must be something wrong with the distribution of foodstuffs in this country. There seems to be no purpose at all, no definite aim in connection with providing our people with the things they require. It seems to be a matter of enterprise, saying, "Well, let us get control of the food and we will deliver it if there is money in it. If we cannot get our price the people will not eat. If the people cannot pay for it or if we cannot . get our profit from both the producer and the consumer, then they can do without".
In regard to the matter of research, government assistance in this connection is long overdue, but there is something more needed. For far too long the benefits of the work done by the research laboratories of this and other countries have not been made available to the people themselves. Some private concern gets hold of the patent rights to a particular process and holds it up, saying, "Well, if it is going to interfere with our own industry we shall not let it be used". In other words, if synthetic rubber is going to interfere with rubber business, stop it; if the making of alcohol is going to interfere with the oil business, do not make the process available except at our price. But there are countries that are making progress along this line, and Canada had better wake up. There are countries where the benefits of science and research are being made available to the people as a whole. There, are countries that are beginning

Supply-Agriculture
to use their natural resources for the benefit of all the people, where the concern of the department of agriculture and other government departments is the welfare of the people and not the profits of the few. We should be setting our house in order now'.
The experience of those people who laboured so hard for so many years, only to see their homes deteriorating and their equities disappearing, has created bitterness and resentment against those who have been responsible for the policies of this dominion in the past. A few promises made at election time or a few increases in prices every four years are not going to allay their fears or restore their faith in those who have been responsible for the policies of this country for so many years. The agriculturists of Canada have lost faith. It is plain that there must be a new purpose and new concern on the part of those who govern. The interests and welfare of those who w'ork on the land must be considered before the interests of a few privileged people.
Increased tenancy across this land must be stopped. The w'elfare of agriculture is too closely linked up with the economy, health and social welfare of the people of Canada to be longer neglected. We have to stop the exploitation of those who to-day, apparently assisted by government regulations, are able to make themselves affluent at the expense and the toil of the producers in agriculture across this land.

Before we commence a detailed discussion of the items I should like to bring to the attention of the minister two telegrams received from my own constituency, because they indicate that out there conditions in respect to the marketing of live stock are far from satisfactory.
The first of these telegrams is dated at Lethbridge, Alberta, February 16, and states:
Our information indicates could conservative!}' expect 1275 to 1375 for lambs f.o.b. Choice fed lambs selling St. Paul 16 cents less duty two fifty freight one dollar add exchange 125. Our price now eleven cents and orders light only a few ewes moving at five cents which is ruinous. Cow situation materially improved but offering price for top steers has slipped to 1150 on instructions from Toronto heavy steers very draggy. Feed grain situation deteriorating rapidly due to heavy movement east and United States will be shipping grain back here before fall or else live stock will be liquidated. Government meddling seems to have no end but chaos. If moisture conditions do not improve beyond reasonable hope western stock men face a major disaster as result of this grain policy.
This is signed by C. O. Asplund, for the Lethbridge stock feeders' association.
I have another telegram which reached me this morning. It is dated at Magrath, Alberta, February 17, and is as follows:
Lambs selling two dollars hundred less than last yeaf little demand approximately twenty five thousand Welling Magrath and Spring Coulee lambs heavy should have gone weeks ago no buyers for fat ewes at any price serious situation heavy steers wanted last year this year small cattle wanted choice steers difficult to sell at lower price demand for cows slightly improved no hay oats or barley obtainable wheat prices out of line with live stock prices.
This is signed by E. Pingarie Tanner and Mayor H. Tilston Jones, president of the board of trade.
I have had this matter of selling finished live stock before parliament now for several days. I believe I first mentioned it on February 7. A few days ago the minister dealt with the matter in a rather optimistic manner, indicating that all was well. I point out that if we are to maintain our food production at a standard which will provide plenty for our people, and enable us to contribute as we ought to the rehabilitation of the conquered countries, certainly we must have more intelligence prevailing in the Department of Agriculture than has prevailed thus far in connection with live stock.
I do not know just what is the matter. I hate to think there is neglect or stupidity. I hate to think there is lack of vision; but certainly there is something dreadfully wrong, when we realize that there are 25,000 lambs in Welling, Magrath and Spring Coulee, just three places in my constituency, and that those lambs cannot be moved, although they should have gone long ago. When one thinks of the loss occasioned to feeders who have to keep that live stock in their corrals, awaiting sales, one realizes the extent to which public confidence is being destroyed.
In Canada we have a strange situation. We have had meatless Tuesdays for I do not know how long. We have had meat rationing, and people have been led to believe that there is a shortage. Now look at this! What are we to gather from a situation of this kind? I find myself utterly at a loss to understand. I have not discussed the question of sheep sales on other occasions, but have confined my remarks t.o beef. It seems to me that these two telegrams indicate a serious situation.
Another condition has evidently developed in western Canada as a result of what appeared to be a wise provision, namely, that of sending a quantity of our surplus grain to tihe east. I presume, for reasons which no one would have been expected to foresee, shortages have developed. We find one telegram complaining that they are unable to buy hay, oats or barley, to keep their cattle in good condition. That telegram comes from an area in which vast quantities of
Supply-Agriculture

oats, wheat and barley are produced. Yet the grain has been moved out to the extent that they are now unable to buy it, and a serious condition has developed.
Before taking my seat I wish to discuss one other question, namely, that related to the beet sugar industry in Canada. I find myself completely confounded by the lack of interest in the welfare of our country manifested by many people in high places, so far as sugar production is concerned. I pointed out in 1936, and again in 1937, 1938 and 1939 what ought to be done in Canada in connection with sugar. * But there was a number of wise smart Alecks who thought they knew all about it, and would not listen to anyone, in the belief that we had plenty of sugar. Now we see the position we are in! Sugar rationed painfully! Only five or six days ago the sugar controller announced that we might expect a worse condition, so far as sugar supplies are concerned, in 1944 and 1945. How can men who will allow conditions like that lay claim to having ordinary intelligence?
On behalf of the beet growers in western Canada requests have been made for a rebate of part of the excise tax levied against them, so as to enable them to cover the additional labour costs, trucking and other expenses which have grown out of the war. Thus far we have not had a word from the government. The Minister of Agriculture has not condescended to give us any information in the matter, and the Minister of Finance maintains a strict silence.
Mr. . GARDINER:	The Minister of
Finance had intended at the opening of today's sitting to make a statement with respect to sugar. However, other matters intervened. He had to leave the chamber, and upon leaving he asked me if I would stand aside at eight o'clock long enough to permit him to make that statement. He will be here at eight o'clock to make it.

I certainly appreciate that, because I am disturbed with regard to this matter. In Canada we are able to produce sugar of a very high quality, and at a very low price. There is no reason in the world why the people of this country should be short of sugar or should have to pay a high price for it. As I pointed out to the house in 1941, in 1937 the Canadian sugar factory at Raymond received less than four cents a pound for its sugar, and at that price made substantial profits for itself and the farmers. When hon. members compare four cents a pound with the price we have 
been paying for sugar, not only in 1937 but in subsequent years, they will realize that something is terribly wrong. Somebody is mismanaging the whole show. I am glad the minister announced that something is going to be done and I hope the rebate is to be given.
I did not say what was to be done; I said an announcement would be made.

I hope the announcement will indicate that the people in charge of the sugar affairs of Canada do not intend to penalize the Canadian people and make them go short of sugar when we can produce it in great abundance. I wished to bring these two matters to the attention of the minister and let him comment upon them as he sees fit. I do not think I shall say anything more at the present time.

I have one or two observations to make in connection with what was said a little while ago* by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) about research. It is well understood that the prosperity of agriculture and of industry is dependent upon the prosperity of each other. One hundred years ago four-fifths of the products of the farm were used by man; at the present time I understand only about one-third of these products are consumed by the people. Perhaps that is one of our difficulties to-day. We must get more people back on the farms and consume more.
I should like to point out that the chemical industry of the United States invests between two and four per cent of its receipts from sales in research. Agriculture in that country invests only one-seventh of one per cent of its revenue. That is an interesting comparison. In 1938 an act of congress established four regional laboratories in the United States which were to consider the problem of the industrial utilization of agricultural surpluses, by-products and waste products. The discoveries were to become the property of the nation under the general service patent regulations. I mention that only to indicate that the amount of money proposed to be spent by the minister on research is quite small. The results of such research affect not only the farmer but also the industrial worker in the city.

I should like to refer to some of the remarks of the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden). As I remember, his first statement was that Canada had lagged far behind the rest of the world in the price of wheat.

I said that the Winnipeg grain exchange had1 lagged behind.

Supply-Agriculture

At any rate, that our price of wheat had lagged behind the rest of the world. A moment later the hon. member mentioned the price of wheat in the United States. I admit that the price of wheat in Canada is lower than the price in the United States, but it has been higher than in any other country during all the time the hon. member was speaking of.
Except Great Britain.

Except in Great
Britain where it has been subsidized quite heavily.

I suppose European
conditions would be satisfactory to the hon. member? I was just talking about the western hemisphere.

No doubt the
hon. member does not remember what I say in this house at times, but last year I endeavoured to set out what I thought was the position in regard to the world grain situation. One of my hon. friends across the floor of the house mentioned that to-day and said I was about right in what I said last year. I am a little more careful about statements I make in regard to grain and farming and I think I know a little more about those things than my hon. friend. He has made some of the wildest statements in regard to all these things. Many such statements are made from the other side, or at least from that corner. The other day the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) put a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, as reported on page 302 of Hansard, of February 9. He said:
I want to remind the Minister of Trade and Commerce that about fifty-four per cent of the 1942 crop was sold by the farmers on the open market, and that they will get no benefit out of the participation certificates, or any increased price for that wheat.
One would think the bon. member for Weyburn knew what he was talking about when he said that, but that is not the fact. I doubt if my hon. friend knows more about the actual figures than I do, but I should like to make a prediction and I think it will be as true as any I ever made. I would say that there was under forty per cent of the 1942 crop sold on the open market and over sixty per cent sold to the wheat board. The farmers will get participation certificates on that sixty per cent or more sold to the wheat board. That is considerably different from fifty-four per cent.

That is the
information the chairman of the wheat board gave the agriculture committee last year.. The hon. member was a member of that committee.

I do not remember the chairman of the wheat board giving any such information as my hon. friend says he did. I do not think anyone has given the information he is speaking of. The wheat was not delivered at that time.
The 1942 crop.

The 1942-43 crop; that is the 1942 crop. Every time the minister's estimates come up we have criticism year after year by my hon. friends. They have always criticized the policies brought down by the Minister of Agriculture. If they will go back and consider the position of agriculture in years gone by when different policies were brought down by the then Minister of Agriculture they will find that the present minister has been dead right all the time. When he brought down his policy of subsidizing the growing of coarse grains in western Canada my hon. friend and others criticized him sharply, but where would this country have been if he had not brought down such a policy and emphasized the growing of coarse grains for the feeding of live stock?
Who criticized that?
Members on that side of the house; many of them.
No.

Just look at Hansard. The hon. member for Yorkton has criticized the wheat board, but let me say that that board has done a remarkable job in handling the wheat of this country. The same can be said for our railway companies.
A good job for the line elevator companies.

My hon. friend does not know the difference between the line elevator companies and the Winnipeg grain exchange. A moment ago he said that the Winnipeg grain exchange set the price of wheat. The Winnipeg grain exchange is simply a trading place for traders to get together and if; has nothing to do with setting the price of wheat. It is the traders who come there who set the price of wheat when they trade one against the other. No one can set the price of wheat in this country when there is an open market. If we get into the position where we have the policies in force which my hon. friends want to put into force, they will be able to set the price of wheat and then-I was going to say, "God help the farmer if they ever do."
At six oclock the committee took recess.

subtopic: MODIFICATION OF LIMITATION OF TAX ADVANTAGE IN RESPECT OF CHARITABLE CONTRIBUTIONS BY BUSINESS CONCERNS

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MODIFICATION OF LIMITATION OF TAX ADVANTAGE IN RESPECT OF CHARITABLE CONTRIBUTIONS BY BUSINESS CONCERNS
speechtext:
There are two brief statements which I think I should make to the house. The first is in respect of charitable donations.
The house will recall that on January 31 I made a statement indicating the government's intention to introduce at the time of the budget a measure limiting the tax advantage which may be obtained by a business concern making contributions to charitable organizations. I announced at that time that in respect of contributions subscribed after January 31, 1944, the tax advantage obtainable by a business concerned, whether corporate or otherwise, should not be greater than that obtained by a comparable business not subject to tax at the 100 per cent rate.
In the meantime I have received many representations from various organizations asking for clarification and expressing great concern over the possible effect of this proposed amendment on their ability to secure the funds needed to carry on their activities. As^ a result of these representations, and the quite widespread comment on this subject in the press and elsewhere, I should like to make a further statement on the matter.
First of all I should like to explain more fully and restate to the house the facts of the present situation relating to tax deductions in respect of charitable contributions which, to the government, seemed clearly to call for some safeguarding measure.

subtopic: MODIFICATION OF LIMITATION OF TAX ADVANTAGE IN RESPECT OF CHARITABLE CONTRIBUTIONS BY BUSINESS CONCERNS
speechtext: Is this only in connection with excess profits tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MODIFICATION OF LIMITATION OF TAX ADVANTAGE IN RESPECT OF CHARITABLE CONTRIBUTIONS BY BUSINESS CONCERNS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: MODIFICATION OF LIMITATION OF TAX ADVANTAGE IN RESPECT OF CHARITABLE CONTRIBUTIONS BY BUSINESS CONCERNS
speechtext: Not income tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MODIFICATION OF LIMITATION OF TAX ADVANTAGE IN RESPECT OF CHARITABLE CONTRIBUTIONS BY BUSINESS CONCERNS
speechtext:
Oh, that is right; it only affects business concerns. I think I had better not interject anything; it is quite clear.
The present law allows a business concern as a deduction in computing profits subject to tax an amount not exceeding 5 per cent of its income which has been paid by way of donation within the tax year to any charitable organization in Canada operated exclusively as such and not for the benefit of private gain or profit of any person. As a result of allowing this deduction in computing profits for tax !Mr. J. G. Ross.]
purposes, the government forgoes collecting tax which would otherwise be due. In effect, then, the government can be said to be subsidizing charitable activities. Before the war, when the corporation income tax rate was 15 per cent, the government relinquished 15 cents of tax revenue on every dollar contributed to charity by the ordinary industrial corporation. To-day, when the minimum tax payable by corporations is 40 per cent, the government gives up at least 40 cents in tax for every dollar of charitable contributions made by the corporations. The minimum tax advantage to-day in making contributions to charity is more than two and one-half times greater than it was pre-war. It can scarcely be argued, then, I think, that the government incentive towards charitable giving is ungenerous or that the importance of maintaining the flow' of donations is overlooked. It is true, of course, that the heavy weight of taxation, both on business concerns and individuals, leaves fewer dollars to devote towards charity, but while the weight of taxation has increased the incentive towards giving has likewise increased.
I have just referred to the case where a company is paying a 40 per cent tax rate. No problem can be said to exist in this situation. In making a contribution towards charity of, say, $100, the company' is parting with $60 of shareholder money. The situation which gives rise to the problem, however, is where the business concern is paying tax at the rate of 100 per cent on excess profits. In this situation a contribution to charity reduces the company's tax bill by exactly the same amount. Under these circumstances the company which ostensibly makes a donation to charity is doing so entirely at the expense of the treasury. The company, of course, loses its right to a subsequent 20 per cent refund on the amount contributed. In the light of this situation it is easy to understand the statement which I made in the house on January 31 that business concerns are being solicited on a wholesale scale to make unusually large contributions to various nonprofit organizations.
I think I need do no more than mention this situation in order for the house to see the necessity for some safeguarding provision beyond -that now obtaining in the law. Otherwise the way is open for an abuse of the privileges in the law which could result in a very serious diversion of public funds into channels which, while extremely desirable in themselves, can in the war period scarcely be regarded as of an urgency equal to that of finding funds to finance the war.

Excess Profits-Charitable Institutions
For the reasons I have just stated the government does not feel it can depart from the general principle of the proposed limitation on the tax advantage to be secured by business concerns in making charitable contributions. The government is willing, however, to make a modification which I think effectively removes any possible criticism of the proposed restriction. The modification is intended to enable business concerns to continue without loss of tax advantage, the level of charitable giving which they had established prior to the coming into force of the 100 per cent excess profits tax rate.
I wish, therefore, to announce that the limitation of tax advantage which I proposed on January 31, 1944, will not affect any business whose total contributions in any year are not above the average of its donations in its last two fiscal years ending before July 1. 1942, which was the date when the 100 per cent excess rate came into effect.	'
For example, if a company made charitable contributions totalling $8,000 in one of these two years and $12,000 in the other, its average annual contribution for the two years would be $10,000. It will then be allowed to continue to receive the full tax advantage on $10,000 of contributions in fiscal periods ending after January 31, 1944.
The proposed limitation which I announced on January 31 will apply, however, when contributions made are above the average established by the record of 1940 and 1941, as referred to in what I have said. That is. the limitation will apply to that portion of the amount of contributions not subscribed on or before January 31, 1944, which results in the total amount contributed in the tax year of the business being in excess of the average amount contributed in the last two fiscal years of the business concern ending before July 1, 1942.
The present five per cent limitation with respect to the total volume of deductions allowed will, of course, continue to operate.

subtopic: MODIFICATION OF LIMITATION OF TAX ADVANTAGE IN RESPECT OF CHARITABLE CONTRIBUTIONS BY BUSINESS CONCERNS
speechtext: In other words, this means, prior to the time the tax w'ent on, you are taking the previous two fiscal years as your base?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MODIFICATION OF LIMITATION OF TAX ADVANTAGE IN RESPECT OF CHARITABLE CONTRIBUTIONS BY BUSINESS CONCERNS
speechtext: That is right,

subtopic: MODIFICATION OF LIMITATION OF TAX ADVANTAGE IN RESPECT OF CHARITABLE CONTRIBUTIONS BY BUSINESS CONCERNS
speechtext: And upon that base you are making your average so far as charitable welfare donations are concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MODIFICATION OF LIMITATION OF TAX ADVANTAGE IN RESPECT OF CHARITABLE CONTRIBUTIONS BY BUSINESS CONCERNS
speechtext:
Well, yes. It goes further than that, though. I do not want to muddy the waters by impromptu explanations of what I have said, because every word has to 100-42J
be weighed. That base is taken, and if the donation is kept within that base, the full tax advantage is obtained in respect of the donation, just as the law has been up to now; but for any excess, the tax advantage is limited to 40 per cent of the donation.

subtopic: MODIFICATION OF LIMITATION OF TAX ADVANTAGE IN RESPECT OF CHARITABLE CONTRIBUTIONS BY BUSINESS CONCERNS
speechtext: The balance, then, comes under the same category as the minister's statement indicated to the house some weeks ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MODIFICATION OF LIMITATION OF TAX ADVANTAGE IN RESPECT OF CHARITABLE CONTRIBUTIONS BY BUSINESS CONCERNS
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: MODIFICATION OF LIMITATION OF TAX ADVANTAGE IN RESPECT OF CHARITABLE CONTRIBUTIONS BY BUSINESS CONCERNS
speechtext: It is difficult to assess the exact amount of the advantage or modification which the minister has mentioned. I should not like to express myself with respect to that at the moment. At any rate it is not debatable, and I have no intention of doing more than simply making an observation with respect to it. But I am glad he has made an announcement, for the sake of many of the institutions that have been in touch, I know, with the minister and with hon. members generally, and have felt pretty keenly and severely changes which were being made, because I fancy that, apart altogether from the position in which they found themselves, the fact that it came very quickly upon them involved them in a good deal of difficulty in making their adjustments. I am hopeful that, if the minister finds that this is not a sufficient amount by way of modification, he will not close the door entirely against any adjustment which might conceivably require to be made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MODIFICATION OF LIMITATION OF TAX ADVANTAGE IN RESPECT OF CHARITABLE CONTRIBUTIONS BY BUSINESS CONCERNS
speechtext: I feel that this is the final notice of budget modifications in this regard. I think there has to be some finality about it, and I feel that this is the final notification.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is one other matter. During the past few weeks, the government has received representations from various parts of the country regarding sugar beets, and the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) has also drawn the matter to the attention of the house on several recent occasions. Sugar concerns both the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Finance, and I wish it to be understood that I am speaking also on behalf of my colleague, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner).
The representations -to the government have been along two lines. On the one hand there have been requests for additional dominion

Sugar Beets-Mr. Ilsley

assistance. On the other hand the government has been asked to give, not additional assistance, but assurance that the present price structure will be maintained until the 1944 crop has been marketed.
It will be recalled that during the past two years substantial assistance has been given to the sugar beet industry by way of reductions in the excise tax. The first reduction of half a cent a pound was made in the budget of 1942, and a further reduction of half a cent by order in council, effective September, 1943. These reductions added directly to the price received by growers for their sugar beets, the increase in two shears amounting to approximately twenty-five per cent.
In Alberta and Manitoba higher prices resulted in a substantial increase in acreage. In Alberta, plantings in . 1943 were the largest on record, and there is every reason to believe that if weather conditions had been normal at harvest, the crop would have taxed the capacity of the two factories in that province. Unfortunately, there was considerable spoilage, the loss being estimated at around fifteen per cent. In Manitoba, acreage was slightly less than the year before, but in spite of some loss at harvest there was a record yield.
In Ontario, the situation was quite different. The increased price, which was supplemented by assistance from the Ontario government of fifty-five cents per ton, failed to stimulate plantings. Instead, acreage declined from over
20,000	acres in 1942 to less than 10,000 in 1943. Farmers preferred to raise other crops requiring less labour.
I am bringing these facts to the attention of the house because they illustrate some of the considerations which must weigh with the government in arriving at a decision in this matter. For some time the government has been encouraging the production of soy-beans and white beans, crops which are needed urgently, but which in Ontario compete with sugar beets. This is one of the reasons for the decline in sugar beet production in that province. The hon. member for Lethbridge also spoke of sugar beet growers turning to other crops in Alberta. The point I wish to make is that at this stage in our war effort a choice must be made between alternative uses of land and labour, taking into consideration the relative importance of the various products.
I might also add that even though, as some believe and as is probably true, the world outlook for sugar is less favourable now than a year ago, this does not necessarily mean that Canada should divert land and labour to the production of sugar beets in an effort to offset a possible decline in imported supplies
[Air. Ilsley.]
if there are other equally or even more important uses to which these resources can be put.
The experience last year illustrates the variation between conditions in various parts of Canada. In the West, prices were sufficiently attractive to stimulate maximum plantings and should continue to be fairly satisfactory; in Ontario, the existing price level, plus the provincial subsidy, had little effect so far as can be ascertained.
After careful consideration the government has therefore come to the conclusion that it would be inadvisable to increase dominion assistance on beet sugar. Provincial governments have always taken a special interest in sugar beets, and of course I do not know whether they intend giving additional assistance to their growers.
As I said at the outset, some growers have asked for assurance that prices will not be lower during the 1944 crop year. In order to remove any fears that the government might reduce returns on sugar by altering the excise tax, I may say that the government does not intend to propose any increase in this particular tax in the forthcoming budget, nor does it intend revoking the order in council by which the latest half-cent reduction was effected, at least before the 1944 sugar beet crop has been marketed.
The dominion government, through the sugar administrator, controls the importation and sale of cane sugar, and, as additional assurance, I am in a position to say that on the basis of our present commitments and prospects there is no danger of a reduction in the price of sugar within the period during which the 1944 crop is being marketed.
I hope that this statement will provide the necessary degree of certainty as to price levels during the coming year.

Are steps being taken by the government to reopen the sugar factory at Halifax? The Acadia Sugar Company has been closed for two years. This matter has been brought up in the house from time to time by the member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor), and it means a great-deal to the province of Nova Scotia as well as to the sugar supply in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would not increase the supply of sugar in Canada by a pound. I am not aware of the authority under which the -refinery at Halifax was closed or whether it was by governmental direction at all, but so far as I know no steps are being taken to open it. However, I will make inquiries and inform my hon. friend if I find that any change is planned.
