At six o'clock I was endeavouring to answer one or two remarks of the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden) in the speech he made prior to my rising. He was speaking of the wheat board and the way they had handled the wheat crop of the western farmer. I said I thought, and I am sure I am right, that the wheat board had done an excellent job this year in handling Canada's wheat and also all grains for the farmers not only of western Canada but also of eastern Canada and far western Canada. It must be remembered that, following the policy laid down by the Minister of Agriculture of subsidizing the shipment of grain to eastern Canada and to British Columbia for the feeding of live stock a year ago, besides all exports to the old country and to the United States, the wheat board and the railway companies were able to move some fifty-eight million bushels of grain for feed to other parts of Canada from the west. This year, from the 1st- of August, the start of the crop year, to the end of December there has been moved forty-five million bushels, or seventy-six per cent of the total movement of last year. When one considers that millions of bushels are being shipped to the United States, great credit is due not only to the wheat board but to the railway companies and the railwaymen for handling the grain in the way they have done throughout the past year or two. They have had to do this while moving thousands of troops from one end of the country to the other and thousands of civilian passengers besides millions of tons of freight needed for the war. The record made by the wheat board and the railways of this country has never been surpassed, and I think they should be given credit instead of being criticized by the hon. member and others.
The hon. gentleman spoke of the government taking over wheat and not allowing the price to go up. Surely he knows better than that; he knows that was not the case. He knows
that when the government took over the wheat they first of all set a price of SI 231 a bushel for all wheat that was in the hands of the board from 1940, 1941 and 1942 crops, and intimated that a participation certificate would be paid on that basis, less cost of handling that grain. Up to the point of taking over at a price of SI .234 none of that wheat is to compete with wheat of successive years. That wheat goes as lend-lease or is sold for feed or shipped to some of our allies and does not compete in any way with the crop of 1943. The crop of 1943 was taken over at SI.25 a bushel advance price and a participation certificate to the farmer, so that when the wheat is finally sold, whatever price is received for it by the government will be returned to the farmer by the participation certificate, the difference between SI .25 and whatever price the government gets for that wheat.
Why did you not do it four years ago?
We have always done it.
You have never done it.

There was always a participation certificate, and we have always told the farmer that if he sold through the wheat board he would get the participation certificate. We have not done as my hon. friends have done-gone and told the farmers that they would never get anything for it. We told them they would get something for it and they are going to get something for it.
Why did you not close the grain exchange?

The Minister of Trade and Commerce stated in the house the other day that the wheat now being sold to the United States was being sold at an advance, and the figures he gave are equivalent to from sixteen to twenty-two cents a bushel over SI .25. These were the figures he gave, from S1.41 to $1.47 for No. 1 northern. Each year the policy of the Minister of Agriculture has been criticized in this house, but it has paid dividends to the allies in this war. Year by year he has arranged matters so that the farmers of Canada could produce more food, and that food could not only be sold to the people of Canada but be shipped overseas for the use of our allies. He asked for meats and dairy products mainly. He asked the western farmer to cut down the growing of wheat, to increase the growing of coarse grains in order that the western farmer and the eastern farmer could produce more meat
Supply-Agriculture

and dairy products. How successful that policy has been is again shown by the very criticisms that come from hon. members of this house. That is why we are unable to handle all the cattle, hogs and sheep that are coming on the market. It is a physical impossibility to handle them, unless you can get sufficient shipping to take the stuff out of the country as it passes through the packing plants.
I am a farmer, and I do not believe that anybody ought to rise in his place in this house and try to make out that the packers are nothing but robbers. The farmers have done a great job in producing live stock, and the packers and the men employed by the packers have done a great job in handling live stock during the war.
The minister said it was on account of the packing plants that they could not ship.

My hon. friend is babbling away again. The hon. member for Yorlcton then went on to try to prove that the farmer was paying excess prices for prac-ticalfy everything that he had to buy, and that his position was not getting better, as the Minister of Agriculture said it was.
I did not say that.

The hon. member intimated that. Let me say this: My hon. friend should have read the pamphlet that was quoted this afternoon by the hon. member from Souris, the Economic Annalist. The first paragraph reads:
Preliminary figures make it possible to access the trends of prices and production in 1943. The index of wholesale prices advanced 4'3 points over that of 1942 or 4'5 per cent. The urban cost of living index was 1*6 points higher. The cost of farm family living rose i-3 points. Wholesale prices of Canadian farm products averaged 13-4 points or 16-2 per cent higher than in 1942. The index of prices of field products was 15-1 points or 22'7 per cent higher and that of animal products was 8-0 points or 9-8 per cent higher than a year earlier. .	.	. The total index of Canadian
farm product prices was 104'6 in December. It will be observed that this is 2-1 points above the index of wholesale prices of all commodities.
What was it in June?
What was it ten years ago? What is the use of saying that?
What was it in June?
As a farmer I buy .and sell.

What?
{Mr. J. G. Ross.]

I buy the things the farmer has to buy and I sell the things the farmer has to sell. Let me tell my hon. friend this, that there is nothing in the Dominion of Canada that has risen more in prices in the last two years than farm products.
Farm machinery has.

Farm machinery has not. Farm products have risen higher than anything during this war. When this war began I was producing hogs and getting seven cents a pound for them. Take a look at the figures to-day and see what you are getting. Take the figures for cattle and compare them with what they were at the beginning of the war. Take a look at the figures for grains, butter, cheese, every product that the farmer has to raise in this country. The price has gone up farther in comparison with that of anything else in this country, and it is to the credit of the Minister of Agriculture and this government that that has happened.
My hon. friends rise in their places in this house day after day and paint a picture of fear and trembling as to what will happen when this war is over. I am not a bit afraid of what is going to happen when the war is over; not a bit. People have short memories. Many of them think there was a great depression after the last war. There was no such thing. After the last war there were twelve years of the most prosperous times that the world has ever seen; twelve years, and most of it under a Liberal regime in this country.
In spite of a Liberal regime.

Most of it under a Liberal regime. My hon. friend, if he were a farmer, would know that when a Liberal regime is in power he gets good prices for his products and the reverse is true when the Liberals are out of power.
I live in a town just like my hon. friend.

There were reasons for that prosperity after the last war, and the same reasons will hold good after this one. The men who have gone from Canada to the army, navy and air force have received a much better education than any of us in this house ever received. They have been taught to take responsibility. They have seen much more of the world than most of us have seen, and they are coming back when this war is over to take charge of this country and run it as it

Supply-Agriculture
should be run. I am not a bit afraid of our young people coming back here, and I hope they will take charge and run this dominion as it ought to be run. After the last war there was prosperity. Why? Because Great Britain and the United States made some billions of dollars available to the countries in Europe for the purchase of food products and raw material to rehabilitate themselves. That started the prosperity. Then during the last war many new processes and new inventions were developed which were put into commercial use after the war. These things in commercial use created more buying power, more distribution of wealth, and that pros-, perity continued for twelve years. We know now that when this war is over there will not bo a few billions but hundreds of billions of dollars of credits made available by the united nations in ordered to rehabilitate the unfortunate countries of the world. We know also that science and invention have worked out new processes and inventions in this war a hundredfold compared with the last w'ar. I am satisfied that when this war is over we shall have prosperity for at least twenty-five years. But you must have a policy to help it along.
After the last war we had trouble with wheat. We had been asked to place every available acre in wheat during the last war, and the farmers in western Canada based their economy on wheat. When the war was over there was apparently more wheat than could properly be handled in the world wheat trade at that time. After this war it is going to be not only wheat but cattle, hogs, sheep, butter, cheese, eggs and poultry, and practically every farm product that one can think of, barley, oats, rye, flax. We are going to have a surplus of every one of them in this country when the war is over, because we have all of these commodities at the peak of production. What are we going to do with them when the war is over? What is the solution? If this government and other governments do not agree to follow out the Atlantic charter, do not agree to drop tariffs altogether, and allow trade to flow freely from one country to another, then there will eventually be chaos and trouble in the world. But if we will follow sound Liberal policy when this war is over, then prosperity can continue throughout the world and everyone can have more of the world's goods.
The leader of the opposition, the hon. member for Peel, spoke of the discussion that took place last year in regard to research laboratories. I was very glad to note that everyone in the house agreed with the suggestion made at that time that we should go farther into agricultural research in this country, and I am pleased to see that this year the government has increased the amount of money available for that purpose. I agree with the hon. member for Peel, however, that this amount is not large enough even yet. After parliament adjourned I had an opportunity of going to the United States and being shown through one of the large laboratories set up by the government of that country. Of course it had to handle a great many more products than would be handled in any one of our regional laboratories.
Might I ask where that was?

This one was at Albany, California; and the hon. member will realize that with the varied production on the west coast of the United States, they have many more matters to deal with than we would have in any single section of Canada, since their products range all the way from practically tropical fruits to the things grown in the temperate zone. This laboratory cost something in the neighbourhood of a million dollars, while the equipment cost something like half a million dollars. Of course we would not have to expend that amount of money, but if we desired to put up a proper laboratory we would have to spend more than two or three hundred thousand dollars.
A great deal of this work in Canada has been done in the past by the research council, by universities throughout the country and by the Department of Agriculture at its experimental farms. A good deal of research work can be carried on in that way, but if you are really going to get down to the business of research in agricultural products you must locate one laboratory somewhere to get started with, and there is a very good reason for that. In this laboratory you will have different branches, with men working on different products. In order to run it economically and well you will require, above all these different departments, an analytical branch with highly trained men and very intricate machines which cost a great deal of money. Therefore, in order that all the different branches may get the benefit of these highly trained technical men and these machines, it is necessary that the work be carried on in one laboratory. That organization should not be part of the research council here; it should be separate and apart, for
Supply-Agriculture

agricultural research. We must see to it that the newest types of machines are purchased for this laboratory, and I would suggest that before the remainder of the $200,000 runs out on March 31, the minister should see if he cannot purchase some of the machines that are needed, and at least we shall get that far along. Then we can use the money which is to be voted this year, and possibly more in the supplementary estimates, to carry research work farther.	.
Are these machines readily available?

I am. not so sure of that. I do not know. I should think some of them would be hard to get, but I am sure some machines and some equipment could be procured now. No doubt some of the more intricate machines will be very difficult to obtain until after the war.

May I ask the hon. member if he has any knowledge whatever of the workings of the National Chemurgic Society. Has he made any study of the work of that society?
,Mr. ROSS (Moose Jaw): I have read some of their pamphlets dealing with the set-up of the laboratories which have been established in Washington, but I have not attended any of the conventions of the National Chemurgic Society. The work of these laboratories has been considerably changed since the beginning of the war. When they were first started they were intended to work on agricultural products, to find new uses for them; but since the war a large part of their work has been in connection with the dehydration, freezing and packaging of goods in order that they may be used during the war.
M.r. WOOD:	I should like to supplement
the remarks of the hon. member for Moose Jaw. I wish to thank him for his most vigorous speech in defence of the cause of the farmer. I believe that if farming is to retain its rightful place in this country we need more people with faith in that branch of industry, rather than people who are always crying about it. After all, farming is not an easy job; it takes strong, virile men, men with ambition, men who are prepared to pit their physical energies against all the elements. Farming is only for capable people, so that we expect to have sharing in the joys of agriculture only those of our citizens who. are ambitious and physically able to do a hard job.
However, this is not really what I intended to say. I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Yorkton, who complained

because farm, prices in the United States were so much higher than in Canada. Well, you know, it is only human to magnify fault and belittle virtue, and sometimes distant pastures seem green. Let us analyse the situation for a moment. Only about three weeks ago I happened to have a farmer from Michigan in my stable, looking at the hogs I was producing, and I asked what he was getting for hogs in his state. He told me he was being paid $13.90 at his farm, live weight. Well, I was getting close to $13 for my hogs, live weight, and he had to pay a good deal more for his feed than I did. We have had the advantage of the subsidy of $4.50 on freight from the west, and we have had the benefit of the price ceiling, which they do not have in the United States. This man was paying almost fifty per cent more for his feed than- I was paying, so that when the hon. member for Yorkton makes a statement of the kind he did he should at least qualify it by pointing out the different conditions that exist. Farmers in the United States may be receiving more for some of their products, but it is costing them far more to produce those commodities than it costs in Canada, due to our price control policy.
There is another thing I should like to bring to the attention of the committee. In consequence of this unpopular control policy which was inflicted upon us, let us see what is happening. I notice a question was asked by the hon. member for Mackenzie as to the public debt of Canada. The farmers to some extent are responsible for the payment of that debt. The answer to the hon. member's question, as it appears at page 574 of Hansard, shows that on March 31, 1943 the per capita public debt of Canada was $523.44.
I hold in my hand a statement from the Herald Tribune of New York. This issue of February 14 sets out the gross public debt and guaranteed obligations in the United States. The figure is $183 billion, or a per capita debt of $1,410, when spread over their population of 130 million. That is their debt, compared with ours of only $523.44. Our debt will probably increase to some extent, but I am prepared to say that the per capita debt of the Canadian farmer, in so far as his contribution to the total amount is concerned,-is only one-half the load carried by farmers in .the United States.
Does that mean anything to the hon. member for Yorkton? I think he would show a great deal more wisdom if, when analysing these economic questions he would lay both sides of the question before the people, instead of trying to show only those things he wished to show, or attempting to have the people believe only those things he wishes them to believe.

Supply-Agriculture
In his analysis he leaves out important facts which have contributed to the general welfare of the people of Canada.
This evening I intend to discuss these estimates at somewhat greater length than I have in the past. First I would draw the attention of the committee to some newspaper clippings I sometimes tear out of a local newspaper, the Olobe and Mail. I used to take it regularly, and even now I read it occasionally. I got a copy this morning before I had breakfast, because I do not like to read it after I have had a full meal.
That shows the hon. member's poor judgment; do not blame the Globe and Mail.

I will give my judgment of the hon. member in a moment or two. This Winnipeg dispatch states:
Farm Mortgages being Cleared Up
Prosperity among farmers is reflected in the number of mortgages, some of them of many years standing, that are being retired. . . . The Manitoba Farm Loans Association announces that farmers are clearing their holdings faster than ever before, and in this respect the record for the year was about fifty per cent better than for the previous year.
That is where they have had good government for twenty years.

Here is another newspaper clipping which is headed "Farm incomes at high level", and states that farm incomes in 1943 totalled $1,397 million, or almost double what it was at the beginning of the war. That is about five times as much as it was when the party of hon. members opposite had put us in the last depths of degradation and poverty in 1932, as a consequence of their judgment.
I have before me another short item bearing date of February 16, and headed "Farm income from milk up $28 million in 1943." I am not saying the farmers are getting too much, but I do share the view of the hon. member for Moose Jaw who has said that in consequence of policies in force to-day we are making rapid progress, and going ahead probably just as fast as any other country.
In 1932-and I hate to mention this, but I believe I must do so, following the interjection of the hon. member for Peel-I sold pork for $3.25 a hundredweight. To-day I can get as much for one pig as I got for six of them in those days. Of course we know that at that time prices were lower in Canada than they had ever been. One would have to go back to the time of Queen Elizabeth to find a parallel.
In 1930, when the Liberal government was turned out of office, our trade stood fifth
among the nations of the world. That is, there were only four nations which had a greater volume of trade than did Canada. In 1932 we had gone down to seventh place, and we stayed there until 1935, when a Liberal government was returned to power. Some may say that that was a period of world depression. True, there was a world-wide depression; but it was only incidental that Canada belonged to that same world both before and during the depression, and that she was shoved down from fifth to seventh place in consequence of policies in force at that time?
Is the hon. member sure of his facts?
Yes; certainly he is.
I would like to challenge that.

The hon. member has the same source that I had from which to get his information.
In 1935 we stood seventh among the trading nations of the world. By the time war broke out in 1939 we were back to fifth place, and to-day we stand fourth.
Third.
First.
Yes; make it first.
Be generous.

There never was a time when the people of Canada exported as much as they did in 1943. The export trade for January is $64 million higher than it was in the preceding month. My only regret is that so much of that has had to be trading in weapons of destruction, and human slaughter machinery. We do not gloat over that kind of trade.
The fact remains, however, that in 1943 we shipped $775 million worth of agricultural products. That is, we are one of the nations which has been in a position to feed itself, and at the same time sell food products to the value I have mentioned. And on top of that, as Madame Chiang Kai-shek said, we have made the greatest contribution per capita in munitions that has been made by any of the united nations-as well as in our manpower. These things do not happen by accident.
That was an afterthought.

They result, of course, from some of the unfortunate regulations to which we have been committed. But we as Liberals believe we should share the happiness and enjoyments of our country in times of peace with the great masses of our people and by the
Supply-Agriculture

same token, in time of distress, when 775,000 of our boys are regimented into fighting for your liberty and mine, we should share with them some of the burdens and hardships they are asked to bear.
"Regimentation" is a good word to use.

Exactly. When a soldier goes to war he expects regimentation. I think that we civilians should accept with better grace than some of the opposition have the restrictions that have been put upon us. I hope that six months after the war they will be as few as possible and we can get back again where under honest Liberal policies we can carry on with as little a measure of restriction as possible.
You should not have sounded that last unhappy note. Otherwise your speech was pretty good.

I do not propose to make an omnibus speech at this time and try to cover the number of subjects hon. members who have preceded me have tried to cover. I was rather amazed to hear the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Wood) try to explain that during the ten years before this war it was only the Progressive Conservative party that had created hard times. I think most of us who were farmers during the period between the two wars remember that there was a lot of hard times.
Before taking up the subject with which I wish to deal, I should like to say a few words in reply to the hon. member for Moose law (Mr. Ross). I judged from his remarks that the prosperity the farmer is enjoying at the present time-he is enjoying a certain amount-a great deal more than he has done for a long time is due entirely to the Department of Agriculture and the Minister of Agriculture.
A good part of it.

I have an idea that there was a war on and that had considerable to do with the present position of agriculture. The same Minister of Agriculture was in power from 1935 to 1939, four years during which we did not have a war and during which, as I remember, agriculture was not too prosperous. The hon. member also stated that the twelve years after the last war were the most prosperous as far as agriculture was concerned.
As far as the whole country was concerned.

I served four years in the last war. I came back from overseas, took up land in western Canada and bought my

seed wheat in 1920 for $2.60 a bushel, and in 1921 when the Liberal government were in power I got 67 cents a bushel for my wheat.
There was no Liberal government in power in 1921. Mr. Meighen was in power all through 1921.
They were in power shortly after that and prices did not increase very much.
Prices went up.

I sold my wheat at the same price in 1922 when they were in power.
The matter I wanted to discuss was in connection with the price of grass and clover seeds. This year the special products marketing board has taken over the complete marketing of grass and clover seeds, all domestic requirements being handled through that board. The result is not very satisfactory as far as the producers of clover seed is concerned. Last fall when the board took over the marketing of these seeds they intimated to the cooperatives and to the buyers of grass seed that they should give the farmers participation certificates. Some of the buyers complied with this request, but there were others who did not.
The price received by the growers of alfalfa seed-I am dealing with alfalfa seed more particularly, but I think my remarks apply equally well to red clover and alsike seed- last year in the district from which I come was thirty-eight cents a pound for No. 1 commercial seed, and forty cents a pound for No. 1 registered seed, when they were marketed through the cooperative. Last year the ceiling price on alfalfa seed was thirty-seven cents a pound, but there was no restriction as far as export was concerned. Out of a total crop of some 4,500,000 pounds of alfalfa seed, somewhere in the neighbourhood of 2.000,000 pounds were exported. The additional price received on export balanced the domestic price and gave to the producer approximately thirty-eight cents a pound for No. 1 commercial seed.
This year the government has taken over the export of seed and has established certain prices. According to a return tabled yesterday on the motion of the hon. member for York East (Mr. McGregor), the export price is 34J cents a pound. According to information which I have, approximately ten per cent of the crop available in Canada this year will be exported. If these figures are correct, and I believe they are approximately correct, it means that this year the producer of alfalfa seed will receive at the farm only from thirty

Supply-Agriculture
to thirty-one cents a pound for the grade of seed for which he received thirty-eight cents a pound last year.
I realize why the government has taken the step it has this year. Last year a large proportion of our seed was exported, and in the spring of the year we found that we did not have enough to meet our domestic requirements. The result was that we had to use a lot of second and third grade seed. I imagine that it was to prevent the same thing occurring this year that the government has taken over the whole crop and is controlling export. However, I do not see why the producer of alfalfa seed should bear the brunt of this action. He is facing a loss of from eight to ten cents a pound.
In almost every other case where the government have acted in a like manner a subsidy has been paid to the producer to give him something near the price he would receive had he been allowed to use the export market. I understand that the government are sending most of their exports to Great Britain. If they were using the United States market they could get a much better price than 34i cents a pound. I have no objection to the government supplying the British market because I think that is as it should be, but I do not think the producers of alfalfa and clover seeds should be asked to take a rap of that kind. A subsidy should be paid to these growers which would give them a price which would approximate what they received last year for their seed.
The growing of alfalfa seed is a hazardous business because it is only once out of every three years that you get a reasonable crop, and sometimes not that. When one considers the hazards and cost of production a price of thirty^eight cents a pound is not unfair. If the figures which have been tabled are correct I would think that the prices received this year will not be such as to encourage men continuing in the production of seed. I happen to represent a district which produces probably more alfalfa seed than any other place in the Dominion of Canada, and I know that because of the cost of production and other hazards the acreage has been reduced during the last two or three years. Encouragement must be given to these people to continue in production because this seed is essential to agriculture in eastern Canada and in other parts of the world. There is a real demand for alfalfa seed outside Canada, one which we will be able to supply if we encourage our producers. I should like the minister to make a statement as to the situation with regard to clover seed and grass seed at the present time,
and what the producer can likely expect to get as a return on his participation certificates if the prices are realized.

I did not intend to make any extended remarks. I had one or two questions I wanted to ask the minister; but I do want to refer to one or two things said by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross). The hon. member for Moose Jaw takes the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden) to task for referring to the Winnipeg grain exchange as setting prices. Well, the hon. member for Moose Jaw ought to know something about the grain exchange. I think he had a good deal to do with some of the grain brokerage firms in days gone by, and probably got to know something about the grain exchange.
Surely not!
Was the hon. member for Moose Jaw a grain broker?
I believe so, although he always tells the committee he was a farmer.
I always heard him say that.
I thought he grew sunflower seeds.
Maybe he did more farming the farmer.
That is mere talk without any knowledge. I was never a broker in my life. I was always a farmer.
Well, the hon. member spent a lot of time in a grain brokerage office.
I may have done that, and the hon. member might have learned more about the business if he had.

I know a lot of farmers who were "broken" after coming in contact with the hon. member's brokerage office. One of the things that the hon. member for Moose Jaw and the Minister -of Agriculture like to do when they rise in their places is to twit those of us who are not farmers with not being farmers, yet daring to discuss agriculture. I make no apology for not being a farmer. The committee may be interested to know that the Minister of Agriculture is not really a farmer either. He supports a farm; he does not make the farm support him.

The farm would support me better than anything you have ever done supports you.

The Minister of Agriculture or the hon. member for Moose Jaw have not fooled very many people. The hon. member for Moose Jaw took exception to the statement which I made regarding the fact that about fifty-four per cent of the 1942 crop was sold by the farmers on the open market. I want to refer the hon. member to the report of the Canadian wheat board for the crop year 1941-42, the year which ended July 31, 1942.
That is the 1941 crop.
The 1941 crop.

The crop year ended July 31, 1942. On page 4 I find this statement:
Of the total marketings of 227-9 million bushels in the west during the crop year 1941-42, producers delivered 100 million bushels to the board, or about 44 per cent of their marketings. In the previous crop year producers delivered 395 million bushels to the wheat board out of total marketings of 456 million bushels.
You were in the right church but the wrong pew.

In other words, the figure was actually lower, but I had in mind that the producer delivered forty-six per cent. As a matter of fact, he. delivered only forty-four per cent to the wheat board that year.
That is the 1941 crop. The hon. member said 1942.
I say that fifty-six per cent was sold in the open market for the crop year 1941-42.
Let the hon member hold his horses a minute.
Let the hon. member for Weyburn hold his horses for a minute.
As I say, he was in the right church but the wrong pew.

The figures on page 4 show what the board price was during that year and what the cash price was on the Winnipeg exchange, and the fact that the market price was higher than the board price accounted, of course, for the fact that fifty-six per cent of the wheat that year was sold on the open market rather than to the board. The fact remains that, while we have not the figures for the 1943 crop, or the 1942-43 crop, the market price during a good part of that year was higher than the board price. The hon. member for Moose Jaw thinks it is probably sixty per cent. I imagine he will find that the figure is much lower.
I have the exact figures in my pocket, and they are more than sixty per cent.
If the minister has the figures I should be very glad to have them.
I am not permitted to give the exact ones, but they are more than sixty per cent.
When are we to get the report?
I do not know.
It will be very late.
Surely; it is "not in the national interest".

As I have said, in the 1941-42 crop year the farmers who sold fifty-six per cent of their wheat on the open market did not receive any participation certificates; and unless the government and the wheat board make some change in policy and revise their arrangements, those people will not get any of the benefit of the subsequent increase in price. Whatever the hon. member for Moose Jaw may argue about 1941 or 1942 does not alter the cogency of the argument that for all of that fifty-six

per cent of the crop which was sold on the open market, the people who sold it will not get any of the benefit of the increase in price. Did I say "the members" from that group? I said "your people."
Well, I do not know whom the hon. member means by "our people." I cannot tell what all "our people" said.
Your machine.

There are just two
machines in Saskatchewan.

It certainly
would be a new fo-rm of government.
I wish to support those who have suggested to the minister that there is need1 of a great deal more money being spent on research into the use of agricultural products for industrial purposes. All of us supported last year the hon. member for Moose Jaw, who, I think, did a real service to the house and to the country in bringing this matter to the attention of the house on many occasions, and, I think, has made a thorough study of the question.
I was surprised when I saw that, of the $200,,000 that had been voted, not all had been spent. I imagine, of course, the minister will have the explanation-and I should think the explanation is reasonable-that it is very difficult to get machinery for pilot plants, and to procure the proper laboratory equipment. For this reason there can be no serious criticism, because in war time, naturally, war plants have priority. But I believe the government should, in the hope that they can get the equipment, make a much larger appropriation than is now proposed. The figures stated by the minister as being expenditures by his department and the Department of Trade and Commerce are somewhere between $400,000 and $500,000. It is a mere bagatelle compared with what has to be done. We are spending millions in other fields.

I should make myself
clear on that point. No part of the $200,000 voted in these estimates is to be carried into the next year. If any amount is supplied it will have to be brought down as a supplementary estimate.

Yes. But I think the minister will agree, as most members of the committee will, that if the government were to bring down an estimate for ten times what is now provided it would not be a bit too much. From three to five million dollars is not a large amount of money considering the tremendous era that chemurgy and the use of synthetics open up for both farming and industry in western Canada. I am hoping therefore that, especially as we come closer to the end of the war, the government will be prepared either to vote large sums of money to go into research work itself or to make grants to the cooperatives, for instance, who would be only too anxious to take up research along these lines. I had the privilege of attending a meeting with the hon. member for Regina. City (Mr. McNiven) in Saskatoon a year ago last fall, called by the cooperative organizations in Saskatchewan. They were studying the feasibility of going into the making of synthetic alcohol from wheat, and had they been able to get a substantial grant from the government the cooperatives in Saskatchewan would have been prepared to invest considerable sums of money in research along the lines I have suggested. If the government itself does not feel like undertaking research on such a large scale, I suggest that it might be prepared to grant assistance to some of the cooperatives and the farmer organizations, who I am sure would be ready to do this work.
In regard to departmental administration, I notice in the auditor general's report, page A9, expenses of the Minister of Agriculture

amounting to $2,661.42. I should like the minister to break that down and give us an idea as to how much is travelling expenses and so on. The reason why I ask this has no reference particularly to the Minister of Agriculture. I ask the question because there is a matter I have been wanting to raise for several years during the war, namely the fact that in every department there is a vote of $2,000 to every cabinet minister for a car. Originally, I understand, cars and chauffeurs w'ere supplied to cabinet ministers, but that practice was discontinued, and in lieu of that the ministers were given $2,000. During this war time some of the ministers do not drive cars. Indeed, many of us have put our cars away, and so have some of the cabinet ministers. I doubt very much, therefore, whether that grant is still necessary. I have no objection if the government wants to add the $2,000 to a minister's salary because I am not suggesting that we should take anything away from them, but in my opinion a grant of $2,000 for a car is a rather unnecessary expenditure at a time when we are talking to people about economy.
The $2,000 for a car also raises a very deli-' cate question which the minister himself placed before (he house the other day when speaking on a question of privilege. As reported at page 423 of Hansard he said:
This leaves the ear which is at headquarters in Regina, No. 20456, and which is placed at my disposal when I am in the province. I drove this car to the constituency, used it i.n certain occasions while there and drove it back to Regina later. I paid for my own gasoline while it was out, as I always do. The government did not pay for any gasoline in any car used for political purposes during that election, and no one of the cars listed above excepting 20456 -was used for political purposes to my knowledge.
It seems to me that to make a grant of $2,000 to cabinet ministers for a car, then place another car at the minister's disposal while he is in the province, and then have estimated expenses of $2,600, makes a considerable amount for travelling expenses at a time when we are talking about cutting down expenditures.
I wish the minister would enlarge on the statement he made with reference to grain crops during the coming crop year. I was not quick enough to catch the figures he gave, but he wanted the same amount of wheat acreage and 102 per cent of barley and 106 per cent of oats.
101 per cent of barley and 106 per cent of oats.

How does he propose to get that acreage? What are his plans to get the farmers to sow approximately
*MY. T, O. Douglas.]
the acreage he wants? The reason why I put this matter before the minister is that my impression, after going over a considerable part of the province of Saskatchewan this fall, is that ever since we have had the announcement of the new price there is every indication that a good many farmers will go back to increased wheat production. I wondered what the minister had in mind in order to keep the farmers growing the amount of coarse grain he wants them to produce for the purpose of raising live stock and also supplying feed to eastern Canada where the farmers may raise the live stock which we have pledged ourselves to produce for Great Britain.
I noticed, in the brief which the federation of agriculture presented to the government a week or two ago, that one of the things they asked the government to do was to make a statement as early as possible with reference to the price which would be paid this fall for coarse grain. I think that is important. I do not believe that even the subsidy of fifteen cents a bushel on barley and ten cents on oats will be enough to persuade the farmer to sow coarse grains as against wheat, even with the delivery quota on wheat.

The ten cents on oats and fifteen cents on barley are not a subsidy. The plan by which that ten cents on oats and fifteen cents on barley is raised is this. We sell a certain proportion of oats and barley in the United States and a certain amount in the eastern part of Canada; the amount obtained for both lots of grain is'pooled, so to speak, and we guarantee that there will be ten cents earned on what we sell to the United States in order to be spread over all oats sold. The same is true of barley. But at the same time a participation certificate is given which will net the farmer more if the grain is sold for more; that is to say, the price plus the ten cents and fifteen cents constitute the floor return, but any additional price for which it is sold the farmer will also get.

I understood that, but while I know that this has to do with the Minister of Trade and Commerce, in view of the fact that the Minister of Agriculture is charged with production and with the task of getting the kind of production he thinks is most necessary for the war effort, it seems to me that the government ought to make some announcement in the not far distant future as to what prices will obtain for coarse grains; that is the initial price plus whatever price will come from this fund, and then of course the participation certificate. I think if the government would make an announcement of a floor price and what it is likely to be, whether

Supply-Agriculture
it- will be the same as last year or better, and make it before the farmer starts to seed, the minister is more likely to get the acreage announced this afternoon than he will otherwise.
There is one other point. The minister has made no announcement-at least not while I was here; I came in a moment or two late; I was called away while he was speaking-as to whether or not the wheat acreage bnous is to be dropped

I announced it while the hon. member was out of the chamber.
Mr. DOUGLAS CVVeyburn): If we may judge by the estimates it is to be dropped, which means a drop of about $28,000,000. The wheat acreage reduction bonus was paid to the farmer mainly to encourage him to go into the growing of coarse grains, and also to summer-fallow. But it was also paid in lieu of the fact that from that time on there was to be a restriction as to how much wheat he could sell. That is, he was to be allowed to sell only sixty-five per cent of his basic acreage. It was a compensation. It was not a bonus in the sense of a gift or a subsidy. It was a compensation to him because, instead of being able to sell all of his wheat, or even all of his basic acreage, he could now sell only sixty-five per cent of his basic acreage. It seems to me if the government are going to drop the wheat acreage reduction bonus and thereby reduce the agricultural income by roughly $28,000,000, they ought to give consideration to announcing to the farmer that they will take all of his basic acreage, that they will take all the full quota and that it will be based on his entire 1940 acreage or whatever the minister considers to be a fair basic acreage. It seems to me that to continue to take only sixty-five per cent of his basic acreage and to remove the wheat acreage reduction bonus looks very much as though the government have given the farmer a $1.25 price with one hand and have taken away the $28,000,000 compensation from him with the other hand. I ask the minister to give some thought to that.

This general item gives one an opportunity to say a few words of a general nature with respect to the estimates of the Department of Agriculture. From the -observations made so far it is readily apparent that there is not the same degree of criticism from members of the house with respect to agriculture as has been the case on previous occasions. I believe that bears out the statement that has already been made in this debate to the effect that the policies of the Department of Agriculture, particularly during
this period of war and leading up to it, have been sound. I believe that when the history . of this period is written, so far as agriculture in this country is concerned, those who are fair-minded will admit that the minister's approach to the general agricultural problems from one end of the country to the other has been sound.
Mr. GR.AY DON: That shows the influence of John Bracken.

In every instance where it has been necessary to deal with specific problems and specific products these problems and products have been dealt with in a reasonable manner. May I point out that at the outbreak of the war all the facilities in this country were jammed full of wheat. Facilities were tied up; there was no apparent place to which to move the wheat, and at the time the sensible thing seemed to be to turn our production from wheat to some other form of production. A demand was undoubtedly coming for live stock products. The minister announced his policy in that regard. I recall that I looked up some figures at one time-I think it was three years ago-with respect to the general feed situation on the North American continent. I found that from the point of view of feeding units per animal unit on the north American continent the tendency was to show a lessening of feed supplies. Now, with the greatly increased live stock production on the north American continent that situation has developed to a much greater extent than any of us thought possible at that time. Therefore the development which has taken place in that regard and the policies carried out by the department have proven to be sound.
I wish to say a word with respect to a matter that is of particular interest at this time, namely research. I notice that my hon. friend, the leader of the opposition, immediately jumped into the debate to make a speech on the necessity of agricultural research. That is all right; that is to be expected; but I am bound to say that I think all hon. members who have taken part in this debate to-night have failed to recognize the research activities that have been earned on by the Department of Agriculture over a long period of time. If they look at the estimates tabled they will find that we have experimental farms, which are largely research, one might say almost entirely so. Science services are largely research. and even under the prairie farm rehabilitation vote there is a great deal of research work undertaken.
That brings me to say one other word with respect to the prairie farm rehabi'itation
Supply-Agriculture

organization. I come back to the very fine speech made a few days ago by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNieol) on reclamation policies for western Canada. I think he might have included in that address some of the wonderful work that has been done under our experimental farm system and under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. I have before me a rough statement which indicates that the number of large projects undertaken in water conservation in the western provinces amount to 64; dug-outs, 14,108; irrigation projects, 785; or a total of all projects of 18,278. I asked the official who gave me this information particularly about the community pastures, and as to the number of live stock that might be provided for in those community pastures. The estimate given was fifty thousand head. I know that in the section of the country from which I come the live stock population would not have increased nearly to the extent it has had it not been for the work done in water conservation, and particularly the development of those small dug-outs on the various farms. I think that applies to a large part of Saskatchewan as well. It certainly applies to a large part of Manitoba. Therefore, hand in hand with the government's policy has been the work carried on under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, particularly with respect to the development of water supplies.
May I return to the question of research? Last year officials of the Department of Agriculture appeared before the agriculture committee and outlined some of the research developments undertaken by the department. I am prepared to say here to-night that I do not think the officials of the Department of Agriculture have been given sufficient credit for the research activities they have carried on. Much of their activity has been linked in with the national research council, and I fear that some of the credit has gone there that more properly could have been directed to the Department of Agriculture. Be that as it may, it is all directed in the proper way. In addition to the matter of research, I do not think anyone connected with the government can start out a research policy and have it completely divorced from the research activities of other similar bodies under other institutes in different parts of the country. We have a vast variety of conditions throughout Canada. All of [DOT] our agricultural colleges and universities are carrying on certain types of research work, particularly applicable to their own communities. That is research work. We hope it may be continued and linked together.
In the discussions taking place to-night it seems that most hon. members in speaking of
[Mr. Weir.l
research have in mind a vastly expanded programme, a programme that will undertake the processing of agricultural products for nonedible purposes and try to develop new uses for them, new methods of preserving them and taking care of them, and perhaps the introduction of new varieties and things of that kind. That is all to the good; and we hope that the minister's efforts in this regard may be fully carried out. I point out in passing that we have a very creditable system of agricultural research activities being carried on at the present time. I recall, looking back over the reports that were secured last year, some of the developments that have taken place during the period of war which, as in many other instances, has given an impetus to things of this kind.
I point particularly to the developments that have taken place in connection with the drying of eggs, a completely new operation which was not carried on in this country to any great extent before the demand of war forced it upon us. That is a brand new development which may completely revolutionize the poultry industry of Canada. The same can be said for the dehydration of fruits and vegetables, particularly potatoes and things of that kind, and the evaporation of milk. All these things mean increased use of agricultural products, and their wider distribution. If our activities can continue along these and other lines, I am sure Canada stands to gain much from research work of this sort.
I want to go on and say a word or two with regard to the speech delivered this afternoon by the hon. member for Yorkton. I do not know what impression he intended to leave with the committee, but I am bound to say that the impression I was given was one of absolute pessimism as far as agriculture in his part of the country was concerned, and I do not believe that is right. If that is the sort of argument he puts forward with respect to conditions in his part of the country, it is no wonder his people are dissatisfied and complaining about matters in general. I do not live so very far from his constituency, when one considers ithe country as a whole, and I am bound to say that the situation in Manitoba is not like that he pictured here this afternoon. In this connection may I refer for a moment to figures recently released showing the cash income of ithe farmers of Canada in 1943. The figure given is 81,396-6 million dollars, the highest on record as far as the agricultural income of this country is concerned. That income is given by provinces, but I shall not take time to place those figures upon record. That was the cash

Supply-*Agriculture
income of agriculture, without any of the bonuses that have been paid through government subsidies or otherwise. Just here I should like to ask the minister if he would be good enough to place on record the various bonuses that have been paid on agricultural products through the various government agencies, for any convenient period of time.

Has the hon. member the percentage that represents of the total national income?
' Mr. WEIR: No; I do not think that is relevant. Again, when the hon. member goes ahead to argue about parity prices in the same breath, I do not think it is fair to take individual items in an attempt to establish parity prices. I believe that when you take individual items you fail to recognize changed production conditions, the introduction of new varieties and things of that kind. But I point out that even in regard to that feature, and having regard to the argument of many hon. members that the parity period is the average for the period from 1926 to 1929, while unfortunately my figures only go up to 1942, still they show that receipts from the sale of farm products for that year, on an index basis, were 112-2. In Manitoba along they were 124-2.
What was the cost of living index?

I can say to my hon. friend that every major agricultural product with the single exception of wheat is at parity or better at the present, time, and that the increase in the prices of agricultural commodities has been in advance of the increase in the cost of living.
I want to go one step farther, having particularly in mind the observations of the hon. member for Yorkton. I hold in my hand a statement, applicable to Manitoba only, dealing with the Winnipeg division of the Canadian farm loan board, showing that first mortgages in arrears on April 1, 1941, totalled: $99,500; on the same date in 1943 such mortgages in arrears totalled only $43,200, while on February 1, 1944, that total had dropped to $14,300. Second mortgages in arrears on April 1, 1941, totalled $149,500; on April 1, 1943, they amounted to $30,100, and on February 1,	1944, they
amounted to $8,500. Moreover, there were only ninety-seven first mortgages in arrears as at February 1, 1044, of which thirty-one were for less than $50, twenty-seven for between $50 and $100, and fifteen for more than $200. At the same date there were forty-four second mortgages in arrears, of which seven were for less than $50, ten for from $50 to $100 and
twelve for more than $200. Between April 1, and' December 1, 1943, 260 first mortgages had been fully repaid, and during the month of January alone there were two mortgages repaid in full for every day of the month including Sundays. I also looked at the record of the land titles offices. I am. sorry that only goes up to 1942, but it shows a continuous improvement in the number of mortgages discharged through those offices in the province of Manitoba. These include mortgages on farms as well as on business and residential property, and the total number so discharged between 1939 and 1942 was 18,367. So that I cannot stand quietly by and ignore a speech such as that made this afternoon by the hon. member for Yorkton, leaving such an impression as he left, while I know the facts as they are shown in the statements I have presented this evening.
Mr. ROSS* (Souris): For years they have had a different government in Manitoba from the one they have had in Saskatchewan.

But you did not do very
much toward helping that government in Manitoba.
Did you?
Why not?

I am, always willing
to reason it out.

There is another feature which my hon. friends appear to like to play up. They try to make the people believe they are the sole supporters of the cooperative movement in this country. As I standi here to-night I take second place to no one in my sympathy for and interest in the cooperative movement. But I suggest to my hon. friends that this movement is not built on a dollars and cents policy alone, or on any advantages it may obtain, from governments or otherwise as compared with other kinds of business. The cooperative movement is more than a business; it is a sentimental affiliation as well. There is an attachment to it; it is a mode of doing business which is entirely different from the ordinary method; but I point out that while hon. gentlemen in the far corner attempt to take credit for their interest in the cooperative movement, that movement has progressed in this country on a very sound and sensible basis, and has done so under the so-called capitalist party system of government. What more does the cooperative movement need in that regard? 1 look back to the time following 1921 when there was established in the Department of Agriculture here a cooperative branch. The men affiliated with that
Supply-Agriculture

branch have constantly given encouragement and assistance to the cooperative movement, and have done much to help build it up to the point it has reached at the present time. So that I hope the time will soon come when our hon. friends will no longer attempt to say they are the only people interested in the cooperative movement.
Is the hon. member in favour of charging the cooperative movement income tax?

That is not part of the discussion at the present time. Is my hon. friend in favour of that?
The hon.. member for Yorkton referred to the farm implement business, and I thought he tried to make out that on account of the unduly high prices of farm implements the farmers of Canada were being exploited. He failed to say that the farm implement business, as does all business in Canada, operates under a price ceiling, and that there has been no increase in prices of agricultural implements during the time of war. I will go this far with my hon. friend and say to him that I believe there is a more economical method of retailing agricultural implements than now obtains. From that I hope the cooperative movement can develop something more economical in merchandising procedure.
Here again, however, I say to the hon. member for Yorkton that if he will go back to the report of 'the farm implements inquiry of 1936, he will find the record shows that the greatest reason for the increase in prices of farm implements was that of increased labour cost.
I want to go one step farther. The hon. member for Melfort by way of interjection referred to his coming back after the last war and buying wheat for seeding purposes. He said that at that time he paid something over $2 a bushel for it, but had to sell it for sixty cents. That just shows how loosely figures are handled. I am not saying he did not have some misfortune with his crop; probably it was frozen or damaged. But I have the fact noted here, and I am bound to say it, that I have before me the average prices by months, and by the year for both 1921, 1922 and other years. I find the lowest price of wheat in the 1922-23 crop year was 99-9 cents a bushel. I realize, of course, that that is basis Fort William-[DOT]
And No. 1.

No doubt the hon. member would be selling at a local point, and he may have had low-grade wheat. But I am
	-
saying to him that he left the impression, so far as the majority of members in the house were concerned, that the Fort William price of wheat for the year was sixty cents a bushel.
No, no.
I have the floor, and I am just saying what the impression would be to a man who did not know what it meant.

I rise to a question of privilege. The hon. member has stated that I had quoted the Fort William price. I was quoting the price at my local point, with respect to wheat sold in the fall of 1920 at my own station. That price was $2.57 a bushel. The price of No. 3 wheat in the fall of 1921 was sixty-seven cents a bushel at that station.	.

My hon. friend says it was sixty cents a bushel. I leave it to hon. members to figure out w'hat they thought the price was set at. I admitted to my hon. friend that perhaps he was quoting the local price, but I am saying that the impression he left in the minds of the majority of members in the house was that he was talking about the Fort William price.

The hon.
member cannot speak for the majority.
And I did not say sixty cents; I said sixty-seven cents.

Then my hearing is faulty, and I regret it. One could go on and say much more with respect to the policy of the Department of Agriculture, and at a later time I hope to have an opportunity to do so.
Before taking my seat, however, I should like to suggest to the minister some of the possibilities of recent new developments in the field of agriculture. Particularly in Manitoba we have seen a wide diversification in respect of such crops as black-eyed rape, soya beans, sunflowers and, of course, corn, which has been grown with considerable success in southern Manitoba for some time. I believe all those crops have a future, and I am hoping further attention will be given to them.
The main point, however, with respect to such crops as sunflowers and, to some extent, rape seed, is the development of what are known as expelling plants, so that the oil may be extracted more readily. These are bulky products, and it seems unfortunate they have to be moved to eastern Canada for further processing. Having regard to post-war development and to the need for such products, I suggest to the minister that there should be greater diversification in the form of local

S apply

Agriculture
industries in western Canada, and that particular attention should be given to processing plants for these new crops. I think further that the present situation in respect of the meat and live stock industry affords opportunity for the establishing of a general policy which would have for its purpose the development of quick-freezing plants, and other improvements of that kind, so that our products could be utilized to greater extent locally, and further processed. I believe the west needs something of that kind as much as it needs anything, and I am hoping the minister will use his influence to see that in any research activities consideration might be given to offering further assistance in the development of local processing plants for specialized crops in western Canada.
Madam Chairman-
Madam Chairman-
I saw the hon. member for Qu'Appelle.

The ladies generally see me. To-day when the item was first called I suggested that the minister might facilitate matters by making a general statement covering most of the items in a general way. He did not see fit to do so, but I think he will now agree with me that it would have been better if that course had been followed1-with the exception, of course, of those estimates contained in the war appropriation measure.
I would say the discussion has got almost out of bounds. We have heard members from different parts of Canada discussing almost everything one could imagine. One would have thought that part of the time we were discussing the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce, because we heard a great deal about wheat shipments, wheat prices, wheat board activities, participation certificates, the international food conference, and matters of that kind. One could have gained the impression that two or three departments were before the committee at one time. I will agree that there are some parts of the Departs ment of Trade and Commerce which might better be handled- by the Department of Agriculture-and in saying that I believe I am paying the Minister of Agriculture a compliment. I refer particularly to the production of grains, and their marketing on the domestic markets. Possibly some time in the not too distant future we shall see a consolidation of those two departments.
This evening we listened to one or two stirring speeches. The hon. member for Moose Jaw came to the rescue of the minister. He seems to be the pinch-hitter, so to speak, for the minister, and the Minister of Agriculture
seems to be the pinch-hitter for the government. Whenever the government needs to have a speech of that kind delivered, he is generally the one called upon to make it. The hon. member for Moose Jaw, together with the hon. member for Macdonald came to the rescue of the minister, but there is not very much to reply to in what they said.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw referred to the fact that a price of $1.25 a bushel had been set in September. He said that that was a pretty good price, and I agree, but it might well have been set much earlier. That price could have been set in July. The government had all the information as to what was likely to happen, they knew they were going to do it, and they could have saved some of the discussion that has taken place to-night in connection with the farmer delivering to the open market had they set the price in July. If that had been done, all the 1943 crop would have gone to the wheat board. The hon. member for Moose Jaw came to the defence of the packing plants, and he tried to give credit to the Minister of Agriculture for the increase in prices. He said that these advances were due to the policies of the minister. However, I think he has been answered by some of the hon. members to my extreme right who mentioned the fact that the war had brought about this condition. No matter who was Minister of Agriculture, we would be getting better prices for our farm products to-day. I think the farmer should be given credit for the way in which he has changed his methods of production, his system of farming so to speak, in order to meet the need.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw was most encouraging when he forecast that there would be . prosperity for the next twenty-five years. I hope he is right and perhaps he can see farther into the future than most of us. But if we have that prosperity I am afraid he will not be around to give credit to the present government. Before many years we shall have another government and, if we have the prosperity he forecasts, it will be some other government that will get the credit.
The hon. member for Macdonald made a very good speech, with much of- which I agree. I do not take a back seat to anyone as far as farming experience is concerned. I started out in 1900, and in 1906 my brother and I produced 65,000 bushels of grain. We have not done that very often since, but that was a good production for that time. We were forced to build an elevator in order to accommodate our crop, and we got into that business. I learned a lot about the elevator business from 1906 on. I might say also that along with many other farmers in the west I made a few trades; I bought a few

ms
options. At times I traded in a certain office with which the hon. member for Moose Jaw was connected for a time. There were lots of brokers in those days and many farmers gained a lot of experience.
Was the hon. member for Moose Jaw a broker?

I leave that for him to answer. The hon. member for Macdonald made some very sound statements. To-day the farmers in the west are better off financially than they were three or four years ago. I know that from my own experience. I am not a calamity howler; I do not believe in standing up and giving the people of Canada the impression that the farmers are all down and out. But our farmers should have had better prices years ago, better even than what has been received this last year. I have maintained right along that we should have a broader basis for all farm products. I do not want to repeat, but I do think the farmers are entitled to a better price.
The initial price of $1.25 a bushel could easily have been made $1.40. The hon. member for Moose Jaw referred to what has happened within the last three or four days. We understand that 175,000,000 bushels of wheat are going to the United States at a price considerably above the initial price. Then we know what the British farmer is receiving for his grain. So that I say that our farmers are justified in asking for a better price. All they want is a square deal. We should be getting a parity price. As the hon. member for Macdonald says, we are getting parity prices for everything but wheat. Give us a parity price and we shall be fairly well satisfied, but give us that price for a term of years, not just for one year.
Both hon. members referred to the benefits derived from the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. I should like to ask who initiated that legislation, who made those benefits possible in Saskatchewan? The hon. member for Moose Jaw cannot recall, but I think the hon. member for Macdonald will because he was sitting back here somewhere when that act went through this house. The Minister of Pensions 8nd National Health, the hon. member for Wood Mountain and other hon. members will recall the opposition there was at that time to the bill. That legislation was passed to create water storage and furnish supplies of water to parts of Saskatchewan which were what one might call deserts. I take considerable credit for the fact that that legislation was initiated by the government I had the honour to support from 1930 to 1935.
We are supposed to be discussing the minister's estimates in a general way, but we seem

to have got far afield. I would not have been so far afield had it not been for the two or three speeches we have heard. I have been waiting to hear thd minister give a reply to the one or two speeches which seem to have caused so much irritation on the part of the two hon. members. These estimates are practically the same as we had last year. There is a reduction of about $43,000 in the main estimates, and then when the specials come down there will be a reduction of $28,000,000. This reduction has been referred to already. The minister has stated that in th6 agriculture part of the war appropriation there is a provision which he does not want to have discussed while we are discussing the main estimates.
Later on, supplementary estimates will be brought down. It is possible the minister may be going out to Saskatchewan during the Easter recess, or he may have occasion to go a little sooner if certain developments out there require his presence. I understand that certain things have been suggested in the Saskatchewan legislature and that there is to be a rebate or write-off of the seed grain debts where they have been paid to the extent of $4,000,000. There will have to be supplementary estimates to take care of that, as well as other items about which we do not know.
The speech from the throne referred to certain measures that will be introduced in connection with floor prices. There is no question that the Minister of Agriculture will play a very important part in any legislation dealing with agricultural matters, and in this respect he can have a considerable say to ensure that justice is done as far as having a price somewhere near parity, or a just price, the floor price. There are 138.700 farmers in Saskatchewan-the third largest number of any province in the dominion. All our Saskatchewan farmers want, as I have said, is a square deal. They have not had their proper proportion of the national farm income. If they can be assured of it by the establishing of a floor price, and it is on a parity basis, I think it will be fairly well received, provided that it extends over a term of years so that they will have the assurance of some security.
Much has been said about cooperative organizations. The hon. member for Macdonald became quite heated in his remarks on this subject in reply to members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party. I do not find any fault with them on this score; I think they are on sound ground when they plead for fair treatment of all cooperative organizations. We have some in Saskatchewan. I think all credit and assistance possible should be extended by the government to these organizations if they are

Supply-Agriculture
properly operated. Having some knowledge of their accomplishments, I say that they have been marvellous, and any government should give them all possible assistance to carry on that sort of work. Nobody has more experience of the workings of this kind of organization as it pertains to agriculture than the farmers themselves, and on behalf of our
138,000	Saskatchewan producers, a great -many of whom belong to cooperative organizations, I make a special plea that they be given every assistance possible, and hope that the minister will be just in that respect.
-It is also my hope that the minister will give consideration to setting up a board of live stock commissioners. The time has arrived when such a body could do a lot of good. It should, of course, include proper representation of the producers, because no one knows better than they do what is just and proper in these matters. Such a- board could do a lot for the marketing of live stock products at the present time. We need enlarged markets; we want to create a demand for agricultural products, including the expansion of the home market. I believe a live stock marketing board could do much in that direction.
I believe it was the hon. member for Macdonald who referred this evening to diversified farming. We have to consider some policy which will diversify farming operations in western Canada. There is great room for it. Many more people could be gjven employment and established on farms if the system were more diversified. I need only cite my own case. Last year we had only two men on our farm: a farmer and his son operating a combine harvesting fifteen or sixteen thousand bushels of grain. Do you not think that, by a system whereunder other products than grain were grown there, many more people could be employed, real farm homes established, and adequate facilities for farm life created, with lasting benefits to agriculture? It -is something to kee-p in mind.
There are other matters which can be discussed later, item by item, but I have one short reference to make at this time. Last year-the hon. member for Macdonald might listen to this-the agriculture committee met long after the house opened; we heard from a good many chairmen of boards and officials of departments; and we western members were asked to give way to the eastern members. They said they had heard too much about the west, about wheat and other grain, and they blamed this condition on two or three C.C.F. members of the committee and myself in particular. They said "Forget about wheat and so on this year and let us
have a chance." We did it, and did it gracefully, but I will say that we had to come to their rescue quite often to keep the thing going properly. With all due respect to the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) who is sitting in front of me, we knew as much about eastern farmers' problems-producing the same products that they do in eastern Canada-as the eastern members themselves. However, we had a very interesting time, because we heard such a variety of witnesses and evidence. We drew a report on July 16, 19 and 20, and then we did not have the courage to rise and move its adoption, although we had advocated many of the things which have been advocated here to-night, such as research laboratories and so on.
The minister must have read the report, then.
Maybe he did, but the chairman of the committee did not have the courage to rise in his place and move that it be adopted.
That was not the only report which was not moved.
That just shows you.
What is the point?

What is the use of members going to work for two or three months and drawing up a report, leaving it until the last day or two, and then not moving the adoption of the result of all that work? What is the use of taking up our time?
You learn something. You just admitted that you learned a lot.

The chairman did not even move the adoption of the recommendations. I have the report in my hand; it contains several sections.	I myself moved three
amendments of the report. Two of them were turned down and not put in the report, but the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce have adopted them
They knew a good thing when they saw it.
The hon. member knew what was coming up.

Therefore I hope the Minister of Agriculture will insist on this committee getting to work in good time. We can gather much more information similar to what we had last year, carry on from there, and do some useful work.

To get back to these estimates: the details of the items on page 4 are given on pages 54. 55 and 56 and pages following. I grant that there is not much change since last year except under "special"; but if you examine these pages you will see a large item, for travelling expenses, set out at the end of each section. For example, "publicity and extension, travelling expenses, $5,000"; "departmental administration, travelling expenses, $8,000"; "science service, travelling expenses, $900"; "animal and poultry pathology, travelling expenses, $4,000"; "bacteriology and dairy research, travelling expenses, SI ,300' ; "botany and plant pathology, travelling expenses, $15,500". In one division, namely entomology, travelling expenses are shown as over $39,000. I contend that in every branch the travelling expenses are absolutely out of all reason and could be curtailed to a very considerable extent.
I have the auditor general's report here and the figures with. regard to the P.F,R.A. are illuminating. It gives the number of men employed, field men, and so on. In one branch there are 281 and in another branch 300, and the expenses run from $300 to $1,800, besides salaries.
Many are part-time men.

prairie farm assistance.

and the expenses are given. Then there is the wheat acreage reduction outfit. They have a large expense account running from $300 to $2,000.
