by item I shall have something to say. In the meantime I think the minister should answer some of the questions that have been put to him to-night.

I am not a parliamentarian
but a dirt farmer. I am not familiar with the rules of the house and I want to take this opportunity, while the discussion is broad, to say what I have to say. Listening to some of the bon. gentlemen who have already spoken, I was reminded of the fact that I am an immigrant to this country. I read' a book that brought me to this country, and when I heard the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) I thought he was the author. Then when I heard the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Wood)
I thought the book might have come from Ontario. But when my hon. friend the member for Macdonald (Mr. Weir) rises in his place and says the same things, I know it was the Liberal party.
Are you sorry you are here?
You didma go back.

I never made enough to go
back.
I have tried many times to become better acquainted with the Minister of Agriculture, and in fact on one occasion I drove 200 miles to make his acquaintance and to ask him some questions, but I had to be satisfied with a shake of his hand. He expressed his sorrow that he could not spend any more time with me. In the house a few days ago the Minister of Agriculture talked about how well off we were in Canada-in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and other provinces engaged in mixed farming. I should like to call the attention of the Minister of Agriculture to a few facts. I could take steers I sold in Winnipeg for Ilf cents a pound and send them to St. Paul and make $35 dollars more on each of them. I could run steers to St. Paul for seventy cents a hundred and the exchange in my money would pay the duty.
Talking about cattle, I want to ask the minister why he always argues that I do not need a spread in feeding my steers. When I buy a steer I want a spread on it. I want a two cent spread to enable me to break even. To take simple figures, we will say that the feeder market is ten cents. If I buy a steer of 700 lbs. at ten cents, that is $70. I have to put 300 pounds on his back before I can put him back on the market, and that will take me 180 days. I do not know whether other farmers can do better than that, but that is the best I can do. That steer will eat two tons of hay which, at $7.50

Supply-Agriculture
a ton, means $15 added to the $70. When I take that animal home he will eat five pounds of chop a day, and when I put him away he will have increased that to fifteen pounds a day. However, suppose we strike a happy medium and say ten pounds a day; that means he will eat 1,800 pounds of chop. I can get $1.25 per 100 pounds for my grain at the elevator and another twenty-five cents to crush it and handle it. That comes to $1.50, so that you have to add another $27. To keep him in good shape and put a good shine on his coat I have to give him oil cake meal, and he will use fifty pounds in those 180 days. He will need bone-meal and salt. Put on $1 for that and the steer has cost me $114.25. If I sell him on a twelve cent market at Winnipeg I will get $120. I have only $5.75 left for transportation, commission, insurance, labour and depreciation on my buildings. I want to ask the minister how that can be done without a spread. I can buy cattle in the spring at ten cents and sell at ten cents - and make more money feeding them grass, because I do not feed them inside. I want the minister to answer these questions.
I want to say something about hogs too. In the new regulations we are to get $27.45 for select hogs, $3 premium paid by the government. On a "B-l" hog we will get $26.45, a $2 premium. We are to get S23.45 for a "B-2" hog, which is a dollar reduction. I should like to know why there should be this dollar reduction. A "B-l" hog is a light hog, a hog that the packer is willing to pay more money for because when you go into a restaurant and ask for pork chops you do not get them off a 200-pound hog, you get them off a hog dressing around 120 to 135 pounds. If this is a penalty or a fine to the farmer for selling a light hog, why put it into the pocket of the packer? Why not give it to the Red Cross? A "B-2" hog will bring $23.45; a "C-l", $22.95; a "D-l", $22.45. These five grades can go into the export trade, or at least a part of them. There are eight different grades from the producer to the packer. There are twenty-four grades from the packer to the meat board, and from the meat board to the British food ministry there are two grades "A" and "B". If the hog that I produce is fit for export bacon I should get that export bacon price for it. The way it stands to-day it is to the advantage of the packer, not the farmer.
I should like to make another comparison. There is only an imaginary line between Manitoba and that portion of the United States situated to the south of it. The United States farmer raises hogs and sells them at from 200 to 300 weight. His hogs average 250 pounds. We have all these penalties on
this side of the line. If I get a hog up to 200 pounds, I can put from two and a half to three pounds a day on him. He will make very rapid gains at this weight. The United States farmer is paid $26.90 for his hog, and he has the extra weight. If you follow this hog along you will find that it could go to the same packing company as the Canadian hog and they are both sold to the British market at the same price. Because of the way grading is set up now, only about thirty per cent are select hogs. This new grading puts a penalty on the average producer. I am not satisfied with the new system. The hon. minister knows that. I have made quite a study of this problem. The man who grades a hog has only six seconds in which to do it. He has to satisfy himself that it is twenty-nine inches from the hip bone to the shoulder bone, that there is no more than two inches of fat on the shoulder. There has to be no more than one and a half inches on the loin and a little less on the hips. These hogs pass steadily before the grader. I have timed them repeatedly and the time is six seconds. I claim that is one of the reasons why when I send a lot of hogs in and the returns come back I get nine or ten selects, and from the very same boar and the same brood sows I get only two the next time. There is something wrong with the system. I have spoken to one of the big packers about it. He says that if he cannot kill 500 hogs an hour he will shut down his plant, Let us get two graders in there and give the farmer a square deal.
Another serious grievance that I should like to mention is the price of grain. There is a subsidy on grain. When a man is feeding his own grain he does not get that. I should like the Minister of Agriculture to do something about that, because unless that position is cleared up there will be fewer hogs by October. I know throughout my own settlement people are not going to feed the grain. It is at a good price, and they will not feed it to the hogs when they can get the price for it. I know arrangements have been made whereby a man who is feeding hogs can go and get the bonus back, but the man who produces the grain is not getting the benefit of that.
The hon. member for Macdonald spoke about the experimental farms. I have received quite a lot of benefit from them, but there is one thing I should like to say here. If those experimental farms could be brought more in line with the conditions that the average farmer has to face in producing his hogs they would be more educational. Hogs are raised by the agricultural college in Winnipeg, but they are pampered hogs. You
Supply-Agriculture

could not work in the field all day and give hogs care like that. If we had conditions on these experimental farms similar to. those on the average farm a better comparison could be made. I had the pleasure of taking one of my constituents around the agricultural college. I said to him, "How would you like this, or what would you do with it?" He said: "The wife and I would move in right away." The conditions to which I have referred must be improved so that they will be of some benefit to the rank and file in the country.
I should like to say to the hon. members who have spoken that I have not been one of fortune's favoured few since I came to this country. I sold hogs in some of these good years for S2.65 a hundred. I sold steers for two and a half cents a hundred.
The Tories were in then.

You are all tarred with the one brush. I sold butterfat for twelve cents a pound. If we wanted a packet of matches we sent two dozen eggs to the store. Do not forget that. We had twelve years of that.

I was very much interested in the remarks made by the hon. member for Selkirk, a Scotsman with a Scotch tongue. I know he knows something about cattle, because I come from a Scotch constituency. These people came out from Scotland many years ago and settled in what I think is the best riding in Ontario, that of West Middlesex. There we have some of the best cattle feeders in the Dominion of Canada. In the little village of Ailsa Craig, near where I live, there were more cattle shipped out in the old days than anywhere else in Canada with the exception of the city of Calgary, Alberta. The coming of the trucks interfered with that shipment and we have not been able to keep up that record for that point. After listening to the remarks made by my hon. friend with respect to cattle and the feeding of cattle, I say in all sincerity that a Scotch farmer knows how to feed steers. I think the hon. member for Selkirk knows something about it. I agree with the hon. member that it is impossible for feeders to go out and buy cattle unless there is some spread, though the producer who fattens that steer is all right with the prices we are receiving to-day. In the district from which I come, however, where the producers depend upon the feeders to buy up these stockers in the fall, feed them during the winter and sell them in the spring or summer, we believe there must be a spread. At the present time the spread is not as great as it should be, TMr. Bryce. |
but the feeders of cattle in my district are going ahead., believing that they will receive a good price for their product during the coming summer.
I must admit that there is a little consternation at the present time among the cattle feeders and those who have steers to sell, because the packing houses in Toronto, where we in western Ontario sell our steers, have sort of lain down and are not buying. The drovers who buy cattle from the farmers and ship to the Toronto market are having difficulty in selling their cattle; as one of the commission men claimed, if the offerings were light, say, only two hundred head of cattle, the prices would remain just the same. On that market there seems to be a tendency on the part of the packers-I may not be right in this, though I believe I am-to reduce the price of cattle. Hon. members may wonder why I say that. Well, the government has told us that if the packers reduce the price below the floor price, then the producer or feeder can send in his cattle to be slaughtered and the government will take care of it. I quote what the secretary of the meat board said last year to the committee on agriculture: "We are giving some consideration to one system which might be adopted, based upon the fact that on almost every main market there are public slaughter houses. If a producer of cattle felt that the prices offered by the packers were not fair, under this system we would be prepared to have these cattle slaughtered at these public slaughter houses." That is something we in western Ontario fear. We feel that the packer to-day is endeavouring to force the producer or feeder to send his cattle in so that they may be slaughtered on a rail-grading basis, and that is one thing we do not want. The cattlemen of my district, at any rate, will not stand for that. We will not have the rail-grading of cattle, and I hope and trust that at the proper time the government will step in and see that this is not made necessaiy. I have every faith that this will be done.
There is one thing in connection with the shipment of cattle to the stock yards that has often bothered me, and perhaps the minister can enlighten me in this regard. When a drover ships cattle there is condemnation insurance kept off the price. I think that insurance varies in different parts of Canada, but it runs into several hundred thousand dollars every year. The producers had nothing to say about that; the condemnation insurance is collected under an agreement between the packers and drovers which dates back to 1910 and which is still in effect. In Ontario the rate is twenty cents a head on steers and fifty cents on cows, while in the west it is

Supply-Agriculture
one-half of one per cent. In the United States there is no condemnation insurance. I should like to know if the packers ever gave an accounting of that money, which came out of the drovers and producers in the first place. Perhaps the minister can explain that to me.
I am completely in agreement with what has been said regarding the movement of cattle across the line into the United States. No one could be more in favour of that than I am. I am a free trader; I believe in the free movement of goods from Canada to the United States and back again. I hope the day is not too far distant when our cattle may once more move across that line to the stockyards and packing-houses in Chicago, St. Paul, Buffalo and other cities.
And not only cattle.

No; at the moment I am only referring to cattle, but it applies to other products as well. At the present time, however, that may not be possible; if we need the meat in Canada, or if the mother country needs it, we are in duty bound to send it where it is needed. I think it is the feeling of all Canadian cattlemen that if Britain needs the meat they are willing to take their loss and send it over there. But again I express the hope that the day may not be too far distant when our cattle will move freely across the line once more.
One thing to which we in the eastern part of Canada object strenuously is the freight bonus paid to the packer on dressed meat coming from the west. We in Ontario feel very much incensed about this, when our own stockyards and packing houses are not able to take care of the cattle coming on to the markets here. We feel that this bonus should be removed. It was taken off once, but was restored later on. I believe that no class of people in this country have done a better job than has been done by the farmers. They are always willing to do their part. I will admit that in the early days of the war prices were not as good as they should have been, but now those prices have reached a level where I believe most of the people are satisfied. I realize that we are all human and that we like to get the highest possible prices for our farm products, but I feel that the majority of Canadian farmers are satisfied. There may be some inequalities, but they will be looked after.
In southwestern Ontario, from which I come, we are getting more and more into diversified farming, and there is one product on which we are now counting a great deal. I refer to the growing of turnips, which is being done by a great many farmers in that district. We are able to ship them under permit across 100-43
the line, but I think a great deal could be done to increase the market in the United States. I believe an educational programme should be carried on throughout the length and breadth of both Canada and the United States to promote the consumption of -turnips, because I feel that this product offers a great future for many Canadian farmers. The same may be said of beans and other products, of course; but if you go to the United States and ask some of the leading people there, they will tell you they have never tasted turnips. If you go to Philadelphia, AVashington or New York you will find that turnips are not even on the menus of the leading hotels, so that I believe a great deal could be done by way of an educational programme in regard to certain of these farm products. I want to repeat in all sincerity that no group in Canada is more willing to do its part, under great difficulties through lack of help, than Canadian farmers, who will do everything possible to see that this war is brought to a successful conclusion.

A few moments ago the hon. member for Qu'Appelle made some reference to the expense accounts of officials of my department, and the hon. member for Wey-burn made some references to my own expense account. I desire to give the same explanation in connection with the expense accounts of the minister and those of the inspectors and officials of the department. As hon. members know, this country extends from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and in each province there is a considerable agricultural area. As long as I could satisfy the Prime Minister of this country that I ought to remain as Minister of Agriculture I could hold down the position much more easily by remaining here and simply administering the department from my office. But I venture to say that while there has been criticism to-night of some things that have or have not been done in the department, if I had been in the Department of Agriculture-as I have been for eight years -and had never gone out through this country in order to learn at first hand what the problems of the farmers are, there would have been a great deal more criticism than there has been up to the present time. That is the only explanation I wish to make in connection with the expense accounts, so far as my own expense account is concerned. Incidentally, it has been throughout those whole eight years one of the highest expense accounts among ministers of the government, and I am rather proud of that fact. The nature of the department requires that from time to time I visit all of the activities which have been spoken about to-night, and concerning some of which some kind things have been said.

Supply-Agriculture

For example, the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act administration is scattered throughout the southern part of the three prairie provinces. Many of the activities connected with fruit production are carried out in British Columbia, in the maritime provinces or in the southern part of Ontario. Activities in connection with stock raising, generally, are carried on throughout the whole length and breadth of the Dominion of Canada. Anyone who desires to become familiar at first hand with the problems of the farmers, and the people who deal with them, must of necessity from time to time and, indeed, quite often more than once in a year, visit the different parts of Canada to understand the problems confronting the farmers in the different seasons of the year. Therefore I make no apology whatsoever for having an expense account of $2,600 for 1942.
Having said that, may I add that there is no inspector in the Department of Agriculture who is inspecting agricultural activities throughout the rural areas who would be worth his salt if he did not have a high expense account. His work is to travel, and if he does not travel and see what is going on on the farms throughout the country, and make his inspections at first hand, then I say he is not doing the job for which he was employed. Generally speaking, a good man on the road spends at least as much on his expense account as he receives in salary-and quite often he is required to spend more than that. So that I make no apologies for the expense accounts found in the estimates for this year. I only compare them with what has been spent in preceding years under all governments, in provinces as well as in the dominion, and I suggest that our expense account will compare favourably with those for similar work, no matter where that work is carried on.
There has been some discussion to-night with regard to hogs. The hon. member for Moose Jaw and the hon. member for Macdonald called attention to the fact that it is very easy to make statements respecting one's personal experiences, or based upon statements heard here and there throughout the country, and it is possible to make the complaints sound plausible. But when one gets down to actual statistics having to do with the matter under discussion he sometimes finds a picture very different from that which the general statement would lead one to believe.
For example, a few moments ago the hon. member for Selkirk left the impression that a great many hogs grading other than "A" and "B-l" entered into the export of bacon
IMr. Gardiner.!
and hams from Canada. I have in my hand the last statement which came out dealing with the preceding week in connection with the marketing of hogs, and it is a statement which would be borne out by any week one might wish to choose throughout the year. This is what it says:
Hog marketings eased off somewhat in the week ended February 12, showing a decrease of approximately 10,000 head below the previous week; nevertheless the increase over the same week last year was more than 125,000 head.
That is, we are down 10,000 in the week ending February 12, as compared with the previous week; 'but we are up 12)5,000 head as compared writh the same week in the preceding year. The statistical statement continues:
In the week ended February 12, exporting plants slaughtered 224,763 head
Is it not a fact that "B-3's" and "C-l's" can go into export bacon?

"B-3's" may, but not
"C-l's". The fact that they can go in is not proving that they do go in.
Where do the hogs go?
If my hon. friend will read the agreement which was made with Great Britain he will find that if "B-3's" do go in they do not bring the same price, either to the packer or to anyone else.
Is it not a fact that when a carload of hogs is graded at shipboard they pick out one or two bales and that satisfies the inspector that it is export bacon?

I have only five minutes and perhaps my hon. friend will permit me to answer the question. I have not the privilege of being a Scotsman although my ancestors came from Scotland, but I think any Scotsman coming from Scotland will know that no inspector is going to take every bale out of a shipload and make individual inspection. If he did that, the bacon, would never get out of the country.
With regard to cattle, my hon. friend says that he needs a margin in order to produce steers during the winter time. I am not going to argue that question with him, but I should like to tel! him that there is not ten per cent of the beef produced in this country that is produced in commercial, feed lots or from cattle purchased from someone in the manner described by the hon. member for Selkirk and converted into beef.
Then I can sell my grain.

Ninety per cent of the beef produced in this country is produced by people who breed live stock, who raise their own grain to feed to that live stock. What I have said since the beginning of the war' and what I continue to say is that we are not going to get a proper policy upon which to handle ninety per cent of the beef produced in this country if that policy is based upon the needs of the people who undertake the commercial feeding of cattle. My hon. friends across the way try to leave the impression that I am just a poor schoolteacher who never farmed.
Supply-Agriculture
Not a poor school teacher.

I can go into the Moose Jaw or Regina market and buy a steer in competition with any hon. member over there and pay at least one cent a pound more than he can afford to pay if he is a commercial feeder. I can take that steer to my farm and feed my own grain and make more money than he can. That is the reason why commercial feeders are not able to buy cattle on the market under the present condition. They are not able to get them because the farmer, the man who produces his own live stock, the man who produces his own grain, the man who carries the whole operation right through, can do the job at a lesser cost and make more money than the chap who goes into it in the other way. He can buy a few steers and put them in with his own and take the cattle away from the commercial feeder.
I know there are fellows who live outside large cities like Winnipeg who pride themselves upon being farmers, but they spend most of their time in Winnipeg sitting on boards of one kind or another. They boast considerably about what they are able to do. Probably they can go on to the market and buy some of the poorer fed cattlfe, cattle which are well bred but which were not fed before they were sent in; they can pick them up at a low price and freeze out the farmer in the country who sent them in and who did not know just exactly what he was doing. They can take them out, buy some grain, feed them, take them back in and make some profit. But one reason why that is becoming less possible is that we have our inspectors and our agronomists going around the country advising farmers how to finish their stock, how to feed them, how to put them on the market in the proper form.
Some of our hon. friends who are connected with farm organizations would be doing a better job for the farmer if they were to advocate the setting up of local markets into which a farmer could go to purchase cattle before they are ppt on trains and shipped hundreds of miles to a central market. After reaching the central market they are then shipped fifty, sixty or 100 miles to be finished, and the shipping costs and the cost of feeding are added before the cattle get back on the market again. Markets should be organized in different areas so that the farmer who has not sufficient grain to finish all the cattle he has can take them to that market in order that some neighbouring farmer who has the grain may buy them and feed them.
{Mr. Gardiner.]
The next time my estimates come up I am going to place on Hamard a letter written by a farmer in my constituency which I read in a newspaper a short time ago. I am not sure but that he was a Scotsman. He said that he could give some lessons on feeding to some farmers who talk like some hon. members in this house who talk about farming. He knew they w'ould be very helpful. For instance, he said that he raised and fed two pigs for $25, and sold them for $25 each. Then he says that he takes steers, just the same as my hon. friend said he did, weighs them, weighs the feed, feeds them and puts 200 pounds on them in less than six months.
I said 300 pounds.

After he had fed the steers he made 81.25 a bushel on his oats. I would rather listen to stories of that kind than listen to the kind of stories we have heard to-night coming from men who claim they know all about feeding live stock, men who spend their time going around the country telling farmers how they ought to run their farms and how hard up all the farmers are. I would rather listen to farmers who are home farming. They have spent their time feeding cattle and feeding hogs and growing grain with which to feed them, and then they have seen to it that they are marketed at the! proper time and thus have secured the highest possible returns for them.
Item stands.
Progress reported.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Monday, February 21, 1944
The house, met at three o'clock.

subtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT ON TUESDAYS UNTIL FOLLOWING THURSDAY

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT ON TUESDAYS UNTIL FOLLOWING THURSDAY
speechtext: That when the house adjourns on Tuesday, the 22nd instant, it stand adjourned until Thursday, the 24th instant; and, unless otherwise ordered, when the house adjourns on Tuesday evenings, it stand adjourned until the following Thursday, and that standing order 2 be suspended in relation thereto for the present session.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT ON TUESDAYS UNTIL FOLLOWING THURSDAY
speechtext:
When the Prime Minister mentioned on Friday his intention of introducing this motion I was of the opinion that, under

Wednesday Adjournments
the rules of the house, the motion was one that required the usual notice, and subsequent inquiries, I think, have substantiated that view. The Prime Minister, however, was good enough in any event to allow the matter to stand over until to-day for discussion.
The question raised by this motion is one that goes perhaps a little farther than its phraseology would indicate. So far as our party is concerned, we are opposing the motion, and we do so after very careful consideration of its merits and demerits. May I indicate some of the reasons why we have arrived at that conclusion.
I think it will be readily apparent that there is need in this house for a better division of the average private member's time. If our party were of the opinion that this motion would in some way contribute to that end. we should be of course more inclined to give it favourable consideration; but when it is proposed that we should suspend sittings on Wednesday, many points naturally occur to one's mind as to the advisability of such a change. In the first place, I believe that Wednesday will be generally regarded by the members of the house, putting it on a comparative basis, as a particularly active parliamentary day. Coming in the middle of the week, it is a day on which the business of the house is usually given great care and attention, and that is not to reflect upon any other day on which we sit. It does seem to me that to take Wednesday out of the week, as this motion would do, even for the express purpose indicated by the Prime Minister, namely, to enable the committees to meet instead of the house, would be a backward rather than a forward step, if we have in mind the expedition of the work of the House of Commons.
In support of that contention, when we speak of the committees utilizing Wednesday for their sittings while the sittings of the house itself are suspended, I would point out that for years-I do not know whether there is any special1 reason for it-the committees in the main have not made use of their Mondays and Fridays to the full. While therefore that is the situation it does seem to me that there is a very strong argument against taking away one of the principal days of our sittings and utilizing it for committee work until at least the committees have found that the time allotted to their operations, from Monday until Friday night, has been entirely filled. That, I think, is one of the matters which the government ought to consider seriously before suspension of these sittings takes place.
There is another reason which must not be lost sight of, although I do not place
special emphasis upon it. Since the government has asked private members to suspend the initiation of such matters as are normally introduced by them, it is not in the public interest to take away another three hours of an important day in the week when private members can have these deliberations.
Nor is it sufficient for the Prime Minister to indicate in introducing this motion that we are getting three hours' on Friday evening. That is hardly in accordance with the fact., and although I know the Prime Minister was not making a special point of it, I want to clear it up in case it is in anybody's mind. There is no justification for our not sitting on Friday night, because that period is always available, according to the rules, for the house to sit. That is to say, we do not depart from any custom when we sit on Friday nights, and it should be our regular habit to do so, particularly in time of war. So that what we are really doing is taking three hours off our regular weekly sessions, st a time when, I believe, the public expect this parliament to give a full week's attention to a full week's job. For these reasons I trust the Prime Minister and the government will reconsider this proposal.
I now come to a consideration which is important from the point of view of the government, but not of parliament. We may as well face the fact that one of the main reasons why the suspension of Wednesday afternoon sittings is sponsored by the government is that the cabinet finds itself at certain times very much overworked. I am not going to dwell upon that, but I suggest, before the Prime Minister decides we should give up these important three hours, that he might well give thought to a reorganization of his ministry. I say this in the most kindly and friendly spirit. I notice two ministers applauding; I hope the Prime Minister does not see either of them, for I am bound to say that I do not think the work of the cabinet ministers is very equitably divided, if we on this side are in any position to judge. I am not reflecting on any cabinet minister, but there are some ministers who work very hard and others who do not have any more, to say the least, than enough work to do. That being the view, I believe, of parliament and the country, it seems to me that some way should be found whereby the cabinet's work could be so apportioned that it could spare enough men io handle Wednesday afternoon sittings to the satisfaction of the house, the government and the public.
Here is another strange thing. Last year seven parliamentary assistants were appointed, and we were asked to vote money for the
IFednesday Adjournments

purpose. My understanding was that this step was taken to relieve ministers in their parliamentary work. It was stated quite freely, I believe, in this chamber, that these men were not to be simply glorified deputy ministers, but were to be parliamentary assistants, as their title implies. Some very good men have been appointed, and I do not intend to criticize any of them. What I do criticize is the system under which they are operating. We have not noticed that to any great extent they have taken the places of ministers, except on very rare occasions, in debates in the house. Seldom does it happen that ministers are not here just as they were before, answering questions. It seems strange therefore that if pressure of work on the cabinet is the reason for suspending Wednesday afternoon sittings, the change was not proposed before these parliamentary .assistants were appointed. On this point I come back to the question of distribution of work in the cabinet. I do not want to make any reflection on the Minister of Justice, or to contrast his work witli that of the Minister of Agriculture. But it has always been an open question to us why, for instance, the Minister of Justice should have a parliamentary assistant. If he needs one I have no objection; both he and his parliamentary assistant are held in very high esteem and regard in this house. Anything I say is directed against the system rather than against those who hold the positions. But there does not seem to be much argument about this, that if the Minister of Justice needs a parliamentary assistant, the Minister of Agriculture, who has a tremendous burden to carry, should also have one. I mention this so that the whole problem of the distribution of government work may engage the attention of the Prime Minister from now on.
Further, if Wednesday is set aside as a day for committee meetings only, there arise such questions as provision of rooms and staff for the committees, and whether the committees will sit all through the week. More particularly this point must be in the minds of hon. members. Before the special committee on rules and procedure have held more than two sittings, this announcement is made. It seems to me that the government might have referred to that committee the question of Wednesday afternoon sittings in order that we might have expert advice as to how it would fit in with the general scheme of changes in rules and procedure which may be recommended to the house.
If a better system of expedition and dispatch in the work of the house can be devised, I am all in favour of it, and so is our party. We have called incessantly for a better system whereby the work of the chamber may be

facilitated, but it does not seem to me that the taking away of some of the time of the house in the middle of the week is the right way to achieve this laudable object. And, having in mind that so far as the house is concerned Wednesday is one of our active days in legislation, I express my own views and the views of the party which I lead in this house as opposed to the adoption of the motion of the Prime Minister.

subtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT ON TUESDAYS UNTIL FOLLOWING THURSDAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is one occasion on which I am sorry I shall not be able to support the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon). I am rather in favour of the motion. Personally I find, as I think every other hon. member finds, that if I do my work properly a parliamentary session is a tremendous grind. I have often told my constituents that if a member of parliament is to do his work as it should be done he can be the busiest man in the world; or, on the other hand, if he does not want to do his work properly he can be the laziest man in the world. I am under the impression that there should be a complete change in the hours of parliamentary sittings. Sometimes it is hard for us to break away from. custom, but I should be delighted to learn that the committee being set up to consider the rules of procedure was to review the matter of the sitting hours, in order that, we might facilitate the business of the house and also facilitate the work of members of parliament. We meet at three o'clock in the afternoon and sit until eleven o'clock at night. Some may regard that as a short day because it involves only six hours, but many of the provincial legislatures sit only in the afternoon. When I tell some of my people that we sit at night, they are quite surprised. When I tell them further that one gets down here at nine o'clock in the morning, or thereabouts, and looks after his correspondence, then goes into a committee at ten or eleven o'clock and stays there until one, then attends the sittings of the house beginning at three o'clock and again at eight o'clock, that seems like a pretty good day's work. Before I am here very long I begin to feel the effects of that work.
I do not believe we should have to sit so late at night in order that hon. members may properly represent their constituencies in this house. I am sure we all want to facilitate the business, but at the same time we want to retain our health, and there is something in that. I believe we should let up a little on these hours. Therefore I am in favour of the motion to do away with the Wednesday sitting. It does not necessarily follow that this will help us very much, because I know that the

Wednesday Adjournments
committees will sit that day, but they may meet ia the morning and afternoon and still leave us Wednesday evening free.

subtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT ON TUESDAYS UNTIL FOLLOWING THURSDAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are a good many reasons,
I think, why the motion of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) should be supported by the house; most of them have been given already. We fear, however, that if we do not sit on Wednesday that day may not be utilized as well as it might be. At the present time Mondays and Fridays are off days; usually we try to avoid taking votes on those days, because many hon. members who live in the vicinity of Ottawa go home for the week-end. If we had another day, Wednesday, without a sitting of the house, my colleagues fear that we would be simply prolonging the session and not utilizing that day so as to get the most out of it. Personally I must confess that I would welcome being relieved of house duties on Wednesday. I agree with the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) that those of us who have very heavy correspondence, who are trying to operate something of a major political movement, without facilities and from one small room under this roof, would from that point of view welcome an additional day.
With the position of the government I think every hon. member of this house must have a great deal of sympathy. I often wonder how the ministers manage to attend the meetings of cabinet council, which must be a great strain upon them, and at the same time attend in the house as frequently and as assiduously as they do. I agree with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) that hon. members who last year supported the proposal to appoint parliamentary assistants hoped that these assistants would relieve the ministers of constant attendance in the house, and would be able to speak for them on more occasions than they have in the past year.
Our fear, sir, is that this day may not be utilized in the manner in which it ought to be utilized, and for that reason some have grave doubts as to the wisdom of the proposal now made by the Prime Minister.

subtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT ON TUESDAYS UNTIL FOLLOWING THURSDAY
speechtext:
It is not my intention, Mr. Speaker, to argue the wisdom of the motion of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), or to discuss the question of facilitating the work of the cabinet or of hon. members who are serving on committees. I should like to submit that if our sittings must be suspended one day during the week, it might be more practicable and more advantageous to hon. members if that day were Friday. As the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has just pointed out, many hon.
members go home on Friday for the week-end and, since half the membership of the house does not serve on committees, to suspend the sitting on Friday would give those hon. members a chance to go home and look after their business during the week-end. I submit that Friday would be a better day than Wednesday.
I shall not move any amendment to the motion of the Prime Minister, but if my suggestion is approved by the house I hope the government will agree to it.

subtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT ON TUESDAYS UNTIL FOLLOWING THURSDAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 20, 1943, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) introduced his motion to appoint parliamentary assistants to the ministers, and I opposed that motion as best I could. I was satisfied at that time that I was right, and I am now doubly satisfied, because the Prime Minister has to come along with this motion notwithstanding the fact that, as my leader has said, we have appointed six parliamentary assistants. I do not want these parliamentary assistants to feel that anything I am about to say is intended as a reflection on them, for they were perhaps the best the Prime Minister could have selected from his side of the house, and my remarks have no reference to them or the work they have been doing. Personally I could not see why any red-blooded minister would want to be bothered with a parliamentary assistant. In this regard I am happy to hold up the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), as a shining example to other members of the cabinet. Last year when the Prime Minister introduced his motion for appointment of parliamentary assistants he said, at page 2346 of Hansard of April 20 of that year:
I need not elaborate upon the necessity of securing assistance for the ministers of the defence departments, of the Department of Munitions and Supply,, the Department of Labour and the Department of Agriculture.
But the little Napoleon from the west does not need a parliamentary assistant, and I doubt if any minister in the cabinet has a more responsible or more difficult job to handle. I congratulate him upon his ability to handle his department. I have said that he is a little Napoleon; I might have said as well that he is a walking dynamo, and I congratulate the government upon having in the cabinet a man with the capacity of the Minister of Agriculture. I do not want anyone to think I am supporting what he does; I am speaking of his ability in handling his department.
I can picture a minister having a parliamentary assistant come to him for information. The minister will tell his assistant what to say in the house, and must take the responsi-
Wednesday Adjournments

bility for what is to be said. Naturally this takes the time of the minister. He would be much better occupied in attending to some other business. I never could see why, in this country of merely 12,000,000 people, and with its nineteen or twenty ministers-more I believe than we ever had before-parliamentary assistants were required. I was opposed to the whole business, because it was a useless expense to the country.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

subtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT ON TUESDAYS UNTIL FOLLOWING THURSDAY
speechtext: Order. Will the hon. member remain in his seat? I had begun to say that I was for many years a business man; I was connected with big business for many years, and I ought to know something about how to run a business. It would seem that the Prime Minister now finds he has to cut out Wednesday sittings. What will happen? Many members do not come to Ottawa until Tuesday night. Under the new arrangement there will be no necessity for them to come until Wednesday night. Then, many of them go back on Thursday, and the result will be that they will be in Ottawa one day in the week. If it is necessary that we have more time for committee work, why not take the whole of Wednesday night and Friday night for committees?

subtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT ON TUESDAYS UNTIL FOLLOWING THURSDAY
speechtext: I do not want to work every night.

subtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT ON TUESDAYS UNTIL FOLLOWING THURSDAY
speechtext:
I realize the Prime
Minister wants to have more time. Those two nights are available, and I should think he could use them for committees.
What do we find? In the list before us are some fourteen parliamentary committees, and I think the country ought to know just what those committees are. First there is the committee on privileges and elections. Well, it may meet once in a session, but I doubt if it meets at all. The next is the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. Railways are not being built any more, so that that committee is likely to sit only infrequently.

subtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT ON TUESDAYS UNTIL FOLLOWING THURSDAY
speechtext: It has not sat for several sessions.

subtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT ON TUESDAYS UNTIL FOLLOWING THURSDAY
speechtext: The hon. member for York-Sunbury says it has not sat for several sessions. That crosses that out, so far as work goes. The next is the committee on miscellaneous private bills. What time does that take which would interfere with the House of Commons?

subtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT ON TUESDAYS UNTIL FOLLOWING THURSDAY
speechtext: It is just a matter of considering divorce bills.

subtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT ON TUESDAYS UNTIL FOLLOWING THURSDAY
speechtext:
And divorces are handled by the other house. The next is the committee on banking and commerce. This year that committee may have a good deal to do, because of the revision of the Bank Act. So far in the list that is the first committee which will have anything to do.
The next is the public accounts committee. I do not know whether that is the same as the committee of which the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver) is chairman. If not, then the public accounts committee has nothing to do. I realize of course that the other committee about which I have spoken has much to do.
The committee on agriculture and colonization, next on the list, I presume has much work to do, although I do not know. The committee on standing orders would need to sit only about once a month. Then, what is done by the committee on marine and fisheries?

speechtext: Nothing.

Then there is the committee on mines, forests and waters. Again these matters are under the control of a very able minister, the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar)- and I pat him on the back as being one who does not require a parliamentary assistant.
The next is the committee on industrial and international relations; is it meeting any more? I have been in the house for years, and for a long time I have not noted any sittings of that committee.

Eight
years ago.

The committee on debates -has that anything to do? The committee on printing-well, what does the printing committee have to do? The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) smiles. I must tell him right now I was most surprised that he accepted a parliamentary assistant. I thought he was a big, strong, red-blooded man, and could quite easily take care of his department by himself. I am sorry I was disappointed.
The next is the committee on the library of parliament. Has it anything to do? Then, the committee on the restaurant. I do not suppose it has much to do. The committee on railways and shipping-

subtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT ON TUESDAYS UNTIL FOLLOWING THURSDAY
speechtext: It has a lot to do.

subtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT ON TUESDAYS UNTIL FOLLOWING THURSDAY
speechtext:
It does not do much. Then the committee on the revision of standing orders. I presume that was the special committee appointed this year. Then the committee on The Dominion Elections Act. That committee has little to do; I hope our work will not take long.
The last on the list is the committee on reconstruction, which is now meeting. Out of that list of committees, how many are going to meet on Wednesdays, occupying the whole of thdt day?
I should like to support the Prime Minister, because he has a terrific job. I have no desire to add to his burdens; rather I would have them lessened. How'ever I cannot see how the turning over of Wednesdays to the meeting of committees would relieve the congestion in parliament. I should like to see my own work lessened. I represent a large industrial riding, and I have a heavy correspondence. Rarely do I get away from these buildings until twelve o'clock at night. I am in my seat every sitting day, and I find that all my time is occupied. Certainly I should like to have more time to myself, but I am satisfied that the proposed arrangement for Wednesdays would not help me. In fact I would be afraid it would lengthen days which are now altogether too long.
The house knows where I stand, and I shall vote against the proposal.

subtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT ON TUESDAYS UNTIL FOLLOWING THURSDAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not question the right of the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) to speak; but from a sign I thought he gave me I concluded that he had finished his remarks. However, in that I was mistaken.
I do not agree with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) when he says Wednesday is the most important day in the house.

subtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT ON TUESDAYS UNTIL FOLLOWING THURSDAY
speechtext: I did not say that.

subtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT ON TUESDAYS UNTIL FOLLOWING THURSDAY
speechtext: Perhaps I am wrong. To my mind Friday is the most important day, because, with the Tuesday-and-Thursday men at home, we get some business done. The leaving of Wednesdays for committees is a good suggestion, but to those in charge of making arrangements for committees I would say they should see to it that every hon. member is on a committee, so that no one may be idle. I believe the suggestion with regard to Wednesdays is wise, because no hon. member wishes to sit in committee when the house is sitting. Every hon. member who speaks in the house is worth hearing, no matter from which side he may speak. For these reasons 1 support the proposal.

subtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT ON TUESDAYS UNTIL FOLLOWING THURSDAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that I am opposed to this motion to suspend Wednesday sittings of the house for the present session. As has been so well pointed out. the passing of this motion would mean that there would be only two days in the week which would be available from the private members' point of view. As is known, many eastern members go home on Thursday evening or Friday morning and come back on Monday evening, and some understanding seems to have grown up in the house that important votes and important discussions will not take place except from Tuesday to Thursday inclusive of each week. If we do not sit on Wednesdays we shall have only two days for important matters.
The Prime Minister has pointed out that the sessions are strenuous for the cabinet ministers who must attend cabinet meetings and do their parliamentary work as well. I understand that when the parliamentary assistants were appointed a year ago it was done to relieve the ministers of much of their work in the house I agree with some of the remarks that have been made as to there being no necessity for some of these parliamentary assistants, although I think others of them were quite necessary.
I am convinced that this proposed arrangement will lengthen the session of parliament. I am one of the many who come from a considerable distance to attend the sessions. We are forced to stay in Ottawa over the long week-ends. We are faced with the expense of keeping up our homes in our constituencies. The cost of living in Ottawa is high, and we are not allowed to make deductions on our income tax returns for living expenses when we are away from home, as is permitted some of these dollar a year men who advise the government.

subtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT ON TUESDAYS UNTIL FOLLOWING THURSDAY
speechtext: And the ministers.

subtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT ON TUESDAYS UNTIL FOLLOWING THURSDAY
speechtext:
Never mind the ministers just now. I think all in all that the motion of the Prime Minister is a most unfair one. The other day my namesake, the hon. member for Hamilton East (Mr. Ross), a supporter of this government, was referring to the labour order, and is reported to have said at page 365 of Hansard:

many occasions the Prime Minister has set forth his great respect for parliamentary traditions. I am satisfied that the people of this country have great respect for the worth-while traditions of parliament, but I must confess that during the past few years under this regime parliament has fallen into disrepute in the minds of many of the people across this country. I think we should be careful not to allow further progress to be made in this respect. Just the other day the Prime Minister rose in his place and pointed out the trend that had taken place in connection with the formation of new groups. He stated that we were simply repeating what had happened in France, I would remind him that all this has taken place under his leadership and with so-called Canadian unity.
One hon, member pointed out this afternoon that he finds the long hours he has to put in on his parliamentary duties a strain on his health. T would point out that our men overseas must work much longer hours and under more difficult conditions than we do in this country. They should be considered when we think of ourselves in these times of stress and strain. In a period of war we must all make many sacrifices, but since coming here in 1940 it has become apparent to me that if present conditions continue we shall have a state of affairs in Canada under which only the very wealthy or those who have no substantial incomes or businesses will be able to come here as members of parliament. The average business man or farmer could not afford to make this sacrifice in ordinary times, but as I say we must all be prepared to sacrifice to the limit during war time.
I am opposed to the motion., because I do not think it is in the interests of the country. It will certainly lengthen, the session and not help us with our legislative programme. *

Mr. Speaker, I feel that I should make my position clear on this motion. I am not particularly opposed to the motion, because I have every sympathy with the cabinet ministers in the work they are doing; but as has been already pointed out, parliamentary assistants have been appointed who we thought were going to take some of the burden from the shoulders of the cabinet ministers.
As far as the general committees are concerned, it has been the custom since I have been in the house for them not to begin to meet until the middle or latter part of the session. I understand that it is the special committees that will meet on Wednesdays, and anyone who looks over the membership of this house must know that a great many members are not members of any special committee. The brains of this house are not all concentrated in a few people. I think every hon. member has his part to play and something to contribute, and I do not see why every member of the house could not be put on one of the special committees. Take the committee on reconstruction and rehabilitation. Probably no one is more interested in that committee than the farmer members, but there are only four 100-441
farmers on that committee out of a membership of thirty-five. It seems to me that that is hardly a fair distribution.
Some of us who are not members of special committees will have nothing to do if the house does not sit on Wednesdays, except perhaps our ordinary work. We might of course devote the time to something of educative value, but so far as the work of this house is concerned we shall have nothing to do. If it were going to shorten the work of parliament I would be all in favour of the motion, but personally I cannot see it that way.

Mr. Speaker, I agree that we are spending a little too much time in discussing the motion. I think it would be much better to take a vote now7 and let the members decide what they want. For myself I am not in favour of prolonging this debate. I wish to warn the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), however, that the adoption of the motion is not going to facilitate very much the work of the house, by having the committees sit on Wednesdays. What the Prime Minister needs to do is to appoint one of his ministers, who may not have so much to do as some of the others, to organize the work of the house and of the committees so that as many committees and as many private members as possible will be working every day. No one wants to be sitting around this house without something to do. Personally I have plenty to do whether the house or the committees are sitting or not, but I can understand that others may not have enough to do. The work of the session should be so arranged, and it should be someone's responsibility to so arrange it, that after a committee is appointed it should be set expeditiously to work and continue at its work until it has completed rvhatever piece of legislation is referred to it.
I support the motion and I hope that we can soon get on with the work of the house.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think this motion will have the effect of either aiding the government or shortening the session. On the contrary I think it will tremendously increase the length of the sessions. I think it will do other things as well.
The three most important committees of this house, in view of the speech from the throne and the possibility of new legislation, are the social security committee, the reconstruction committee, and the banking and commerce committee. If we have all Wednesday for the social security committee to sit, I am quite certain that every individual in Canada with his own pet theory on health or security
Wednesday Adjournments

or social planning or some other panacea will wish to be heard before that committee, and a tremendous amount of irrelevant and extraneous information will be put before the committee, so that when the committee gets down to its work of making a report and perhaps helping to draft legislation, there will be such a volume of material before it, and so much of it, with all due respect, quite useless, that we shall not be serving the country as well. I believe that to get a committee functioning properly there should be a sense of urgency pervading it; but if this motion goes through we shall be inclined to sit back and say, "We have all Wednesday", and people will come before us and present everything. That is why I oppose this motion.
Last year the house spent over a month in the debate on the speech from the throne, and approximately a month on the budget. Fortunately this year the debate on the speech 1 from the throne has ended. But I suggest that the government might limit the debates on the address and on the budget so that the house will retain its function as a deliberative and legislative assembly, and so that we shall not have members speaking for certain special and local interests in order to get their speeches on Hansard.
I think this motion will lengthen the sessions, will not make the committees more efficient, and will not assist the government in the efficient prosecution of this country's war effort.

subtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT ON TUESDAYS UNTIL FOLLOWING THURSDAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am opposed to this motion because, contrary to what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) expects, I think its tendency, if adopted, will be to lengthen the session, and that has serious repercussions for those of us who live a long distance away from Ottawa. The other day the Prime Minister referred to the fact that in Great Britain parliament for a great part of the session sits from Tuesday to Thursday. But in Britain the distances are so short that a member can go home over the week-end and mingle with his constituents and come back on Tuesday with something of the point of view of the people he represents. We are in a totally different position because of the vast distances in Canada. We are here five or six months of the year, and those of us who live a long distance from our constituents seldom can get back home during the session and get their point of view and discuss their personal problems which they want us to bring before the House of Commons.
I do not think Wednesdays should be taken away. It is true the Prime Minister says

that we have three hours on Friday night, but I think we should have that time anyway, and I think we should do committee work on Saturday, so as to allow members to get away by June or July. Last year it was the 2nd of August before I left the city, and many other members were a day or two later than that. That is a long time to be out of touch with the people whom one represents.
The second point is this. I have every sympathy with the main contention of the Prime Minister, that the cabinet ought to have more time. I agree with that, but some other arrangement could be made. I suggest that on one day of the week, either Thursday or Friday, or whatever days the government may choose, the war committee of the cabinet could meet, and that day could be devoted exclusively to estimates or other matters concerning departments whose ministers are not on the war committee of the cabinet; ministers who are on that committee could be represented by their parliamentary assistants. This would give one day of each week to the war committee of the cabinet for the discussion of matters which they are called upon to consider in carrying the great burden which each of us recognizes they are called upon to bear.

I am in accord with the views expressed by one or two hon. members who have spoken before me, especially those from the west. From my experience, a great deal of time is wasted, and it is a mistake to cut out Wednesdays. The last speaker referred to committees. If on Wednesday six or seven committees are meeting, you will have the whips running around 'and there will be great difficulty getting quorums together, because certain members are on two or three committees. Many of us are on two committees, and last year I found it difficult when attending one committee in which I was interested to find time to attend another committee meeting which I should like to have attended.
It is very unfair to members west of Fort William to ask us to forgo Wednesday sittings, because they never get a chance to go home. We used to sit on Friday nights, and as hon. members will recall, one or two ministers generally opened up their estimates earlier in the session than others and took advantage of that night. In that way we have accomplished a good deal. It would have been a good thing if many of the members who are present now had been in the house on Friday night last, because we had a very informative discussion and obtained much information which I am afraid half the members who were absent will not take the time to read. In my

Wednesday Adjournments
opinion it would prolong the session to adopt this motion and it is not fair to keep the western members here six and seven months. In the 1942 session we were here nearly seven months and last year about six months. From that point of view I am opposed to the motion.

There are just two points I wish to discuss for a moment. First of all, I intend to follow the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) in this vote, and in view of the peculiar circumstances under which I was elected I should explain that statement. I am voting against this motion because, from my short experience in the house, during which time I have served on a number of committees, I am not satisfied that the work in any committee on which I have served warrants a suspension of the work of the house in favour of committees. Most of the reports of these committees are tabled in this house but few if any of them are ever brought to the house for consideration. If the estimates or other matters are passed on to committees, the majority of the members of the house will have no opportunity of discussing them.
The second point on which I wish to protest is this. Suggestions have been made in this house that members, particularly from the Toronto area, are accustomed to absenting themselves from the house on Mondays and Fridays. I would ask hon. members to look over the house this afternoon. If they do they will find that practically every member from Toronto and the Toronto area is in his place. I want that made quite clear. Because we come from Toronto or the Toronto area does not by any means indicate that we are not here in our places on Monday or Friday.

subtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT ON TUESDAYS UNTIL FOLLOWING THURSDAY
speechtext:
I am glad there is sufficient elbow room in this group to permit us to disagree with one another. Personally I am in favour of the motion presented by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). I do not,think it is going to extend the session five minutes, for the simple reason that we have not been sitting on Wednesday nights, nor have we been sitting on Friday nights. The proposal before us definitely states that we shall sit on Friday nights.
The reason, however, why I am in favour of the motion is that I am anything but satisfied with the way the committee work is conducted, and I refer particularly to the special committees. We have the reconstruction cofnmittee, the social security committee, and the committee on war expenditures. The work being carried on by these committees is
just as important as, if not more important than, the business of this house, because these committees are actually planning the future of Canada, giving the house guidance as to the legislation that will go through. My experience in the past two years, so far as committees are concerned, has been this. You leave a stenographer at eleven o'clock or at ten-thirty and rush to a committee with a file full of papers which you have not had a chance to read. Then you sit in and listen to a presentation from the manufacturers' association, the chamber of commerce or some other organization with a battery of experts, and the committee is doing nothing but listening. The chairman is watching the clock to see when twelve-thirty arrives so as to announce the adjournment of the committee and then you bundle your file under your arm and go back to your office and before you get .a chance to read it you meet someone else. That is not satisfactory.
My conception of the motion which the Prime Minister proposes is that we shall set aside Wednesday specifically for that committee work, and then it will be the responsibility of the chairmen of committees to see that their work is so organized that these committees will meet from ten in the morning until any hour in the evening necessary for them to complete their business. If the time is utilized in that way I think it will be a step in the right direction. But the responsibility will rest on the government side of the house to see to it that the chairmen of the respective committees so organize the work as to give those on the committees an opportunity of properly preparing their case, analysing the evidence, and getting some understanding of the deliberations of the committees.
I am in favour of the motion on the understanding that that time be properly utilized and the committee work be properly organized so that the committees may be in a better position to advise the house with respect to the matters that they are called upon to consider.

speechtext:
My hon. friend has touched a point which I am glad he brought up. He has in mind the absence at certain times of a number of members. I ask him what this house is here for, whether it is here to get through business or to accommodate members who wish to be absent one day and present another? I am not the keeper of the consciences of hon. gentlemen in this house. If a member is not sufficiently interested to attend the different sittings of the house, that is his affair and the concern of his constituents; it is not the affair of the government. The government's concern is to try to get through all the business we possibly can. To ask that we should consider arranging the business of the house so as to accommodate those who wish to be absent part of the time instead of being present all the time is to prefer a perfectly unreasonable request.
May I say again that I hope the public at least do not believe that the amount of work which is accomplished in this parliament is to be estimated by the amount of talk, the amount of discussion. As a matter of fact, one of the hopes I cherish is that, having Wednesdays free, some hon. members at least will take advantage of that day to prepare themselves for debates which they expect may follow later on and will thereby be able the better to express themselves in a few words, instead, as so often happens, of getting their first knowledge of a matter which is being discussed when it comes up upon the orders of the day.
If hon. members will stop for a moment to consider how the parliament at Westminster conducts its affairs, they will realize that it is an absurdity to talk about the work of this parliament being dependent upon the number of hon. members that are in the house from day to day. I take it that every hon. member knows that in the British House of Commons
they have seating capacity for something like 400 members, and that there are 615 members returned to the House of Commons. It would be just as reasonable to suggest that no meeting of the British House of Commons should be held to discuss important matters until the whole 615 members could be brought into the chamber. But Britain has realized that what counts is not talk but argument and the importance and the weight of argument, and that the important thing to accomplish in parliament is the business of the country, and to expedite the business which parliament has been summoned to consider. Perhaps that is one of the reasons why this house on different occasions has got through so much business on a Friday evening [DOT]-because there have not been present others than those who were really interested in the matters under discussion. I think that disposes sufficiently of the matter of attendance in the house.
As to committees, if there can be an organization of the committee work in a way which will make it more effective, the government will be only too happy to lend itself to further that particular end. I ask hon. members, has there been a session of this parliament at any time when the work has been better organized than it has been from the beginning of this session up to this moment, and when more has been accomplished in an equivalent period of time? I say there has not been; and I believe that if hon. members will cooperate with the government in its work, much more in the way of expedition can be attained.

subtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT ON TUESDAYS UNTIL FOLLOWING THURSDAY
speechtext:
Let me come to the real question. I have spoken twice in the house on this matter; if that had not been the case, I would have taken a different attitude now. I have told hon. members quite frankly that at this time of wrar, with the great issues that are facing the government and the world and the tremendous responsibilities that are on the shoulders of the government in dealing from day to day with these vast problems, the government needs more time to devote to the careful study and consideration of war problems than it has when parliament is in session, with the sessions carried on as they have been in the past. I made that very clear both times I spoke, but I noticed that this afternoon most hon. gentlemen carefully avoided that side of the question. It was not the government that was being considered in any particular, though I would impress upon this house again that the government has the responsibility of carrying on the war effort of this country at this time. In turn each hon. member who has risen has for the most part spoken about what would suit his particular convenience. Well, it is very human for all of us to think about ourselves first, but I do submit that at a time of war such as this, when hon. members know the responsibility that is upon the government, it is very little to ask that when we are dealing with these questions the government should receive consideration, perhaps in the first instance, in the matter of the business of the house.
Perhaps I can say what I have to say pretty much in this word. Since the beginning of this war the prime minister of Britain has told the House of Commons what time he felt the government required to conduct the business of the country in a time of war, and he has arranged the sittings of the Commons accordingly. Mr. Chamberlain did that; Mr. Churchill has done it. Each of these prime ministers told the House of Commons in Britain that at a time of war the responsibility on the government was so great with regard to the questions which the government alone could consider if it was to deal with them properly in an executive way, or deal with them efficiently when coming before the House of Commons, that the government needed so much time; and, as I pointed out here, since the beginning of the war the House

of Commons in Britain has sat an average of only three days a week. That is, the House of Commons in Britain has found it necessary to sit only three days a week, not that committees may sit or that others may do this or that, but that the prime minister and his colleagues and those who have to do with the executive part of the work of carrying on the war may have opportunity adequately to discuss the great questions that are before,them, and have the necessary time for consultation. If the prime minister of Great Britain has found it necessary to say this to the Commons and the Commons has accepted his word, I think I might claim that, having undertaken to see if possible that this government will carry on until the end of the war, my colleagues and I are entitled to the consideration of this house in the matter of the conditions under which we are to carry on.
I do not want hon. members of this house to forget that, enjoying the confidence of this country as we do; having had it from all sides, from the opposition as well as from the press of this country practically with one voice, that we should continue to carry on until this war is over, I believe we are entitled to have our request immediately met when we say to hon. gentlemen opposite that we need an extra afternoon to confer on the great questions that are coming to us day by day. If we cannot get that cooperation, then we shall have to consider what our responsibility is. I must say that what has taken place this afternoon has not made me believe any more strongly than I did hitherto in the cooperation we can expect from hon. gentlemen opposite. I hope the citizens of this country will take today's Hansard and read the debate that has taken place this afternoon-

And may I add that instead of reducing the number of parliamentary assistants I am going to find it necessary very soon to add to the number, just because the work that is on the shoulders of some of the ministers is becoming so much heavier at this time than it has been heretofore. I think I am entitled to say to hon. members of this house that they must remember that we are now in the fifth year of war, and that those of us who compose the government, particularly those who are on the war committee of the cabinet, have had over four very heavy years in dealing with these questions. Our position is not made any easier or our burden any lighter by the fact we know of circumstances affecting the future now hanging over our heads and the heads of others in similar positions the like of which have never before hung over the heads of members of any ministries in the world.
These matters cannot be dealt with lightly. Take the position this very day, this very week; and when I speak of myself I speak for my colleagues asvwell. I began my work at nine o'clock this morning, trying to deal with some matters that are of immediate importance, trying to consult officials of the departments over which I preside, trying to make sure that at least some acknowledgment was made of some of the most important letters; I had to be in the cabinet council with my colleagues at twelve o'clock, and we were kept there until a quarter to three this afternoon. I had then to be in this house at three o'clock to debate the present motion. One of the questions we were discussing in cabinet council to-day was a question on which we are expected to give Great Britain an answer by Thursday of this week. It is a very, very important question, which we could not settle in the two and a half hours we met to-day, a large part of which time was devoted to a discussion of it. When I say that the government needs time to consider some of these matters, so that it can have an uninterrupted sitting of the necessary duration without feeling that its members must jump up in the next five minutes and rush off to be in the House of Commons to answer questions, I think I am entitled to have my word in that respect accepted.
