I come back to the position of the British parliament. There the ministers have their parliamentary secretaries, their financial secretaries, and many more assistants than our ministers have. It is true that they have many more important matters with which to deal, but the decisions that have to be made there are not more important relatively. The weight of responsibility is not any less, and I wish to say now to the house as Prime Minister of this country that it is not possible for the government of Canada at this time of war; knowing what lies immediately before the Canadian people and our armies in the field, to give the time required to the consideration of those problems which are coming up before us, the time which they should have, and which the interests of the country and of the war demand, unless we find it possible to have more time for continuous consultation while parliament is in session. I can think of no way in which that end can be achieved which would be less of a handicap to anyone than that of taking Wednesday afternoons for that purpose, and resuming the practice of having sittings of the house on Friday nights.
When my hon. friend interrupted me, I was speaking on some of the matters which we have to consider and how time is taken up in unexpected ways. Something has been said in the house about the wages control order. On ' Wednesday of this week the government is to meet with representatives of some of the railway brotherhoods, and I understand is to hear their representations, on this and other matters. Can my colleagues be excused from that? If they are absent, then there is comment on the fact that the government is not as respectful as it should be to the railway brotherhoods.
On Friday of this week we have an engagement to meet with representatives of the Dominion Trades and Labour Congress. After that we have a meeting with representatives of the Catholic Syndicates, to discuss also with them matters pertaining to the wage

order. I hope that all my colleagues will be present with me at both these meetings. This will take most of the entire morning, and past the hour at which the cabinet meets. This is all apart from ordinary business which we have to take up independently.
Reference has been made to the absence at times of ministers from the house. Hon. members when they look up and see a minister absent ask, "Why is he absent?" The likelihood is that he is meeting with a delegation which has been waiting for days to see him, or conferring with regard to some of these matters which have to be left to the government, and which the cabinet has to decide.
I repeat that we are asking this house to give the government what it feels is necessary by way of time to consider matters which relate to the war, and other important matters which are coming up. And I am quite prepared to have a vote taken, if hon. members feel after what I have already said that they wish to vote on the matter.
Now I come to what my hon. friend has said. At the beginning of his remarks-and I am referring to the leader of the opposition- he referred to "our party" as opposing this motion. speechtext:
The committee on war expenditures, as the house will recall, was not set up until July 17 of last year. The committee was immediately convened. We held three meetings of the main committee between the 17th and the 24th of July when the house adjourned'. The committee did not meet in August. Most members

War Expenditures-Mr. Cleaver
had been away from their ridings for many months and required to return to them. The committee, however, reconvened in September and worked continuously through the fall until the middle of November, and it reconvened again a week before the house opened, for the purpose of completing its reports. During this period the main committee and its various subcommittees held ninety-seven meetings at Ottawa in addition to many visits to war plants across Canada.
During the recess our meetings were exceptionally well attended this time, and I think it is only fitting that I should now pay a well-deserved tribute to the members of the committee and to the committee staff for the loyal and efficient way in which they carried on their duties and for the substantial results achieved.
Members of the house will have noticed from our reports that subcommittee No. 1 reported on shipbuilding, both as to cargo and the shipbuilding programme and as to naval vessels. Subcommittees Nos. 2 and 3 were grouped together for the aluminum inquiry. That was an exceptionally heavy inquiry and the committee thought it wise to assign that work jointly to those two subcommittees. Subcommittee No. 4 made the inquiry into the supply of agricultural implements and brought in a report with respect to that subject.
While the committee worked very diligently and lost no time, from the time it was appointed, and worked continuously throughout the fall, much of the work which we should have done has not yet been completed, and we are consequently much pleased that the house has taken notice of our fifth report, which was a recommendation that the committee this year should be set up as promptly as possible on the opening of the session.
Since most of our meetings have been in camera, the work of the committee has received little publicity, and I think it is only fair, only right that I should say that the war expenditures committee, much maligned as it is by some of our daily press, has saved many millions for Canada's war effort. This saving has been effected both directly and indirectly. A reference to the reports will disclose many of the direct savings that have been brought about, but in addition to the direct savings the indirect influence, I am convinced, is quite as important.
I believe it is commonly agreed now that the very fact that a war expenditure committee is sitting and is vigilantly watching government expenditures has a most salutary effect. While no major scandal has occurred in connection with Canada's war effort, and we are all very proud of that fact, yet many
mistakes have been made-honest mistakes. War is wasteful. I will say this, however, that whenever mistakes have been made and whenever waste has occurred the mistakes have been remedied and the waste checked as soon as it was brought to the attention of the minister in question; and in the few instances where actual wrongdoing has occurred the wrongdoers have been punished.
Quite recently one of the Toronto dailies criticized the war expenditures committee for referring, through the minister, to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, criminal charges for investigation and for prosecution if prosecution proved to be justified. I was amazed to read that editorial because, speaking for myself and, I believe, for every member of the house, I do not know of any other way in which a crime, even though connected with the war effort, should be treated than by reference to the R.C.M.P. for investigation and to our criminal courts for punishment if crime actually was committed.
During the last year the committee followed its established practice of holding most of its meetings in camera. We have already had debates in three previous sessions of this house with reference to the practice of holding most of the meetings in camera, and the merits both for and against such meetings have been fully discussed in these debates. In Great Britain, as hon. members know, all meetings of the war expenditures committee are held in camera. In Great Britain also the subcommittees have not even the power to hold any of their meetings otherwise than in camera. In Canada, while the committee has full power to decide itself on the type of meetings to be held, our practice in the main has also been to hold most of our meetings in camera.
As to our subcommittees, we have not tied their hands, and every subcommittee that has been appointed by any war expenditures committee since 1941 has had the fullest power to decide whether its meetings shall be held publicly or in camera. In view of the fact that our Canadian practice as well as the British practice is so well established, I had hoped that there would be no further discussion about the matter. However, in listening to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) in his opening speech this session, I became fully aware of the fact that the point must be argued all over again.
May I call attention to the actual words used by the leader of the opposition. They are quite expressive though perhaps not too dignified, and I just wonder if, when the leader of the opposition uttered those words, he fully appreciated the fact that he was speaking to the British House of Commons in regard to their conduct of war expenditures-

The hon. member says, "Nonsense". That is the hon. member's own opinion. If he thinks it is nonsense I am very much encouraged to go on in the same train of thought. These are the words, Hansard, page 26:
It is about time that the lid was blown off these in-camera sessions of the war expenditures committee. It is little short of a national disgrace that the people of Canada should not know something about the investigations of these contracts. I am opposed to the whole system of pulling down the blinds, closing the shutters and locking the doors when public contracts are being investigated.
\ ou will notice that the leader of the opposition has accused the war expenditures' committee of this House of Commons of acting in a manner which constitutes a national disgrace. These words demand a frank answer, and I welcome the opportunity of giving it. I say that no one knows better than the leader of the opposition, the Toronto Globe and Mail and the others who are carrying on this agitation against in-camera sessions of the war expenditures committee, the reasons why they are carrying on that agitation. They know there are good and sufficient reasons for the meetings being held in camera, and I shall be pleased to enumerate them a little later on.

The very fact that our hearings are held in camera and that the witnesses are not subjected to trial by press and press headlines leads to the greatest possible frankness and greatly assists the committee in pursuing its work. From the incident I have just related I can assure hon. members that if any evidence comes out in the war expenditures committee that is of

War Expenditures-Mr. Cleaver
particular interest, there is not the slightest danger of its being hidden. In the light of past experience we have nothing to fear from bashful reticence on the part of the opposition if anything comes up which they think will advance their political fortunes.
With apologies to the house I should like to outline briefly why the British war expenditures committee as well as our own committee have found that better work is done when the meetings are held in camera. In the first place there is much information brought out which, if disclosed, would give either aid or comfort to the enemy, and at the time you are taking evidence in regard to war contracts you never know when a witness is going to blurt out something which would have that result. In the second place we have found that witnesses, when giving evidence as to contentious matters or matters where honest mistakes have occurred, become very reticent and practically "freeze up" if the meetings are open to the public. They know in advance that the meeting is going to be in camera and that they are not going to be subjected to trial by the press, so they frankly tell the story. Some people may question that; some may say the witnesses should have more courage, and so on. However, we must face up to the fact that this state of affairs does exist; and if we want to do a thorough job as a war expenditures committee; if we want to acquire all the evidence we need as to contentious matters or matters in which mistakes have been made, we simply must hold our meetings in camera. In the third place-and this reason applies to all members of the house-in public meetings hon. members are prone to make speeches. When we are engaged in serious, hard work as a committee the same progress is not made if hon. members are making speeches in order to get in the headlines.
For these reasons we believe we achieve better results by having our meetings in camera. We know we get no publicity; we get nothing but hard work and results.

I trust, Mr. Speaker, that this time will not be charged against me, but I believe I can find the reference for my hon. friend. The only change of which I am aware was the change requested in the report tabled on July 19, 1943, paragraph 5 of which reads as follows:
In cases where consideration of national security precludes the publishing of certain recommendations and of the arguments upon which they are based, to address a memorandum to the Prime Minister for the consideration of the war cabinet, providing that the committee shall, whenever it has exercised such powers, report the fact as soon as possible to the house.
As I understand the British practice, it is this. If any matter arises which for reasons of security should not be tabled as a house report, a confidential report is made to the Prime Minister for consideration by the war cabinet. The war expenditures committee must notify the house, however, that it has made such confidential report, though not indicating the contents of it. I might add, Mr. Speaker, that in requesting this additional

War Expenditures-Mr. Cleaver
power the committee adopted exactly the wording that is contained in the reference to the British war expenditures committee.
When the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) asked this question I was about to say that another reason for setting up the committee on war expenditures was to permit private members of the House of Commons actively to take part in Canada's war effort, and to make a contribution to that effort. If hon. members will be good enough to read the debate which took place in the spring of 1941 I think they will find the answers to most of the charges-in my opinion unfair charges, though other hon. members may not agree with me-which are now being levelled by some of the daily newspapers and some members of the opposition with respect to the functioning of the war expenditures committee. I would suggest to my hon. friends of the opposition that if they want the lid blown off, as their leader mentioned the other day, or if they want fireworks, there is another committee to which they should go rather than the war expenditures committee. It is quite true that the fear of losing the war has passed, and that we can confidently look forward to final victory. But I suggest to yourself, Mr. Speaker, and to the house, that the 'need for economy in the war effort is just as great as it ever was, and that if there are any members who must indulge in fireworks, and who must regale themselves with charges about $400 rugs, which never did exist, and with other pieces of fiction, they can satisfy this desire for public stunting before the public accounts committee.
But why harm the war expenditures committee, a serious-minded committee which was set up for the express purpose of saving money in this country's war effort? Why attempt to hamper them in their work by putting on a demonstration of that kind?
Just to-day the Toronto Globe and Mail published a very misleading editorial in which they soundly criticize the committee upon its shipbuilding report. I should like to take the time of the house for a moment to refer briefly to our shipbuilding report. Late in 1940 Great Britain, on account of the submarine menace, needed cargo vessels very badly. Representatives from the British government came to this country and surveyed the possibility of building cargo vessels in Canada. For fifteen years prior to the war no steel cargo vessel had been built in this country, and we had little in the way of shipbuilding facilities.
As a result of that survey the British representatives found three firms in Canada with possibilities. Prices were negotiated with
those firms. The final agreement was that $1,859,000 was to be spent for cargo vessels to be built on the Pacific coast, and $1,784,000 for cargo vessels to be built in the St. Lawrence. The shipping problem became progressively worse, and in April, 1941, an order in council was passed authorizing the incorporation of Wartime Merchant Shipping Limited. Canada then branched out on an aggressive policy of cargo shipbuilding. We had only three suitable yards. The industry was expanded to the greatest possible extent; new yards were built, and contracts were awarded to eleven shipyards in Canada. The prices in these yards were agreed upon as the prices which had been negotiated by the British representatives. The result was that by the end of 1943 Canada had built and delivered 232 cargo vessels, in addition to something over 400 naval ships.
In September, 1943, Sir Oliver Lyttelton, British Minister of Production, told a press conference that Canada was launching ships, exclusive of the larger types of war ships, to an extent equal to the volume of launchings by Great Britain. Ships were urgently needed. We had little in the way of shipbuilding facilities; we had little in the way of trained personnel, but we did produce the ships.
What about the cost? Some of the daily press and some of our hon. friends in the opposition are commencing entirely to forget the emergency, and to criticize the costs? Well, what about those costs? All of the original contracts were negotiated and signed at the price which had been arranged by the British delegation. That is the first item on cost,

Subcommittee No. 1 completed its investigation into the shipbuilding programme, and tabled its report on the 26th of last month. I refer hon. members to that report and ask them to read all of it. It is not long, and I should like to read into the record one paragraph with respect to cost to show that we did bring to the attention of the public in the fullest possible way exactly what had happened. I read from page 140 of the committee's minutes of proceedings as follows:
The original contracts for cargo ships were for a fixed price but when it was found that a ship could be built cheaper than anticipated renegotiation of contracts was undertaken. At the time renegotiation commenced about eighty ships had been delivered and about forty-five more were in various stages of construction. A flat fee of $50,900 for each North Sands ship was agreed upon and as to shipbuilding firms performing additional services, certain additional allowances were negotiated. This, it was reported to your committee, resulted in a reduction of approximately $300,000 per ship. These renegotiated contracts wen; made retroactive and were effective back to the date of the first ship, with a resulting reduction in cost of between thirty and forty million dollars.
It is all very *well for my hon. friends of the opposition to say now that we wrere too generous in the prices allowed for these ships, but I would remind them that we had not yards, that we had not constructed a steel cargo vessel in the fifteen years prior to the outbreak of the war. We knew nothing of what it would cost to build these ships, but we did know one thing-we needed ships. What did this government do? Mr. H. R. MacMillan was appointed the head of the shipping company, and I challenge hon. members to give the name of any other man who would have done a better job of heading up this merchant shipbuilding company. He was an aggressive man, and he carried his aggressiveness and his insistence that we have ships almost to the point of ruthlessness. But we got the ships.
There are other points I should like to cover which -were referred to inferentially in the editorial in the Globe and Mail. The suggestion was made in that editorial that we were trying to conceal facts, that we had not produced evidence in regard to the cost of some naval vessel and that we had not produced comparative costs as between the government-owned yard and a privately owned shipyard. I take it that the editorial refers to two motions moved by the hon. member for York East (Mr. McGregor) in the subcommittee. They were negatived and I am told that only the hon. member voted for them. They were then brought before the

Many times the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) has indicated to this house that it is not in the public interest to disclose contract prices with respect to ships. In order to leave the correct impression you must give considerable qualifying material because no two yards do the same amount of work on a ship and without the qualifying material a correct impression *cannot be given. My first reason as to why the motion was defeated would be that the figures were given to us in confidence. The next objection to releasing the figures was that they had been compiled by company auditors and were not subject to an independent audit. We had no assurance that the two sets of figures were properly comparable because *different firms of auditors have different ' methods of setting up head office costs, [DOT]weighting overhead and the like. I should like to conclude with just one thought. The work on the war expenditures committee was interesting, but it was hard. Members of the committee spent two or three or four months of their time between two long sessions and they made real personal sacrifices. I would hope that in this debate on the setting up of the committee we might lose perhaps a little of the spirit of the arena and retain more of the spirit of the workshop. With practically no exception every member of the committee cooperated to the fullest extent. I never asked any member of the committee, be he Conservative, Social Credit or Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, to perform a task which was not willingly and efficiently performed. I would ask hon. members, especially those who were not on the committee, to keep before them the reasons why the committee was set up. It was not a propaganda committee and it was never intended to be such. It was not a scandalhunting committee. Our sole job was to look for economies and try to save money in carrying out this country's war effort.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for reasons that I shall give I want to oppose concurrence in the report of the war expenditures committee now before the house. I do this because the conclusions, at least in the matter of my criticisms of the aluminum agreements, are borne out neither by the evidence itself nor by the body of the

report submitted to this house. The subcommittee dealing with the Aluminum Company of Canada finds that none of the allegations I made in this house is substantiated by the facts. I will endeavour to show, and I believe I can show, on the contrary, that the main allegations not only were substantiated by evidence placed before the subcommittee but are in fact in the main confirmed by the report itself.
To the extent that I erred, I erred in important respects in understating the case. Only in one particular would I modify what I said about the agreements last session, and that is when I said that the labour conditions in the plant were both scandalous and inhuman. What I would say now, after having seen the conditions in the plant, is that the labour relations of the corporation have been and are bad.
My allegations fall under several main headings. First, I stated that the aluminum group had, and continues to have, a monopoly in the production of this important metal in Canada. The New Oxford dictionary defines "monopoly" as "the exclusive possession of the trade in some commodity." Now for forty years the aluminum group has been the sole producer of raw aluminum in Canada, and it has had the exclusive possession of the trade in this commodity. There is no question then that my allegation, that the Aluminum Company of Canada was and is a monopoly, is proven conclusively.
The report takes refuge in the hope that there might be future competition in this metal in Canada. This is as improbable as it is irrelevant. The fact is that there is a monopoly and we ignore it at our peril. Yet the report says that none of my allegations is substantiated.
As to future competition, the huge tax and other concessions given the company during this period of war have enabled it to tighten its strangle-hold upon this vital metal. It has acquired, as the report clearly shows, vastly expanded modern plant and equipment, alt fully paid for out of war production, and a power plant three-fifths paid for to enable it to produce the cheapest electrical power in North America. The report tries to minimize these advantages by suggesting future competition from plastics or from secondary aluminum. As to plastics, they will probably enter many fields; but without a knowledge of comparative costs and relative uses no intelligent appraisal can be made, and neither the evidence nor the report attempts any such appraisal.
As to the competition from secondary aluminum, raw aluminum must be made before scrap aluminum is possible. There is no second-

War Expenditures-Mr. Coldwell
ary aluminum industry in Canada, and if they were, scrap aluminum, I am advised, could be used only for low-grade castings. It is therefore not a competitor with the virgin metal.
I said that restrictive clauses were included in the power contracts. The report confirms this, but explains that they had never been used. The fact is that they were there, and this, in my opinion, was a sufficient deterrent to any possible competitor, particularly in the earlier years of the company's history and development.
In the Shawinigan power contract, to which I specifically referred, the clause remained until December, 1943, after the subcommittee had adjourned; yet the report concludes that none of my allegations was substantiated.
I said last session that our minister at Washington had been counsel for the Aluminum Company of Canada up to the time the agreements between the governments and the company were made. That was admitted in this house. I said, too, that he was still vicepresident and director of the parent company, Aluminium Limited. This was confirmed last session; yet the report declares that none of my allegations is substantiated.
I said, too, that the aluminum group had paid many millions for the water rights which had been alienated in the province of Quebec twenty-six years before for $40,000. The evidence and the report confirm it; yet the report states that none of my allegations is substantiated.
I said that Aluminium Limited, the parent or holding company, was an important member of an international cartel, the organization of which was arranged in Canada. I said that this cartel was formed to establish a production quota and to fix buying prices. This was amply confirmed by the evidence. I stated that Aluminium Limited was set up in 1928 and that the Aluminum Company of America transferred to the new Canadian company all its foreign holdings. I alleged that the share capital of the new company was distributed to the shareholders of the Aluminum Company of America as stock dividends. That was admitted in the evidence, which also shows that in 1939, the latest year for which We have records, the officers and directors and their immediate families, together with the important Mellon interests, held fifty-six per cent of the share capital of the United States company and over fifty-one per cent of the share capital of Aluminium Limited, the owner of the Aluminum Company of Canada. The president and five of the six directors are United States citizens; yet the report says that none of my allegations is substantiated.
As to the cartel itself, the Alliance Aluminum Company of Basle, Switzerland, the report now before this house confirms everything I said about it. Let the report now before the house speak for itself in this regard. This is what it says:
An agreement was entered into to limit the production of the members of the group.
The group which form Alliance Limited, the cartel.
In addition, an agreement was reached as to the price at which the group would purchase aluminum from its members; Aluminium Limited Subscribed approximately 28 per cent of the total stock. The other members were the aluminum producers of Great Britain, Germany, France, Italy and Switzerland.
Later, the report mow before the house adds that the Alliance corporation, the cartel, is still in existence. Aluminium Limited carries its shares in the cartel on its own books at the present time as an asset. The German nazi-controlled interest is still there and its shares are apparently unaffected. The report says, and the evidence amply confirms the statement, that this cartel set a world-buying price; yet the report draws the remarkable conclusion that prices were unaffected by this cartel and declares again that none of my allegations, including my charge that Aluminium Limited was a partner in a world cartel, was substantiated.
To-day at noon in the city of Toronto, speaking before the Canadian club, the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Turgeon) said this:
International cartels which control markets and rob the people of legitimate benefits of inventions must be ruthlessly destroved by government.
The same afternoon we are asked to concur in a report which attempts to whitewash one of the largest cartels in the world. Now, whatever miracles of production the aluminum group has accomplished, with united nations funds, since 1940, my statement that they jeopardized the war efforts of the united nations still stands. They restricted production before the war while Germany's domestic production greatly expanded. Under a cartel agreement the Aluminum Company of Canada supplied Japan with large quantities of metal, enabling her to destroy Chinese cities. In 1940 and 1941 our nations gathered aluminum pots and pans while our Chinese allies and our own kin paid with their blood the price of the cartel agreements. High prices and scarcity quotas are the ways of these irresponsible privately-owned cartels. They are above governments; they are above human suffering, and they conclude private treaties for their own advancement among their own members; and the Aluminum Company of Canada,

War Expenditures-Mr. Coldwell
through its parent company, Aluminium Limited, and the aluminum interests of nazi Germany are, as I said, at this moment fellow-members of the aluminum cartel. The report says so, and then, extraordinarily enough, goes on to declare that none of my allegations is substantiated.
Next, I said that the price of aluminum to the united nations is exorbitant and completely out of line with production costs. I alleged that in 1937 the cost was at least as low as 8-943 cents a pound. The report confirms this figure. The Price Waterhouse figures establish the cost in 1939 at 8-31 cents a pound. This was a figure which, I cannot understand quite why, was omitted from the report; and may I say that that figure is higher than one would have expected with the greatly increased output of the new and more modern facilities. But of course we had to accept Price Waterhouse figures throughout, in the absence of any other auditor. Let us remember that Price Waterho-use, an internationally famous auditing firm, has been declared guilty of gross negligence by a United States commission in connection with the auditing of the financial operations of another internationally known firm. I do not propose to elaborate this; but I have the data, the official report of the securities exchange commission, Washington, under my hand. I was not aware of this until recently, or I would have been still more insistent that the committee in its deliberations engage independent auditing advice. Be that as it may, the cost of producing aluminum at Arvida in 1939 was, according to Price Waterhouse, 8-31 cents a pound. The evidence shows that Great Britain that year paid twenty cents a pound for it. There were no advertising or selling costs to be added, so that the profit in that year was apparently 140 per cent of the cost price. Yet my allegation that prices were exorbitant is included among those declared to be entirely without foundation.
In the war contracts the company was protected against increases in costs by an escalator clause whereby the price rose in proportion to increased costs of transportation, labour and so on. In 1942, according to the auditors, the cost had risen to 11-56 cents a pound, with, as I said before, a vastly increased output of aluminum. The selling price that year was 21 cents a pound, a mark-up of 9-44 cents a pound.

The public engaged in the war against the fascist and nazi aggressors and the Japanese imperialists; that is the public who pay for it. The public grant rebates, special depreciation and allow for income and all other taxes, and then the company makes for its owners a further profit of nearly sixteen per cent, or, to be exact, 15-93 per cent of the ingot cost. Even the attempt of witnesses to minimize the extent of the profits still showed an enormous return to the owners of the Aluminum Company of Canada; that is to its owner, the Aluminium Limited; yet the committee declares that none of my allegations is substantiated.
The prospectus of the company, placed in evidence and available to any member of the committee who wishes to obtain a copy, states that at the end of the war the company's new plant facilities will have no funded debt; all extensions will be paid for during the war, whether the governments take the amount of aluminum contracted for or not, and this was confirmed in the evidence and is confirmed by the report. I said last session that the company took no financial risk in regard to these new facilities. The evidence confirms this; yet the report charges that none of my allegations is substantiated.
In the report much is made of the cost of carrying Shipshaw and the Arvida facilities by the company, should we encounter a post-war depression, which I submit the committee report implies will be inevitable. But the company's own prospectus, placed in evidence, has this to say:
Facilities being brought into production are financed partly out of earnings and partly out of the aid of various allied governments on the principle that such facilities should be substantially self-liquidating in the period of the war.
Later, the prospectus adds these words:
Many unprejudiced authorities also believe that the age of light metals is just beginning. If it is not, we will have unneeded facilities which we can either demolish without loss or hold for eventualities, and a business of prewar dimensions -which alw-ays managed to earn a profit for its shareholders.
That is the opinion of the company itself. In other words, it is a case of "heads we win, tails you lose". The chairman of the war contracts depreciation board told us that there tvas veiy likely to be a post-war value in connection with Shipshaw as a power project, altogether aside from the production of aluminum. Yet the report, in order to defend the vast concessions made to the company, tries to. say that they may have little or no value, and upon that assumption declares that another of my allegations is not substantiated.
As to Shipshaw, this power development was planned as long ago as 1925, when aluminum production was neither as important nor as voluminous as in recent years, particularly during this war period.

The other question I was deliberating was as to the references he made respecting his information as to things which happened in the committee. That appeared to me to be relevant, but I would say that the hon. member cannot refer particularly to any particular item where evidence has been given in camera, with the distinction the hon. member has placed upon it. But as I listened to the hon. member I was convinced he had transgressed paragraph 568 in the third edition of Beauchesne's "Parliamentary Rules and Forms", where it states:
Until the report and evidence have been laid upon the table, it is irregular to refer to them in debate, or to put questions in reference to the proceedings of the committee.
Then it points out in paragraph 569:
That when the evidence is before the house it may be debated at length, but members will not be permitted to discuss the conduct or language of members of the committee, except so far as it appears on the record.
My conclusion, therefore, is that as long as the hon. member is referring in general terms to his interpretation of the evidence given in committee, he is entitled to do so. I told the committee upon my return from New York, and I remember one of the members objecting to my having information that other members of the committee did not have. I said I had been so advised when I was there on January 15. And may I say that that power used in Toronto, and supplied from the source I have mentioned, gives Toronto to-day very cheap power indeed.
As to Shipshaw's creating new unusable power, may I point out that in 1939, when there were 400,000 workers unemployed in this country, a large number of whom were in Quebec, that province of Quebec had a surplus of power of only thirteen per cent. Yet the report bemoans the fact that we should have this great new source of power available, one which I contend ought to be used for rural electrification and for industry after the war, and again states that, none of my allegations is substantiated.
In conclusion, I wish to make it abundantly clear, as I said at the outset of the inquiry before the subcommittee-if I may refer just this once to anything that happened there- my criticisms are not for one moment directed against the administrators, the technicians and the workers who planned and executed this marvellous project. This, though, in my opinion they could have done equally well for the people and for the government of Canada. On the contrary I have nothing but the highest praise for the industrial miracle



War Expenditures-Mr. Coldwell
they accomplished. And my high hope is that we may, as a Canadian people, through our democratic institutions and for our people devote equal energies and equal abilities to the development of our country in the postwar years.
My criticisms have been, and are directed against the financial interests in the background who, as I said, were in a position to hold a pistol at the heads of the united nations in their extremity. I have been told, for example, that the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe), the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) and the metals controller all wanted to see this project started early in the autumn of 1940, a year after the outbreak of war when Britain was being heavily bombarded from the air and needed aluminum to make planes. But the company refused a fifty per cent write-off offered on Shipshaw, so that it was not started until April, 1941.
The committee in some particulars relied upon and quoted extensively from a decision of a United States district court, as is indicated by the report. But that decision did not concern itself with economic realities but with definitions of company control embodied in existing United States law. The court failed to take into account several common holders of stock in both companies. Furthermore, the decision is under appeal and would have been decided by now but for the fact-this will appear curious to Canadians-that the supreme court of the United States cannot get a quorum together to hear the appeal. Why? Too many of the judges are disqualified because of their participation in earlier indictments of the Aluminum Company of America. Thus for this house to rely on this decision of a lower court in a foreign country, no matter how friendly the country may be, would be to say the least most remarkable.
I,	therefore, say without reservation that all my major statements regarding this project were amply confirmed by the witnesses appearing on behalf of the oompany and the government. Indeed, I would say to hon. members of this house that if they will take the trouble to read the report now before the house they will find that it confirms those statements. Yet the same report says that none of my allegations is substantiated. To vote concurrence in a report so obviously designed to whitewash the deal and the company would be in my opinion to do violence to one's own intelligence. Surely, Mr. [DOT] Speaker, this house dare not approve the report submitted to it on behalf of the war expenditures committee.

I expected that we would hear this afternoon from the chairman of the committee a resume of some of the work accomplished, but all we are asked for is concurrence in a report based upon evidence which I doubt one member out of three in this house has gone over or is in a position to cast an intelligent vote on. Hon. members are being asked to decide on a very serious matter, one of the most important matters that have come before this House of Commons by way of committee.
When we first thought of having a war expenditures committee each and every hon. member believed that he was going to have an opportunity to be of some service to his country and to help out with the war effort. How well I remember when three short years ago we were told before we went into the committee room that politics would be left right at the door, that they would not enter into the deliberations on war expenditures. speechtext:
I regret that I was not present in the earlier part of the evening, but I have been trying to catch up on some engagements which it was impossible to meet earlier in the day. Discussion however, it is apparent, has arisen over the question whether or not evidence which is taken in camera by one of the select committees-the committee on war expenditures-may be disclosed and. in the words of the amendment, "be tabled."
This is the third or fourth session at which we have had occasion to appoint a war expenditures committee. On each occasion I have pointed out that it was necessary, as suggested at the outset, by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson), I believe, to have a committee of this house to examine war expenditures for the purpose of guarding against extravagance, waste and any kind of fraud or wrongdoing. In speaking on the appointment of the committee I have on each occasion drawn attention to the fact that it was a very simple matter for this house to decide whether or not it would have such a committee and how the committee should function, because there was at Westminster, and had been not only throughout the present war but during the last war as well, a committee appointed at '"estminster to deal with national war expenditures. I stated on each occasion that the motion which was being brought forward in this house was in identical terms with the motion which had been adopted in the house at Westminster. In a time of war there are a number of considerations many of which are not apparent on the surface, of which the government, the House of Commons and parliament must take very full account. In connection with the methods of procedure and the evidence taken before the committee on war expenditures, I submit that there must be the best of reasons for having sittings held in camera or the parliament at Westminster would not have followed that procedure in the last war and insisted upon it in this.
Hon. members last year had the opportunity of meeting with the chairman of the war expenditures committee of the British house. He was attending the British empire parliamentary association gathering and many hon. members questioned him as to procedure, why it was that the committee on war expenditures in the British house held their meetings in camera, and why it was that there was so little or nothing at all in the way of debate on its reports. The answer which was given has already been stated in this house and is to be found in Hansard of last session. It was to the effect that the committee exists not for the purpose of trying some case, or seeking out scandal or to prosecute someone for some wrongdoing, but rather that it is a committee appointed for the purpose of assisting the treasury at a time of war, in seeing that in war expenditures waste is avoided and that economies are effected wherever possible. In the course of its inquiries members may come across matters which are evidence of wrongdoing, and in such cases the procedure at Westminster is to have the committee report at once to
710	COMMONS
War Expenditures-Mr. Mackenzie King
the minister whose department is concerned. Without any attempt to do things in public which might divert the mind of the people from the major issue, namely, that of the prosecution of the war itself, the minister of the department concerned is given an opportunity to see that errors are immediately corrected. There is the further procedure, that if a matter serious enough comes to light and the committee feels that it should be brought to the attention of the Prime Minister, this opportunity is afforded and indeed it is the committee's duty to bring the matter to the Prime Minister's attention so that the government itself may take it in hand immediately to ensure that nothing further is done which may be contrary to the public interest.
The reason why the committee holds its sessions in camera is first of all that the evidence itself can be so much more readily elicited than it could be if the proceedings were held in public. To further the efficiency of its work is one of the reasons why the committee proceeds in camera. I need not repeat what was said this afternoon by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver), the mover of the resolution for concurrence, because all hon. members know that officials will not come forward and give evidence in public in the manner in which they are prepared to give it in private. The war expenditures committee is free to call anyone -experts, officials of departments, any person they please. Hon. members will also know that evidence which is disclosed in one direction may be of great assistance to competitors of the concerns affected, and that in a public hearing witnesses will refuse to disclose evidence which they know is going to be of advantage to a competitor.
A further consideration, and a very important one, applies directly to this particular industry which is being referred to at the present time. The expenditures being examined into frequently involve questions of contract with other governments. I am not at all sure that this particular industry has not contracts to which the governments of the United Kingdom, Australia, and the United States are parties, and I have reason to believe that some of these contracts might not have been made had these governments understood that their part in the matter, and the interests which they are seeking to conserve and to hold secret, at all events for the time being, would be disclosed.

I come back again to what I was saying. In addition to the reasons for the in camera proceedings which I have presented, there is the further one of what may be given, wholly unexpectedly, in the nature of aid or comfort to the enemy. Witnesses cannot be examined in public without some of them saying something, quite innocently to them, seeming to have little or no significance, and yet, watched as proceedings are from every side by those who are seeking to further the interest of the enemy rather than the interest of the country, may lead to something being disclosed which may be at least a clue leading in directions very injurious to the war effort. These are all good, sound, substantial reasons.
There is no parliament more desirous of upholding its own supremacy than the parliament at Westminster. There is no parliament which has sought more eagerly than has the parliament at Westminster to preserve the utmost frankness and openness in all discussions. But when one looks through the list of the public men who have given their support to the present procedure at Westminster of the war expenditures committee and finds such names as those of all the prime ministers of Britain during the period of the last war and the present war, and all the leaders of the opposition in the last war and the present war, I feel that to oppose views which these gentlemen all agree must prevail in matters of this kind requires very substantial reasons.
One thing further. .At Westminster, so carefully is the whole situation guarded that the reports themselves are never debated. I do not know whether hon. members are aware of that. I am perfectly sure that if some service was not thereby being rendered the country an attitude of that kind would not be taken by the British parliament. That has been its position from the beginning. The reports are tabled, and never once have they been a subject of debate since this war has commenced. That seems to be a surprise to some hon. members, but the reasons for it are apparent. It does not mean that those who are members of the committee may not come across evidences of wrongdoing which

War Expenditures-Mr. Howe
they think ought to be exposed, and which they might even feel it their duty to expose. Where there are cases of that kind, and an hon. member who is a member of a committee that has been holding its sittings in camera feels that a wrong has been done which the committee is unwilling to investigate, or that the government is seeking to conceal something because it is unwilling to make public proceedings held in camera, that hon. member may rise in his place and prefer a charge against the government, and the government thereupon appoints a committee of inquiry. There is in such a case some responsibility assumed with respect to the charge that is made. A member is not supposed to make a charge that is not capable of being substantiated; rather is he expected to be so sure of his ground that he is quite prepared to substantiate his charge. There were many times in the last war when the government of the day had to consider whether it was going to investigate rumours and accusations which might be put forward by its opponents, and the government of the day-quite rightly-took very strongly the position that it was not the business of the government to take up the time of the country and parliament in discussing rumours and running down this and that for the purpose of obtaining what little bit of political or party advantage might be gained by some party, but that if an hon. member rose in his place and seriously preferred a charge in the manner I have referred to, an inquiry would be granted.
Then there is always opportunity for hon. members to discuss matters before the public accounts committee if they have reason to believe that there are situations which should be discussed there. But I wish to make it clear that it would not be possible for the war expenditures committee to function as it was intended to function unless its sittings were held in camera; and being held in camera it is not proper that the proceedings should be made public.
I understand that my colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) would welcome all the evidence being made public. His wishes in that particular are shared by every member of the government, but so far as the adoption of that course is concerned it would be a proceeding directly contrary to the procedure which has been laid down at the time previous committees were appointed, and on the basis of which this committee has been constituted. .
Let me repeat that the committee, as the wording of the motion indicates here, is toexamine the expenditure defrayed out of moneys provided by parliament for the defence services, and for other services directly connected with the war, and to report what, if any, economies consistent with the execution of the policy decided by the government may be effected therein.
In other words, this committee is viewed in Britain, and it should be so viewed here, as an adjunct to or ally of the treasury; it is to help the treasury of the country to see that public funds are protected. If there are to be inquiries on other matters, they ought to proceed in accordance with the procedure of this house in such matters.
Therefore I hope, Mr. Speaker, that my hon. friend opposite will not press his amendment, but if he does, I hope the house will support the government in opposing it.

I am quite aware that it would be a breach of confidence, and particularly a breach against myself, if that evidence were tabled.
The committee, in investigating all aspects of the aluminum situation, went very much outside its terms of reference. It investigated expenditures made by the British government in this country by direct negotiation, and investments made by the British government acting through myself as its agent. The terms on which I was appointed agent of the government of the United Kingdom for the transactions I entered into on their behalf were that such transactions would be entirely confidential as between myself and the British government.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in
this debate for the purpose of considering, to at least some extent, some of the charges that have been repeated by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) as far as the

Department of Munitions and Supply is concerned. During the discussion of the war appropriation resolution last year the hon. gentleman made certain charges. These charges were referred to the war expenditures committee and, as the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) has just stated, in essence they were boiled down to some five charges. The hon. gentleman had an opportunity of giving or submitting evidence, since he was a member of the committee; but on none of the five charges has the committee found for him. On the contrary the committee has found against the charges, but that is not the purpose I have in mind in rising this evening; there are other members of the committee, I am sure, wrho will deal with the charges generally, as repeated this evening by the hon. member.
I should like to discuss twq main issues, concerning which the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar repeated his affirmations this evening. Those two issues concern the direct purchases of fabricated aluminum, by the government, and the question of special depreciation on the Shipshaw power development. The Department of Munitions and1 Supply is not concerned with the British, American or Australian contracts, for the very good reason that it had absolutely nothing to do with them save and except as agent for those governments in the negotiation of one contract and in the finality, I believe, of the Australian contract. Neither did the department have anything to do with the plant expansions at Arvida, because these were brought about by the contracts to which I referred a moment ago.
Canada's purchases of aluminum, as everyone knows, in comparison with those of Britain and the United States were very small, and I hope to be able to establish that Canada's war administration certainly was not at fault in connection with any purchases of fabricated aluminum. I hope also to be able to show that the special depreciation which was granted at Shipshaw was the only logical thing to do at the time, and that had; it not been done serious harm would have befallen the war effort.
Canada's purchases of aluminum have been entirely related to fabricated items, such as sheet, rod, tubing, bars, structural shapes, forgings and' castings. Direct government purchases from the outbreak of war to August 20, 1943, total less than $900,000. Again I say that in comparison with the British and American purchases this amount was very small, These purchases were made for the government itself, either on behalf of crown companies or as requisitions were sent in by the service departments. There were other purchases made, of

War Expenditures-Mr. Chevrier
course, by contractors such as aeroplane manufacturers, which were of a far more important nature. In the two and a half years to June 30, 1943, total sale? of fabricated items were $33,984,093, and on these sales Alcan made the modest profit of $714,569. This was made before taxes were computed, and the company made a loss of $1,482,180 after a pro rata share of income taxes had been applied. Again with reference to these purchases, it is difficult to see where and how Canada's war administration has been at fault with reference to purchases of fabricated aluminum.
With the permission of the house, Mr. Speaker, I should like to place on Hansard a condensation of sales for 1941, 1942, and the first half of 1943. This condensation may be taken as reliable. From this it will be seen that the profit of the Aluminum Company oi Canada before charging off any interest or any taxes was 3-6 per cent on its cost of sales, and 3-4 per cent on its sales. Surely no one in this house can complain that in the purchases of aluminum by Canadians there has been any improvidence, there has been any gross profit, or there has been any carelessness in the negotiation of profit margins.

speechtext:
War Expenditures-Mr. Chevrier
The next question which has to be decided is whether or not the transaction granting special depreciation was a provident one, and whether the government discharged its responsibilities to the people of Canada for the production of aluminum for war purposes with appropriate regard (1) for maximum output at maximum speed (2) economy in expenditure (3) equitable treatment and (4) longterm implications.	,
Aluminum, as the house knows, is in great demand for war purposes, chiefly in the manufacture of aeroplanes. It is estimated that from forty per cent to eighty per cent of an aeroplane is made of aluminum. Aluminum is made, as the house equally well knows, from bauxite, cryolite and fluorspar, and the resultant aluminum ingot is fabricated because of a tremendous amount of electrical energy which is put through these three commodities. Aluminum production requires three and one-third horse-power of electrical energy per metric ton of output. For each person employed in the production of aluminum over 100 horse-power is required, as compared with about one-half horse-power per person employed in the Bren gun plant of the John Inglis company at Toronto, and about one-eighth horse-power per person in the average of textile manufacture
The capacity for production of the Aluminum Company of Canada at Arvida from the years 1927 to 1937 was 45,000 metric tons, and its actual production in those years ran as high as 42,600 tons in 1937 and as low as
15,000	tons in 1934, with an average of 28,200 tons, or an average .production rate of 62-6 per cent. The normal place of aluminum in the world market ran usually fourth and fifth, and its production generally ran about 11 per cent of the total, with the United Kingdom by far the largest taker, Japan next at 20 per cent, then the United States, and small demands from twenty other nations.
In 1937 a world race for aluminum began to develop, as it now appears for war. Germany, Russia, Japan and Italy had led the way, with Germany reaching first place in the world by 1938. Influenced by these insistent demands Alcan laid plans to increase its capacity greatly, and in 1939 it turned out 75,200 metric tons, and in 1940, 99,000 tons, which was more than double its pre-war capacity, or over 260 per cent of its output in its best year, which was 1928, prior to the pre-war scramble for raw aluminum.
It should be pointed out that this expansion was initiated and financed by the company itself without any assistance from or intervention from the government.

Then there came three quick successions of contracts by the British government, one in February of 1940, a second in June of 1940 and a third in February of 1941. In these contracts the United Kingdom government contracted with the company to expand its production facilities very much more, and contracted to take the whole of the output of the new additions, plus all the output of the company's previous facilities, reserving only Canada's small demands, and thus until the year 1941 with provision for renewal of the arrangements if the emergency continued thereafter.
These contracts were financed by loans from the United Kingdom to Alcan totalling $55,600,000. They were 20-year three per cent loans. Again the Canadian government had absolutely nothing to do with any of these arrangements.
Next came a succession of four contracts with the United States, commencing with one for 170,000 metric tons, of May 2, 1941, and ending with one for 167,800 tons, of April 1, 1942. These contracts totalled 621,436 tons. The United States contracts called for four further plant extensions involving estimated deliveries when complete as follows:

1942	'	 94,'474
1943		 146,283
1944		 326,216

This makes a total United States expansion of 621,436 tons, or 1,370,000,000 pounds of aluminum. Again the Canadian government was not a party to these contracts, nor did it know their terms until after they were signed.
But after the first contract which was made with the United States government in 1941 it became quite evident that Alcan could not fulfil it without an arrangement with the Canadian government which would permit capital expenditures for plants being charged off as a production cost over the expected period of the war. Otherwise the Canadian government would be expropriating in taxes money provided by a friendly government without which that government's imperative needs of aluminum could not possibly be provided. The same was true with respect to the three succeeding United States contracts. Refusal to agree to this understanding would have been unthinkable, so far as the Canadian government was concerned. The first two United States contracts, totalling approximately S120,000,000 in United States funds, with $50,000,000 in immediate payments, came at a time when Canada's balance with the United States was very unfavourable.

War Expenditures-Mr. Chevrier
Thus they were extremely welcome and clearly fell within the scope of the War Exchange Conservation Act, section 8 of which reads in part as follows:
The governor in council in order to increase Canada's supply of foreign exchange may, on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance, enter into agreements with individuals, partnerships or corporations to grant assistance by way of special tax credits and/or special allowances for depreciation or depletion under the Incom: War Tax Act and/or the Excess Profits Tax Act, if, in the opinion of the governor in council, such assistance is necessary in order that an expansion of the exports of any individual, partnership or corporation receiving such assistance may take place or that the exports of any such individual, partnership or corporation may be maintained at levels higher than would otherwise obtain.
The proposal that the cost of the further plant additions should be charged to production costs was thus completely in keeping with the laws of Canada. This would have been equally true of the two subsequent United States contracts. In June, 1941, the United Kingdom government arranged with the Department of Munitions and Supply to take over the administration of its aluminum contracts. About the same time the government of Australia, which had already been negotiating a contract for a certain quantity of aluminum, arranged for that department to also take over the administration of its aluminum purchases.
As agent for the United Kingdom government the Department of Munitions and Supply subsequently negotiated for a further extension of Alcan plant facilities for the production of raw aluminum. Later the Minister of Munitions and Supply succeeded in reducing the average price for 1942 and 1943 of the British contracts to the same level as the base price of the United States contracts far 1942 and 1943. The successive two United States contracts, the Australian contract, and the last United Kingdom contract and the two final United States contracts, all calling for increased facilities, were superimposed one upon the other, before the previous plant expansion could be completed. Thus there never was a time at which a cut-off could be made, the plants being in a state of continuous expansion on an ever-increasing scale. Therefore it became impossible to segregate either the funds advanced by the various governments or the plants themselves.
The United Kingdom and the Australian contracts clearly could not come within the meaning of the War Exchange Conservation Act and, accordingly, it was decided, some months after the work had been under way 100-46i
and when very heavy commitments had been made by Alcan, that the matter should be dealt with by the war contracts depreciation board. This applied also to expenditures for completion of the Shipshaw power development with which I shall deal in a moment. So much for the facts.
I have dealt with this first in order to establish the tremendous expansion which took place almost overnight at Arvida. The plant at Arvida which had been producing at the rate of 62-6 per cent of its capacity had its production raised to 1,100 per cent over its pre-war capacity, an increase from a production capacity of 45,000 tons a year to 500,000 tons a year. This leads one naturally into a consideration of the Shipshaw power development project.
This was a purely Canadian matter. Neither the United States government nor the United Kingdom government had anything to do with it. The Shipshaw power project was not a new plant or a new project; it was the completion of one started in 1928 and held in suspense since 1931. It was forced on Alcan as a vital necessity to the means of fighting an air war. The down payments on account of the United States contracts referred to a moment ago were not sufficient to cover the full cost of the facilities for the production of the required additional raw aluminum, let alone provide anything for power development. The completion of the Shipshaw project was urged by the power controller as far back as 1940 in the clear vision that this was an air war, that there could not be enough aeroplanes without a greatly increased aluminum production and that such a production would imperatively demand a greatly increased power production as well. The construction of the Shipshaw canal and powerhouse in about ' eighteen months as compared with a normal construction rate of three years for such a work was an extraordinarily fine accomplishment. In the opinion of the power controller of Canada it was the greatest contribution made by this country to the war effort.
As the house knows, almost every war contract involves some additional capital expenditure, such as for new plant, new equipment, new buildings, new machine tools, jigs, fixtures, gauges and the like. It is a very rare exception for the Department of Munitions and Supply to find a contractor who has everything he needs with which to undertake a war contract. The required capital expenditure is usually put up to the department as something that it must find a way to take care of. There has developed over a period of time the following five methods, any one of which or any combination of which the department has to use.

War Expenditures-Mr. Chevrier
1.	By normal or accelerated depreciation granted to the contractor by his own expenditure in his own plant as a part of his production cost.
2.	By special depreciation granted to the contractor through his own expenditure in his own plant under a ruling of the war contracts depreciation board, again as part of his production cost.
3.	By capital assistance through government expenditure in the contractor's own plant.
4.	By the government building an entirely new plant and appointing an entirely new organization to manage it for them, or setting up a crown company to manage it without fee or profit.
5.	By the government purchasing or expropriating an existing plant, enlarging it to suit the requirements, and setting up its own management by way of a crown company or management fee arrangements.
These are the methods that have been used from time to time in the department. These, or a combination of these methods, are the only means by which the department can come to the assistance of a war contract.
The house will-agree with me at once, I am sure, that because of the huge commitments required on the part of certain contractors it is impossible for the government to expect of them that they should, or could, finance their undertaking in all cases. Such certainly was the case with the aluminum company. The government of the United Kingdom realized it from the first when it made to the company the substantial loan of $55,600,000. If the company had not had this money to put up plant expansions, it could not have proceeded. Similarly, the government of the United States made down payments aggregating $75,350,000. The total cost of the whole undertaking, including plant expansions, and power developments, was roughly $250,000,000. When it is considered that the cost of the project was so huge, I think it will be admitted that the United Kingdom and the United States governments were well advised, as was the Canadian government, in coming to the assistance of the company as they did.
This leads me to a discussion of depreciation. Depreciation has, to my way of thinking, three meanings. First, there is the wear and tear of an asset or of an article, the common usage by hand or the use that is brought about by the elements; such, for instance, as the annual depreciation in a motor car. Depreciation has also another meaning called obsolescence; that is, the asset is losing its value
lMr. Chevrier. 1
in the industrial field because other assets are superseding it in the sense of greater production, greater utility at less cost. For example, should aluminum be displaced by magnesium after the war, aluminum will have depreciated because of obsolescence. There is the third phase that has crept into the law, namely, that the asset is entrusted to facilitate our war purposes under the apprehension that should the war suddenly cease-call it what you will -the asset as a value has depreciated to the owner and it becomes of no use in peace time.
Depreciation, therefore, can occur through' wear and tear, obsolescence or disappearance of demand. If, for instance, the demand for aluminum after the war reverts to the position it occupied prior to the war, say, in 1937, depreciation of that plant will be great, because of obsolescence or disappearance of demand.
The principle of allowing depreciation as an item of cost is universally applied in every country which has an, income tax act. It is so recognized in Great Britain, the United States, Australia and Canada.
Generally speaking, depreciation is threefold; that is, normal, accelerated, and special.
Normal depreciation is that which is granted to every citizen by virtue of the income tax laws. As an illustration, machinery is deemed to have a life of ten years, working one 8-hour shift a day, and usually gets ten per cent depreciation per annum, as an allowance which it may charge as an item of cost. This is normal depreciation. If, however, the machinery works twenty-four hours a day, the life of the machinery is deemed to be much shorter, and an increased rate is allowed by the Department of National Revenue, which is called accelerated depreciation. The usual rate allowed in such cases is twenty per cent per annum, as the maximum, even though the machinery may be working three shifts. At the rate of twenty per cent per annum, a perfectly new plant would be written off in five years. I should point out here that there are many expenditures on a plant which are handled under norma! or accelerated depreciation, which are made without any reference to the Department of Munitions and Supply.
Special depreciation is that which is granted under the regulations of a board called the war contracts depreciation board. Where it appears that a manufacturer having a war contract or a subcontract is able to establish that part or all of his assets would have no post-war value, he may apply to the board for special depreciation, and if it is granted, that part which has no residual value may

War Expenditures-Mr. Chevrier
be written off. It is explicit that this privilege can be allowed only when the essentiality of the expenditures can be demonstrated, and then only to the extent to which the plant additions could be shown to have no reasonable post-war value.
In the case of Shipshaw, in the year 1925, the Aluminum Company of Canada filed with the Quebec government an application for authority to complete the Shipshaw power development. This application included the cost of a canal of much the same nature as that which now exists, sufficient to permit of the ultimate development of 800,000 horsepower years, at an estimated cost of $20,000,000 with only three 80,000 horsepower generators installed, out of an ultimate installation of ten such generators.
The company's plan was to instal these additional generators one by one over the years as and when the needs of its aluminum business so required. It estimated that each of these turbines installed would cost another $1,000,000, making the ultimate estimated cost $27,000,000.
The Canadian government, under the dire necessities of the war situation, compelled the company to complete this power development on the larger scale of 1,020,000 horsepower years. This it did under war-time conditions, with high wages and costs of every description greatly magnified, involving a total expenditure of over 870,000,000. How then, I ask, in equity could the Canadian government refuse to protect the company against a difference in cost between its normal expected expenditure of $27,000,000 and this extraordinary war-inflated expenditure of $70,000,000? That is all that the Canadian government did with reference to that projeot.
The impression has been created in the country that the whole of the power development was paid for by the Canadian government. This is not so. Actually it has cost the Aluminum Company of Canada every penny which it would have cost if it had been undertaken by the company in days of peace, namely $27,000,000 to $30,000,000.
As to the special depreciation on the facilities for the production of aluminum, the house should clearly bear in mind that not a single Canadian dollar went into the plants of Alcan. It all came from the United States, the United Kingdom and Australia

with the United States taking much the greatest share. The Canadian government had nothing to do with the way in which these governments chose to finance their needs of aluminum production. They alone decided the method which in their judgment could produce the aluminum they needed with the least loss of time and at the lowest price.
It is not for us Canadians, whose needs for aluminum were always more than adequately provided for, to criticize the decisions of these other nations. It was for the Canadian government to cooperate with these nations and to facilitate their decisions in every way possible. All that the Canadian government really did was to agree not to expropriate in taxes the funds provided by these allies in time of need, without which their needs could not be provided.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar spoke of the great amount of power which would be created in that north country, and how that power would affect eastern Ontario. I say to him that experts who have studied this question say that it is impossible to transport power to Montreal from the Arvida area at a reasonable cost and that because of the distance, which is 340 miles, it is outside the limit of the economic transmission of power, and power at Beauharnois would compete so greatly with Shipshaw power that there would not be the slightest inducement to Alcan to transmit its power there.
It would have been unthinkable for the Canadian government to have expropriated in taxes the very funds expressly provided by the governments of the United States, the United Kingdom and Australia for the erection of the plants, without which there was no possible way for these nations to get the aluminum they required when and as they required it.
I submit to the house that the Canadian government would have been recreant to its trust and false to its duty as a member of the united nations had it pursued any other course than that which it did with reference to the purchase of fabricated aluminum, with reference to the Shipshaw power development, and also with reference to the expansion of plant.
It will be apparent, too, to the house that the charges in connection with the Shipshaw development completely fail of substantiation. In the whole transaction the Canadian government moved quickly as regards production, and on a maximum scale. It moved economically for the completion of a half-developed plant, saving money as well as time. It allowed all that and no more than was equitable in the circumstances, and I submit with deference that no situation inimical to the Canadian position and long-term interests was created by these arrangements.

In rising to support the amendment, may I say that all members of the house were in agreement with the general principles which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) outlined in 1940 when the first war expenditures

War Expenditures- Mr. Nicholson
committee was set up. No one in this house wanted to discover war-time scandals, and I think it was recognized that any individual or corporation who would profiteer during these dark days was undermining confidence not only in this administration but in our democratic institutions. The Prime Minister outlined then and he repeated to-night the advantages of having these committees sit in -camera. All the opposition members of the 'house, I think, were opposed to having the [DOT]committee sit in camera in previous sessions, tunless it could be demonstrated that the evidence to be produced would give comfort to the enemy or would cripple our war effort. On all other occasions it was felt that the committee should sit openly and all information be made available to all members of the house and to the public.
The Prime Minister intimated to-night that if the committees sat in camera evidence would be elicited much more easily and that the members of the committee would be free to call anyone they chose. A year ago I sat with one of the subcommittees while the investigation was made in connection with the administration of wartime housing. Hon. members will recall that on various occasions I discussed the activities of wartime housing and advanced the general position that the taxpayers of the country were not receiving good value for the expenditures that were being made. I argued that the activities of wartime housing had been conducted in too many places in communities where there was a shortage of permanent houses.
