Mr. T. J. O'NEILL (Kamloops):	As a
member of one of the subcommittees that inquired into the aluminum contracts and the allegations made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), possibly I had better read from Hansard just what the hon. member said in those days. As reported in Hansard of June 14, 1943 at page 3619, the hon. member said:

War Expenditures-Mr. O'Neill
I have placed the facts before the committee without invective, I am certain without exaggeration, and I know without misrepresentation. These are the facts as I have accumulated them. I have got them first hand from first-hand sources. I have no doubt that there are certain people who know the people I visited when I was in Washington and know the offices where I got my information. I assure the committee that my information is authentic and gathered from those who were able to give me the information.
All through the hearings of that committee, the chairman, I can say, was very fair. 1 believe that every member of the committee will say that. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. had every opportunity to bring before the committee that evidence which he said he received- at first hand. He did not bring in any of that evidence. He brought no evidence with the exception of one witness, and the committee waited two days after we were ready to rise in order to permit him to bring in that witness, a Mr. Lipkowitz. Mr. Lipko-witz did not give any evidence that in my judgment would support the allegation made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar.
The hon. member goes on to speak of cartels, monopolies and what-have-you. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that the main idea in bringing these matters before this house was to create in the minds of the people the belief that because of the existence of cartels, monopolies, or what-have-you, the people of this country were being fleeced out of millions of dollars on the purchase of aluminum. To support that I read this in the paper:
The peoples of the united nations are being sold down the Saguenay river, said Mr. M. J. Coldwell, leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation.
What paper? The C.C.F. News, of Vancouver, dated February 3, 1944. I do not think the C.C.F. News of Vancouver would misquote Mr. Coldwell. In the same paper Mr. Coldwell has this to say:
The report of the special subcommittee on aluminum, composed wholly of Liberals and Progressive Conservatives except for myself, is a very obvious attempt to whitewash the whole affair.
We have heard a lot of things here about imputing motives and so forth; but I consider that a statement like that, from a man who holds the high position of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, is an insult to every member of that committee. He does not even give us the credit of being intelligent enough to get the point. He says that the committee was composed of Liberals and Conservatives and that a deliberate attempt was made to whitewash the evidence which was given
before that committee. If ever there was an imputation of motives, I think this is one. It imputes the motive of dishonesty to the hon. members composing that committee, and as one of the members let me inform the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that I am not dishonest. I tried to view the evidence as it was submitted and to give my findings accordingly.
To support my statement that the intention was to create in the minds of the people that they were being fleeced, I will read a little more of what the hon. member said. He stated:
Cheap labour, cheap power and high monopoly prices for their product have brought the aluminum interests untold wealth and economic power.
Then he went on to make some remarks with respect to labour. He has since said that he would like to retract the words he used on that occasion, that the treatment of the men at this plant was "scandalous" and "inhuman." But a great deal of publicity and a great deal of importance were attached to the statements the hon. member made at that time in this house; they have been echoed and reechoed over this country. I submit to you, sir, that in so doing a well-known method now used in Europe is being followed, the method of hammering and hammering and again hammering on a certain subject; it does not make any difference what the facts are, if you repeat a statement often enough, whether there is anything in it or not, the public will begin to believe it. But having said these things, the hon. member tonight said he would retract these expressions and would say that conditions were bad.
But he said a lot more than describing conditions as scandalous and inhuman. He said:
Men in the pot-rooms rarely last long amidst the poisonous fumes, and the labour turnover in that part of the plant is appalling.
As regards the fumes, it is well known now that the company has done everything humanly possible in the way of modern appliances to correct that condition. It is also a well-known fact that years ago the work of the pot-room men was very severe and arduous and the fumes were terrific. But today, so far as I have been able to determine, there is no record of any occupational disease in that plant. That should be a fair indication of whether the fumes are there in sufficient quantities to injure health.
As for wages, I do not definitely know the rates, but I am told that the income of a pot-room man is around $2,000. But there are other conditions besides wages to be re-
War Expenditures-Mr. O'Neill

garded. Everything is now being done to reduce the labour of these men. As an indication that conditions are not as outlined by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, when the strike took place last fall at Shawinigan Falls, there were, so far as I could find out through reading the papers, only two matters in dispute. One was, whether those men were to look after six pots or seven pots. They were supposed to look after one more pot in the winter time because the weather was cooler, than they had to do in the summer. One question in dispute was whether they should revert from six to seven pots in the winter time. The other point at issue was a jurisdictional dispute. They were not complaining about working conditions or about wages; what they were concerned about was whether they would have to look after six or seven pots, and whether one union or another union would attend to the interests of the workers.
A word as to housing. This committee visited Arvida and Shipshaw. The housing conditions there were very good. The company builds houses, which the men can either buy or rent, as they choose. They are very fine houses. They have good schools; they have hospitalization, and they have a retirement fund which, of course, is contributory. I found that the washrooms, lockers and such equipment are very much better than we have on ;the Canadian Pacific Railway. I worked for the C.P.R. for a long time and I know that conditions in this respect are not so good as those at the aluminum plants; yet as an old C.P.R. engineer I never considered that we were unfairly dealt with by that company.
It would appear from statements of the sort I have quoted that they may be inspired by another motive. I noticed that just after the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar made his allegation last fall, this appeared in the Ottawa Citizen:
Shipshaw is one of the most valuable pieces of ammunition for the C.C.F. in the forthcoming elections.
That was said by a prominent member of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party, now an M.L.A. in British Columbia.

I shall be very brief in my remarks, Mr. Speaker; I intend to speak only to the amendment and the tabling of the evidence heard by the war expenditures committee. I
was a member of that committee when it was first organized in 1941, and I believe the policy of hearing evidence in camera was the proper policy to adopt, particularly at that time. I think there were many things in its favour then that could not be said in its favour now. Some matters might come out which would give comfort to the enemy and interfere with our prosecution of the war, and so on, so that at that time I was in agreement with the majority of the committee that the meetings should be held in camera. But I submit to you, Mr. SpeakerpthatTIf the committee wishes to have its meetings held in camera it never should make a report such as was tabled in this house on January 26. The committee presumed to take the allegations or charges made by a certain individual and hold hearings on them; then it brought in a report, based on the evidence adduced before it, finding that the charges had not been substantiated in any degree whatever. When a report of that kind is brought in I submit that the evidence must be placed before this house, because there is no way in which hon. members can satisfy themselves as to the correctness of the report except by reviewing the evidence. Either that evidence should be tabled or the report should be withdrawn. We cannot have a report placed before us, the correctness of which is denied by one party- whether it be made up of one man or a dozen-and which is supported by others. There is no way in which' members of this house can vote intelligently unless they have before them the evidence taken in that inquiry. Think of a judge being asked to pass sentence in a case where he did not hear the evidence, where the evidence had been taken in some other place, and when he did not hear it! Then think of his being asked to base a judgment upon such evidence! We are in an impossible position. Either, as I said before, that evidence must be placed upon the table of the house, or the report must be withdrawn.

Mr. Speaker, I think I can confine myself to the rules of the house in respect to the present amendment. What I have to say will take only a few minutes and I shall be finished before eleven o'clock. I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) when he says that the members of this house find themselves in a strange position. They are being asked to vote concurrence in a report or to vote against concurrence without having access to the evidence upon which the report is based. We cannot do that very well. Personally I find myself in a strange position.
A report has been presented to the house which I understand is unanimous, with the exception of one member of the committee. When the report was presented I was not in the house; I was on a train. I read a bit in the newspaper and, as I gathered from the newspaper report-and I suppose this would be the reaction of the public-the report had been presented but nothing had been said. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) gave a statement to the press to the effect that the report was a whitewash. My amazement was considerable. I wondered at the time why the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar did not present to the house a minority report.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND, THIRD, FOURTH AND FIFTH REPORTS OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: The rules would not allow it.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND, THIRD, FOURTH AND FIFTH REPORTS OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I understand since coming here that the rules will not allow it. I think it is a strange rule because I believed at the time that the hon. member should have had an opportunity of presenting a minority report. Then it would have been all in the one report. The statement that it was a whitewash seemed at that time to be a

War Expenditures-Mr. Hansell
bit of a reflection upon all the other members of the committee. What happened? The first opportunity which the hon. member had of bringing in what might have been tantamount to a minority report was to-day. The speech of the hon. member simply means, if we are to believe what he said, that his charges are correct and that the report was a whitewash. Therefore we have to decide whether to vote for or reject concurrence, and we have to do it on the basis of what we hear discussed in this house because we have not had the evidence presented to us. That is a strange position in which to place the members of this house.
I quite understand, on the other hand, for I have acted on the war expenditures committee in years gone by, that all the evidence submitted to the committee cannot be made public property. At least, if the evidence given before the committee on war expenditures last year is similar to some that was submitted in the year I was on the committee, I doubt whether it should be revealed because it would divulge certain matters in connection with our military operations, in Canada it is true, but which we could not possibly have divulged to the enemy. At the same time, however, when it comes to matters such as the charges which the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has made, I cannot see that there could be anything in that evidence that would give comfort to the enemy. Surely it would give no comfort to the enemy to know whether we paid one million dollars for something or whether we paid ten cents for it. That has nothing to do with military operations or military strategy. On the other hand, the public has a right to know how we are spending public money, especially when it is spent for things that have , nothing to do with actual military operations. Therefore, if the government refuses to place the evidence on the table for the scrutiny of members of parliament, and if the hon. member's charges are not refuted satisfactorily to my mind, I am afraid that I shall have to join with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and refuse to vote for concurrence in the committee's report. Although he has been wrong so many times, I am afraid this would have to be one time when I would have to agree with him. If the charges are not refuted, there is nothing else we can do. Personally I think that when the charges were made last year the whole matter should have been sent immediately to the public accounts committee, and not be made necessarily a part of the work of the war expenditures committee.
So as not to embarrass the government in respect of evidence being 'laid on the table which it may not be in the best interests of winning the war to table because it might reveal something of value to the enemy, I have a subamendment to move. I move, Mr. Speaker, that after the word "evidence" where it first occurs in the amendment, the following words be inserted:
respecting aluminum contracts and relative subjects thereto.
That would mean that the entire evidence taken by the committee would not have to be put on the table but simply the evidence relating to the charges which have been made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. It seems to me that we have to make some distinction. I feel certain that if the evidence taken by this committee is like some of the evidence that was submitted to the wrar expenditures committee in years gone by it must contain some things that it would not be wise to reveal. But so far as aluminum contracts are concerned, that is a matter of dollars and cents, contracts, work done, and we have no reason to fear that that is going to give comfort to the enemy.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND, THIRD, FOURTH AND FIFTH REPORTS OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, how will the amendment read with the subamendment?

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND, THIRD, FOURTH AND FIFTH REPORTS OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It will read as follows:
That all the w-ords in the said motion after the word "reports" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"Be not now concurred in but that the house instructs that the evidence respecting aluminum contracts and relative subjects thereto upon which the said reports are founded be tabled and that consideration of the reports be post-poped until the house has had sufficient opportunity to study the said evidence."
As it reads with the subamendment, it says: "the evidence respecting aluminum contracts and relative subjects thereto upon which the said reports are founded." I would point out that the reports are not founded simply upon evidence dealing with aluminum contracts and relative subjects thereto. I am afraid that the subamendment is out of order. If it was adopted the main motion would not be intelligible or consistent with itself.
On motion of Mr. Jackman the debate was adj ourned.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
